## 2026-10-16 — grids: the nature grid goes hex (GRIDS plan steps 1–2)

Branch `grids` (docs/GRIDS.md, DECISIONS round 35). The interval columns
now sit on a hex lattice; every system runs on it, and it renders as hex
prisms. No square/hex switch: the square reference is the `ambient`
branch, run beside it (no fallback paths to keep alive).

- Lattice in common.wgsl (`nbr`, `cellPos`, `cellAt`, `triAt`, `Dirs`),
  mirrored for the CPU in world/lattice.ts. Directions in opposite pairs, so
  every `k ^ 1` (the flux coming back) carried over unchanged.
- Per-pipe rates × 2/3 (water and oil gain, slumping, wind easing): the
  hex Laplacian weights six neighbours 2/3 as much as the square grid's
  four, so things spread at the same continuum rate. `netFlow` normalises
  by 2/NDIR (a uniform flow v puts dot(v, e_k) down each pipe; summed over
  six directions that's 3v).
- Wind is split over the six faces by its positive projections (`dSplit`);
  upwind shelter walks world positions through `cellAt`.
- Hex corners for soft ground and sheets: each cell owns its 30° and 90°
  corners (`cornerTex` 2w × h); a corner's height is the three touching
  columns (weight 2) and the three beyond (weight 1), the hex form of the
  old 4 × 4 tent. Bilinear lookups (shadow, reach fog, shorelines, the
  soft-border vote) became three-centre barycentric (`triAt`).
- Prisms: top fanned from the centre, three sides toward the eye, 36
  vertices. Per-triangle normals showed every hexagon's fan wherever the
  smoothed corners weren't coplanar; the top takes one normal, the
  least-squares plane through its corners. Per-cell colour noise keyed to
  the hex cell (it was floor(world), a square pattern over the hexes).
- Rock carving ported to the prism (six slab tests, the fanned top). The
  map's edge zigzags on a hex grid, and carving rays left edge prisms
  through the notches into nothing: off-map counts as closed. The loose
  sheet's side at the map edge always shows (its corners there can belong
  to a cell on the map, which had hidden it).
- CPU: picks, taps, strikes and the trial's gates go through `cellPos`;
  weather lives in world extent (w + 0.5) × h·√3/2 and samples heights via
  `cellAt`; levels still author in cells (laid row by row: ~13 % shorter in
  y, slightly sheared), points of interest converted with `poiWorld`.

Measured (headless, real GPU, 1600 × 900, the Dam Valley story start;
scripts/perfpass.mjs, new): draw 7.7 ms hex vs 4.0 ms square; the sim's
passes 2.9 ms vs 2.3 ms (sediment 1.06 vs 0.80); 96 vs 120 fps. The sim
costs about what six neighbours should. Draw is 1.9×: every top vertex
reloads all six corner heights for the centre and the normal — next, a
per-cell top plane cached once per frame. The same 40 s storm at speed 6
leaves both at the same place (63 % vs 62 % green), water pooled in the
basin on both.

Draw, following up (same view): 69k instances on both grids, so it was
vertex-bound — 36 vertices a prism against 18 a box. Each cell's top plane
(centre and fitted gradient, per ground / water / drift) is now cached by
render-fields with its corners (cornerTex 5w × h: two corners and three
plane texels per cell): 7.7 → 7.3 ms. The top in four triangles over its
corners instead of a six-triangle fan (the flat normal shows nothing the
centre point added) and plants in their own list at 18 vertices (prisms
30): 6.7 ms against square's 4.0 — the ratio of the prism's vertices
(30/18). A top-only list for prisms with every side hidden would take most
of the rest; not now (the branch's point is the grids).

## 2026-10-16 — grids: structure grids (GRIDS plan steps 3–4, first pass)

A structure grid is a rigid voxel grid in its own frame — position and a
full rotation (yaw, pitch, roll) — over the hex nature grid
(src/grids/structures.ts, src/shaders/grids.wgsl). The CPU only places
structures: it uploads a model's voxels once into a GPU pool and writes
each frame (64 bytes: position, quaternion, dims + pool offset, world xy
bounds). Everything grid-shaped is a kernel:

- project.wgsl (structure → nature, every tick, first): each nature column
  casts its world-vertical line through each structure's rotated voxels (a
  3D DDA in local space) and keeps the top of the first solid run, the
  bottom of the last, and the world normal of the face the line entered by
  (exact for boxes: `foreign`, xy). Merged with the CPU's sleeping bodies
  (integrity.ts now writes `bodyCpu`, rasterised over hex centres), it is
  `bodyProj` — so every system that already respected bodies sees
  structures unchanged: water stands on them, loose ground banks against
  them, wind is sheltered by them. 0.05 ms.
- Sediment (the burial): sand above a structure's top falls only to it,
  and where a column's run is under a structure (or it has none), arrivals
  start a new run on the structure's top — so drifts climb over it instead
  of vanishing under it. Measured with a pour onto a 20°-tilted concrete
  slab: the sand piles on it, runs off its low edge and buries it in a cone
  — a round cone (the hex grid's repose relaxation; the square grid's are
  pyramid-ish).
- structtick.wgsl (the structure's own tick, every 4 ticks, 0.02 ms): per
  voxel, samples the nature grid at its world centre (nature → structure):
  sand cover (inside the loose run there), and moss on its faces open to
  the air where the ground is damp — up-facing faces fastest, undersides
  too; it creeps from green ground and mossy neighbours, rarely starts on
  its own. First tuning grew full cover in under 20 s; now about four
  minutes of damp weather.
- structprep.wgsl: exposed voxels → rotated-cube instances in the body
  format, drawn by the body pipeline (indirect). fsBody shades a structure
  voxel's moss, and the sand drape redundantly: a face point inside the
  nature grid's loose run there (interpolated over the three nearest
  centres, counting only columns whose run reaches down to that height)
  takes the sand's colour, so the sand line on a tilted wall follows the
  drift smoothly rather than the cells.
- Test hooks: `?structure=model,x,y,yaw,pitch,roll[,sink]` (cells,
  degrees) and `reclaimed.grids.place(...)`; scripts/timelapse.mjs (shots
  at marks of sim time after a JS setup).

Not yet: sliding by the projected normal (the normals are there; the
sediment doesn't use them), air inside a structure (one span per column:
an office tower's window grid reads as solid slabs; sand poured onto one
beam slides off — correct, but a solid slab was the clearer test),
structures that move (setPose exists; nothing drives it), breaking them.

## grids: a tilt slider on the sandbox's Place tool

The user found the structure demo hard to poke at (URL and console only).
The sandbox's Place tool now has a tilt slider: at 0 it stamps the model
into the columns as before; above 0 the model goes in as a structure grid
of its own, toppled that far over its quarter turn (E), with a little roll
so no face lines up with the hexes, resting on the ground (bury sinks it).
Then pour, rain, wind and the weather tools act on it. Not undoable (the
undo snapshot covers the layers, not the structure pool); 8 at most.
Placed into the ground, it overlaps: nothing is displaced yet.

## grids: air inside structures — projected intervals and the open air between them

The user: the building should be able to hold air (and other materials)
the way the terrain's columns do — use the same representation. The
projection now keeps every solid stretch a column's vertical line crosses
(project.wgsl), up to three per column, in the layers' own interval form
(`projAt` in common.wgsl reads them as intervals). The surface pass adds the
floor of each stretch of open air they leave (`levels`). The sediment pass
then moves loose ground within one level: a column's run lies in one
(`runLevel`); what a neighbour sends at height h comes into the level open at
h, or steps up onto the solid there (`openAt`) — so a wall is just higher
ground at that height, a doorway or the gap under a raised floor is open;
arrivals in a level other than the run's land on its floor (`landAt`); what
comes from the sky over a structure lands on its top; granular intervals fall
onto the highest projected interval beneath them. The old single-span rule
(everything arriving under a structure went onto its top) is gone.

Wind under a structure: shelter is measured at the run's own height (the
solid upwind at that height, not the tallest thing), and a run with a
structure over it feels wind only if the open air upwind (a column with
nothing over it) comes before a solid within 16 cells — inside a room it's
still, along the line of a doorway or under an overhang's edge it blows.
(The wind field itself doesn't see structures yet.) Nothing goes airborne
from under a structure (it would come down on the roof). Smoothing now needs
the wind to be felt (shelter applied, as for transport): a pile under a hole
in a roof was being spread over the whole floor by the wind outside.

Measured (scripts/roomtest.mjs: a 16 × 16 room, foundation, floor, roof with a
4 × 4 hole, a doorway, slightly tilted, in the sandbox):
- calm: 48 cells of sand dropped under the hole fall onto the floor and
  slump out under the roof into a round cone at repose (peak 3.1); all the
  sand within 26 cells goes 9515.7 → 9563.7 (exactly +48), then stays.
- wind (60 base, 18 felt) along the doorway's line: sand banks against the
  outside wall, blows into the gap under the raised floor (0 → 4.4 cells),
  climbs onto the sill; the jet along the doorway's line spreads the pile
  inside along that line. It stops at the sill when dust from the air
  crusts it into soil (plants bind it), which doesn't blow — sandbox
  behaviour, not the room's.
- cost (Dam Valley, nothing projected): sediment 0.62 → 0.70 ms,
  sediment-out 0.40 → 0.42, surface 0.16 → 0.18; project 0.05 (unchanged).
- also: placing a tilted model rested it on the loose run's base, sunk into
  the sand (heightAt is the base); the pick's height now says how deep the
  sand lies.

Known: water still has one sheet per column, on the top one; a column's
plants are one value, so the ground's plants under a room show on sand that
lands on its floor; nothing is displaced when a structure is placed into the
ground (it overlaps).

## 2026-10-22 — grids: smooth-lit tops

Soft tops and drift sheets already pass through shared corner heights (a
continuous surface), but each was lit with its one fitted plane, so every

planes of the three cells round the point (barycentric over the lattice of

run noise ±0.3 ms on this machine; three plane reads per top pixel).

Also measured on the way (Dam Valley, 1600 × 900): at render scale 0.5
draw falls 5.7 → 2.6 ms, and with a flat-colour fragment shader to 2.4 ms —
draw is now bound by fragment shading (~3.3 ms), not vertices (~1.6 ms).
Emitting near cells first (front to back) didn't help (5.8 ms); storm and

## 2026-10-22 — grids: the field mesh, a prototype (G13 h, option C)

Round 38: the intervals are storage, not a constraint on drawing. The
"density field" is a function evaluated from them on the fly — nothing new
is stored but the mesh (and a scratch grid while it's built).

Behind `?mesh=1` (`?mesh=x,y,r` a region r cells each way round x, y;
`?meshh=` the sample spacing, 0.5; `?meshevery=N`), one square region is
drawn as a mesh instead of prisms, sheets and cubes. Three compute passes:
- sampleField: the field at every sample. Terrain: each column's vertical
  distance to its solid (touching intervals are one solid, below 0 is
  bedrock), blended barycentrically over the three nearest centres.
  Structures: the distance to their voxels' boxes in their own rotated frame
  (the nearest of the 27 round it: solid outside, air inside — an
  occupancy blend rounded the room's edges off). The two joined by a smooth
  minimum (0.6), so sand against a wall makes a fillet.
- makeVerts: surface nets — a vertex per crossed sample cell at the mean of
  its edge crossings, its normal the field's own gradient (central
  differences, so light runs smooth across cells), and how much it's
  structure.
- makeQuads: two triangles per crossed sample edge.
The fragment shader finds the interval the point lies in (a step into the
surface) and takes its material, so the layers and stains still come from
the intervals; a structure's share shows its voxel (moss, sand cover).

Measured (headless, real GPU, 1600 × 900, rebuilt every frame — the worst
case, no dirty tracking yet; scripts/meshtest.mjs):

| region (Dam Valley) | columns | rebuild | vertices | triangles |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| r 16, h 0.5 | ~1.2k | 0.43 ms | 6.3k | 12.2k |
| r 24, h 0.5 | ~2.7k | 0.96 ms | 13.8k | 27.0k |
| r 32, h 0.5 | ~4.7k | 1.77 ms | 24.1k | 47.6k |
| r 24, h 1.0 | ~2.7k | 0.19 ms | 3.4k | 6.5k |

So ~0.37 ms and ~5k vertices per 1000 columns at h 0.5 (~290 KB as stored
now: 32-byte vertices, 32-bit indices), a quarter of that at h 1, which
looks nearly the same at the default zoom. The sandbox room (r 24): 17k
vertices, 1.07 ms. Draw didn't move outside the noise (5.7–6.2 ms against
6.0 on the same view). Most samples lie above everything: skipping them, a
compact vertex and rebuilding only dirty chunks are next.

## 2026-10-22 — setPushes

The GameplayGM units experiment sends its force fields every frame; a frame
with no tick left its pushes queued, the next frame's joined them, and
push() threw past eight. `setPushes(list)` replaces the queue instead; the
throw past eight stays (more than eight in one tick is a caller's mistake).

## 2026-10-23 — snow, leaves, ice and crystal

Round 50's materials. They needed a temperature, which the world didn't

## 2026-10-23 — places, step 1: plans, queries, ops masked to a place

The user gave the go-ahead (via the units session) for places step 1
(docs/PLACES.md). A plan (generated Voronoi or noise bands, boxes and
halls, or hand-drawn SDF rooms) is rasterized onto the hex lattice: one
u32 per column, the top room and (later) the enclosed level's room,
uploaded as the `places` contract buffer with a room → region table.
Adjacency comes from the raster (cell sides shared, border columns, the
border's middle), so it matches what the GPU masks exactly. The plan's
shape (chain or tree) picks a spanning set of connections as
suggestions; connect/disconnect are records until W1 carves. Ops masked
to a place run in one small kernel (placeop.wgsl, one op a tick from a
queue) on the sediment's ticks, before it, so a bury's deposit is
folded in the same tick — the climate pass, after the sediment,
overwrites deposit .yz with snow and leaves, and would otherwise eat
it. A storm held over a place is the ordinary storm with `hold`: it
steers to the centre instead of riding the wind, then fades.
Measured (scripts/placestest.mjs, sandbox 256 × 256): the default
Voronoi plan (spacing 22, groups 1–3, chain) makes 46 rooms (387–2,763
columns, mean 1,425) in 9 regions, 1–9 neighbours a room (mean 4.7), 45
suggested connections (a spanning chain); bands make 29 rooms with 8
halls in 6 regions. A 2-cell sand bury (noise 0.5) adds 1.54 cells a
column in the room, -0.08 in a neighbour (its sand slumps), +0.003
outside; a 1.5-cell flood is +0.28 a column in the room 1.5 s later and
the rest already running out over the flat sandbox (nothing holds it
until W1 shapes rooms); the held storm sits on the room's centre at
full intensity after 12 s. Drain leaves 0.02 (water flowing back in).

## 2026-10-23 — agents: surfaces, fields, units

Round 52: the user wants agents that build and mine, as a layer for many
games ("let's do it", on a new `agents` branch off grids). First the ground
they walk and the way they find. Surfaces come straight from the
intervals rather than a depth peel: each column's solid and loose runs,
merged where they touch, give a surface wherever there's 1.5 cells of air
over the top. Up to four a column, linked to the six hex neighbours within
a step up or a drop, with headroom checked over both. The fields are
distances relaxed in place on the GPU, eight sweeps a tick. Each surface is
recomputed from its neighbours rather than kept as a running minimum, so a
field heals when the terrain changes; past (w + h) × 6 a value counts as
unreachable, which stops pockets cut off from the seeds counting up for
ever (the first field image showed one as a stale red patch). A unit
follows its group's field down the six-neighbour gradient, is pushed away
from busier columns (double-buffered counts) and never crosses a missing
link. Each draws as three voxels through the physics voxel hook, so it is
lit and shadowed for free.

- Surfaces: 65,484 columns with one and 52 with two (under the bridge);
  390,551 links.
- 300 units sent 66 cells: mean distance 62 → 20 in 21 s.
- A 4-high stone wall across the way: they split round both ends.

## 2026-10-23 — agents: thrown, held, knocked over, catching fire

  skids, slams back off walls, is hurt by hard landings, and gets up once
  it settles.

## 2026-10-23 — the world API: smooth sampling, cached views, warmup with debris

The units session moved the hover bike onto the API and asked for three
things.

**Smooth heights.** A rider sampling hex columns steps at every edge. The
ask was for the field mesh's (1 − d)² blend, but the field mesh doesn't do
that: it blends the three nearest centres barycentrically, at a point warped
by hash noise. So `{ smooth: true }` is a CPU port of exactly that, the pcg
hash included. Against the mesh's own up-facing vertices it misses by 0.011
(median) everywhere, and 0.024 where the stepped heights miss by 0.141.

**Cached views.** Typed views of each read are made once, not per call: a
smooth sample is ~2 µs. The field mesh's vertices are now COPY_SRC, for the
check.

**Warmup with debris.** `WorldDef.warmup`, attachSim's third argument and
`sim.warmup()` settle the world with debrisBoost raised, then put it back.
That was the bike's last direct Globals write. It works through the
particles' spawns on dirty ground, so the clean sandbox shows it least: 600
ticks at debris 10 left 4,294 litter, dust and leaf particles against
3,147 at 1.

## 2026-10-23 — world API: layer pulls

The world editor's first ask (DECISIONS round 52) is to grab a material's
layer and pull it. For example, bedrock pulled up through the sand and soil

growing height.

layerpull.wgsl does it per column:
- The material's topmost run grows toward height × the brush (a dome,
  broken at the edge by the material's noise) and everything over it moves
  up with it. With `through`, the solids lying on it crack to their rubble.

  most any call asked of it.

  not twice it.

The hoverbike session wants players to dig caves and tunnels into mountains

  under its top bores into it. The heat gathers per column until it can
  melt the whole span of a round hole about the hit (half height
  √(r² − off²)), then the span goes at once and the rock over it stays (the
  interval split). Melting from the middle out was tried first: the line

  through it, and the bore was a slit 0.4 high, 9 deep.
- The melt runs out a column a tick through a spill texture (two rgba32float
  textures, since the depth kernel is at the 8 storage buffers): to the lowest
  open neighbour, else back along the beam's `dir`, and pours out as lava
  on the first column whose open sky lies at or under the bore's floor.
  With nowhere to go (or after 48 columns) it sets on the bore's floor.
- `terrain.floorAt` also finds the column's own gaps (a cave's floor), not
  only the open air under structures' projected intervals: walkers can
  stand in a bore.
- `WorldDef.slots`: a world can ask for more intervals per column (the
  overhang over a bore takes a slot; a full column can't be bored:
  BACKLOG Q21).

Measured (`boretest`, sandbox, a 14-high stone block, beam radius 1.6,
power 9000, re-aimed each 150 ms): 6 columns in after 9 s, the hole 3.0
high (14.75–17.79 at a hit of 16.27) with 9 cells of rock over it,
36 cells³ of lava out in front of the face, none on the top; floorAt gives
14.75 in the hole and 26.79 from the top. The beam on the open top still
melts it down (25.9 → 16.2 in 5 s).

## 2026-10-23 — perf branch: profile a phone's frame; mesh by default; culling; shadows fitted to the view

Round 61: a `perf` branch to profile and experiment; clear wins merge into
`grids`, and the user judges the feel on a phone.

Tools:
- scripts/perfprofile.mjs: a phone-shaped viewport (412×915 at DPR 2.6;
  low's DPR 1 and half scale make a 206×457 frame). Each variant is a fresh
  page, and every pass is reported as GPU ms per frame: the profiler now
  sums each pass over every frame (`totalMs`), so a pass that runs every
  4th tick counts a quarter.
- `?skip=` (renderer.ts) leaves a piece of the frame out to measure it
  (opaque, tops, plants, prisms, mesh, bodies, structs, voxels, skins,
  water, particles, rain, shadow, prep, meshprep, cull, shadowfit).

Measured on the desktop GPU at that frame, the valley at low:
- Prisms: GPU 3.8 ms/frame. The terrain draw ~1.6 and its instance prep
  0.5 dominate; every sim pass together is ~1.3.
- The mesh: 3.7 ms. Draw 1.1, its shadow pass 0.36, the mesh build ~0.6.
- The sandbox at desktop size (meshtest): draw 1.89 ms with the mesh
  against 3.42 with prisms, plus 0.31 of mesh build.

Changes:
- The mesh is the default in every level and the world API (`?mesh=0`).
  The menu diorama keeps its voxels.
- renderprep culls to the view: a column is emitted only if its box, or
  the shadow its top casts (followed up to 40 cells), shows on screen. The
  camera is bound at 31.
- The mesh's chunks are culled by their real tops, read back from the hash
  pass (+4; zMax until known), not boxes to the sky. In an isometric view
  a box to the sky covered a long strip of the screen.
- The shadow map covers the chunks near the view instead of the whole map,
  and only the chunks inside the sun's box are drawn into it. The light is
  orthographic, so a box floor to sky over the near chunks holds every
  caster whose shadow lands there.
- Shadow map 1024² on low (`shadowSize`), 2048² otherwise.
- The mesh, storm and water tests ask for prisms with `mesh=0` now.

What the desktop can't say: at a 206×457 frame its draw costs are fixed
overheads. The mesh draws 0.64 ms whether 32 chunks or 63, and the culling
moves the total by less than the noise (±0.3 ms). A phone's tile-based GPU
pays for geometry and depth bandwidth far more, which is where culling and
the smaller fitted shadow map should show. A portrait phone sees half the
map even at 3× zoom: the isometric tilt squashes depth. So it's the
user's phone that judges this, through the /perf/ page and `?skip=` A/B
links.

Checks: shadows fitted to the view look the same as the whole-map ones at
4× zoom on a portrait screen. meshtest, pulltest (6/6) and hordetest are
unchanged.

## Round 63 — units carry and throw (agents)

The user's next step for the agents: carry and throw, then dig, fell trees
into logs, make bricks, keep piles, then build. A load has to be ground
that goes somewhere, so the first piece is exact ground ops.

- `terrain.take` / `terrain.put` (edit.wgsl OP_TAKE / OP_PUT): one column
  (its centre and a radius only it lies in), an exact amount off its top
  interval or on top of it. What each did goes to a 64-texel result texture
  at the event's tag (code bits 10-15), read back until every take and put
  in flight has its answer (a frame or two; 0.7–1 s headless, where ticks
  run slow). A put of a new material into a full column puts 0 (Q21).
- `agents.carry` / `pickUp` / `putDown` / `throwItem` / `toss`: a load per
  unit slot on the CPU and in a small buffer the draw reads (the units'
  tick kernel is at its 8 storage buffers; only the draw needs the load).
  Thrown loads fly on the CPU, are drawn by a new `itemDraw` kernel and
  land as ground with a 'landed' event and their hit. Loads are shed when
  a unit tumbles (flung with it), dies or is removed.
- Wood is plant matter (trunks) and can't be ground, so logs will need a
  solid material of their own (next).

Measured (`carrytest`, 8/8): take 0.4 → 0.4 exactly; put 0.75 brick → the
top rises 0.750; four workers each pick up 0.5 sand; two put it down (0.5
each); two throw it 8 cells at five raiders (both land, 0.5 each as
ground; two raiders knocked over); a blasted carrier's 0.5 lands whole.
## Round 63 — pillars of loose ground beside caves (Q16b, Q22)

The user's phone screenshot showed tall narrow pillars of loose ground
against a ravine wall, persisting after storms and explosions; they guessed
the sediment turns solid before it can collapse. Nothing turns loose ground
solid. A probe (`scripts/pillartest.mjs`: craters and storms at ?q=low,
then loose-topped columns over all their lower neighbours, the neighbours'
floors measured from their real intervals) reproduced pillars in the
sandbox after craters and round the arch after rain; not on the valley.

The cause: `slumpOut` measures the drop to a neighbour with `seenAt`, which
(no structure projected there) is the neighbour's whole-column top: the
roof of any cave or overhang inside it. Loose ground beside air under a
roof (a crater's undercut rim, an arch) saw a wall and never slid into the
air, and the face spill (`spillOut`) only spilled buried intervals, not the
run on top.
- `spillOut` spills the run on top too, but only into a neighbour's air
  under a roof (the open air over its top stays slumpOut's, so nothing is
  counted twice).
- A spill that joins or empties intervals left the freed slots holding
  stale copies (the write loop ran to the new count): columns like
  `stone 8.49–9.00 ×12`. The slots in use before the spill are cleared now.
- A trace (< 0.02) of another loose material landing by spill blends into
  the floor's, as `landAt` does: alternating spills had filled slots with
  hairline strata.

Measured (pillartest, sandbox, q=low): 8 craters, 40 s: 61 'hidden'
columns, 208 cells over repose in all, worst 5.4 → 0; with storms, 100 s:
100–118 → ≤ 3, worst 6.1 → 1.8. Sediment 0.70 ms vs 0.73 ms before
(agentstest, the same run); pulltest 6/6, boretest 5/5, spiretest finds
only the same stone pillar with a dust film as before. Found on the way:
overlapping intervals after craters (Q23) and paper-thin solid lids over a
crater's undercut rim (Q24).

## Round 63 — hits that spare groups (agents; the hoverbike session asked)

The hoverbike's lich raises dead (agents in a group of their own); its
fireball and push hurt them too. `HitSpec.groups` (only these groups feel
it) and `spare` (these don't), on `agents.hit` and on a thrown item's hit.
The mask rides in the hit's fire float (bit 0 fire, bits 1-16 a group
each: all 16 floats of a hit were taken). A spared unit can still be
bowled over by the others flung into it (knock-overs are physics), and a
hard landing then hurts it as 'impact'. `sparetest` 2/2: spare [g1]: g1 0
hurt by the blast, g2 6 hurt and 6 thrown (1 of g1 bowled over); groups
[g1]: 5 of g1 hurt and thrown, g2 none.

## Round 65 — the town: Townscaper blocks as real matter (builder)

The user: "a townscraper inspired grid and building system… it plays nice
with terrain and dust"; "you place, it appears". `build/towngrid.ts`,
`build/town.ts`, `townstamp.wgsl` (TownStampSystem), `api.town()`, the
editor's 🏠 tool:
- The grid, Townscaper's (Oskar Stålberg's): a hexagon of triangles over
  the map, neighbours merged at random into quads (a third stay triangles),
  every polygon cut into quads, 40 passes relaxing each toward its
  best-fit square. 1,924 cells of ~32 hex columns on the 256² map, 60 ms.
- A block is a cell and a level (4 high). What stands is worked out from
  the blocks, the way Townscaper picks its pieces: a floor, walls on the
  sides with no block beside (a window in the middle of each, a door on the
  ground floor facing the lowest ground), open to the blocks beside it, a
  hip roof over the top of a stack (rising from its open sides, carrying on
  over a neighbour roofed at its level, leaning up to a taller one's wall),
  pillars at the corners and arches between under a block over nothing. A
  cell's ground floor sits on the highest ground under it, or a
  neighbour's floor when that lines up, on a stone foundation.
- Real matter, not a structure grid: the town rewrites the span of each
  column it touches (on the GPU, one thread a column, in place), so dust
  drifts onto it, moss and vines grow on it (they did within seconds in the
  first shot), the structure pass supports and cracks it, and the agents'
  exact take and put work on it. Loose ground in the span isn't lost: it
  lands on the new top and slides off. The CPU never reads the columns to
  write them (no race with the sim); it tracks the span it last wrote.
  A column over its slots closes its smallest gap (a window filled in).
- Plaster and tile (31, 32): the material table grows to 40 (the physics
  table with it).

Measured (`towntest`, 6/6): a two-level block, one beside it and one over
a gap: the middle column has floors at 13.5 and 17.5 and a roof to 23.9;
the edge a wall 13.5–21.5; every column of the cell roofed; the block over
the gap on 7 pillar columns, 26 of 33 open beneath; taking the upper block
brings the roof down a level. Through the editor: taps on the ground,
roofs and walls build houses, towers and neighbours.

## Round 66 — a streamed world: the window slides, what leaves is frozen (stream)

The user: "prototype the map streaming … building bigger regions
(simulated at coarser detail or frozen)"; first step chosen: a live window
that follows the camera, regions out of it frozen exactly (DECISIONS round
66). `?level=stream`; `scenes/streamer.ts`, `world/streamgen.ts`;
ARCHITECTURE "The streamed world".
- Sliding, not toroidal addressing: Q28 had every kernel's indexing
  wrapping. Moving the contents instead keeps every kernel as it is — a
  slide is a few thousand GPU copies, once per 64 columns of panning. The
  layers aren't copied at all: with the same K in every chunk the chunk
  table is a page table, so a slide hands the leaving chunks' pages to the
  ones coming in.
- What's frozen is what's state (the layers, water, oil, lava, contam,
  moisture, veg, fire, petals, wilt, bend, shake); what's derived each tick
  is shifted with the window (so nothing jumps for a tick) but not kept.
- Hashes and noise of position were in window coordinates, so after a
  slide the trees, tufts, the ground's tint and the woodland patches would
  re-roll. `Globals.org` (the window's world origin) goes into `hash3` and
  `wo()`. The fields were checked identical across a slide (400 cells,
  every field: no difference).
- Generation is per region from world position (noise: continents, hills,
  ridged ranges under a broad mask, lakes below the sea level, cover at
  its angle of repose, snow, plants by moisture). No rivers or caves yet:
  those need a coarse plan over regions (Q33).

Measured (`streamtest`, 8/8): a brick tower 9 high in the west column of
regions; two slides east (8 regions frozen, 8 made): the origin at 128, the
camera moved with the land, the seam where new land meets the old no
steeper than the land beside it (worst 0.31); back west: the tower thawed
exactly (stone 0–19, soil 19–21.7, brick 21.7–30.7, before and after), 12
regions thawed; the sim ticks on; panning south 153 cells: three slides on
their own, the camera kept in the window's middle. A slide: 35–45 ms (one
frame). Frozen regions ~1.4 MB each in memory (Q34). The other tests on
this branch: towntest 6/6, buildtest 4/4, carrytest 8/8, brushtest 5/5.

## Round 67 — the atlas: a world map the stream draws from (atlas)

The user's design (DECISIONS round 67): a coarse map first — continents,
connected components, a partition by Voronoi cells and faults (two
thresholds on one noise), SDF/JFA blending at the borders, patterns from a
bank of tiling fields, climate by latitude, caves — and the chunks streamed
from it. Built as they described it, on the GPU (`src/atlas/`; ARCHITECTURE
"The atlas"). Choices made along the way, and why:
- A torus, so the world has no edge and every noise is periodic (an
  integer lattice period an octave) — no seams at the wrap.
- The macro maps hold only what can't be known locally (a texel's region,
  the region across its nearest border, the distances to that border and
  to the coast); the ground itself is a function of position over them,
  evaluated wherever it's needed. So the whole-world view, a close-up and
  the streamed columns are one function and can't disagree.
- The partition's cells are bent by two octaves of warp at the cells' own
  scale: unwarped, the regions read as paving (straight Voronoi edges).
- Kinds by province (a coarser partition): 85% of a province's regions take
  its kind, so a country reads as one; at 70% the map was a patchwork.
- The region across a border is taken from the four texels a point blends
  (when one differs), not the nearest texel's: past a corner the nearest
  texel's neighbour is a third region and the blend stepped.
- D3D compiles were the cost of starting: the viewer's shader took 27 s
  because the compiler inlined ground() three times (hillshade), each with
  two copies of every region's height and the pattern switch. Now the two
  regions are a loop with a bound it can't unroll, the pattern value comes
  back with the height, shading is from screen derivatives: 1.8 s. All the
  kernels compile at once (createComputePipelineAsync): ~7 s cold, cached
  by the browser after.
- Reaction–diffusion took 14 s as 12000 dispatches; now six steps a
  dispatch in workgroup memory, and only for the patterns a region uses.
- Columns of one batch waited on the last's readback (one parameter
  buffer): each batch has its own now, a slide's four run together.

Measured (`atlastest`, 5/5; n 2048, seed 1): every region one connected
piece (7767 regions, flood fill 8 iterations a run); the borders' JFA
against brute force at 300 texels: worst 0.59 texel, mean 0.13. Building:
base 22 ms, three flood fills ~120–250 ms each (readbacks of the
convergence flag), the CPU's regions 200 ms, JFA 70–80 ms each, the ground
28 ms; kernels compile ~7 s (D3D, cold). Columns: 64² in 5 ms, 256² in
8 ms. The atlas level: three slides east, 12 regions generated, the seam
against the atlas's own ground at the same cells 0 (exact); a slide 120–240
ms when its land wasn't asked for ahead, 9 ms when it was (prefetch). The
field mesh ran out of room in 9 chunks on the atlas's rough land (holes):
its room is a level option now (meshRoom 2.5 for the atlas: 0 full).
streamtest 8/8, towntest 6/6, buildtest 4/4 on this branch.

## Round 69 — forms: what stands on the ground and what's cut into it (atlas)

The user asked for more variety, playing with vertical and horizontal space:
holes to rivers and lava underground, columns of stone, near-vertical cliffs

general generator (crystal spires, spiralling spires, angled mesas). The

  twists, an axis that bends over or a top that tilts, hollow or not, a cap

  as tunnels with skylights or as walled vessels; alcoves in cliff faces;
- each column is marched up as signed values, so surfaces lie between
  samples where the value crosses zero: tops and walls stay fractional as
  the world keeps them, not stepped to whole cells;
- new kinds: spires, escarpment (65–90 over the sea, cliffs all round,
  alcoves), lavafield (lava tubes with skylights, obsidian needles),
  cenotes (water under skylights), crystals; forms added to karst (towers,
  sinkholes), mesa (tilted buttes, arches), badlands (hoodoos with stone
  caps), range and highlands (alcoves, needles), glacier (seracs), basalt

  spires), coral (vessel networks, branches), flesh and veins (vessels).
  New materials flesh, coral, obsidian.

  three deep): springs keep it topped up and molten (a world texture: the
  lava pass was at its 8 storage buffers).
- Physics, the user's way ("if you want it to stand make a stronger
  material"): the ground is terrain; forms of weaker materials are judged
  by the integrity system as they arrive. Sandstone and flesh became
  strength 1: as ground they made whole regions one structure, and judging

  24, packed in 8 bytes); the K limit's loop never ended when the two
  intervals it filled between were different materials (now the closest

  and the streamer refuses it; the whole first window in one dispatch reset
  the GPU (tiles of 64); six chunks of alcoves ran out of mesh room (4, was
  2.5).

Measured: a 64² batch 13–26 ms (crystals: 85 forms, at most 12 runs a
column); the first 256² window 20 ms; slides 6–9 ms prefetched; at the

## Round 79 — the band outside the window; ?win= (places)

Why: the user — the window is a 3D slab of the columns; "Why not also do
what with the 3d cell above the current cell? It will just render
different intervals of the same columns right?" Right: the intervals are

every column's runs outside the window on the CPU. Drawing them is a
second mesh over a second layers buffer; it needn't tick (as the frozen

  the bedrock's top and the samples' base from the layout; a run cut at

  tops in every earlier cliff shot), so the two meshes meet.

  148 675 runs, 31–41 ms on the CPU; 423 k vertices in the band; GPU idle
  ~0.5 ms a frame (hash 0.12, the empty rebuild passes ~0.4). From the mesa
  the block now runs down to the world's floor under the window (it
  stopped at the window's bottom; shots78/tnb vs twb). A z slide 443 ms
  (was 234–320). Memory ~58 MB.

## Round 83 — the terrain's look shaded once a pixel: deferred (perfopt)

Why: the user's first priority, the pixel shader. At low quality (render
scale 0.5, dpr 1: 206 × 457 on a 412 × 915 phone) the camera's zoom is
2.6 CSS pixels a cell, 1.3 rendered — a mesh triangle is under a pixel.
A GPU shades 2 × 2 quads, so each triangle touching a pixel ran the whole
look for up to four, and the surfaces behind the front one too (the round-82
"2.4 ms fixed whatever the pixels": at the phone's size the quads, not the
pixels, are the work). The fix is the old one for tiny triangles: deferred
shading. A `gbuffer` pass draws the mesh into two uint targets (the point's
xyz, its normal packed octahedral with the window/band bit, the structure
word, share and tint: 24 bytes a pixel) and the depth; the world pass then
shades each pixel once from them in a full-screen triangle (one per source:
the window's and the band's layers are different buffers, and the fragment
stage is at its eight storage buffers) and draws the rest over it. The look
is the same function (`meshShade`) as the forward pass. On by default;
`?defer=0` the forward draw (renderer.ts `Renderer.opts.defer`, switchable at
run time for drawbench).

- Tried first: a depth prepass (`?prepass=1`, the mesh's depth, then its
  look tested less-equal): it only removes the surfaces behind, not the
  quads — drawbench draw 3.55 → 3.24 ms (mesh's share 2.47 → 2.16). Kept as a
  flag (it applies with `defer=0`).
- drawbench (still frame at 12304,5457, phone viewport, low; interleaved,
  4 rounds; the laptop's clocks drift with load, so also against renderprep
  — the same work every frame — as a yardstick): draw 3.24 → 1.51 ms, the
  terrain's own share (draw less the draw without the mesh) 2.28 → 0.55 ms
  (−76 %); in renderprep units 8.8 → 4.1 (no mesh 2.5). A second, warm run:
  draw/ref 11.3 → 5.4 (no mesh 3.3).
- Riding (driveprofile, 25 s, phone viewport): the desktop holds 100 Hz
  either way, and at a lighter load its GPU clocks down (every pass, even
  renderprep, reads ~1.8× slower in the deferred rides), so the per-pass
  times there don't compare; draw+gbuffer in renderprep units 10.2 → 7.2.
  The phone's GPU is saturated (p50 30 ms), its clocks up: its frame times
  decide.
- The same picture: shots of the same frame default/deferred differ less

## Round 83 — the rebuild's idle workgroups; a stagger for the change pass that didn't pay (perfopt)

Why: the user's second priority, the mesh's rebuilds. A rebuild's three
passes run over a chunk's whole height of samples (the window's z span),
while its surface lies between its lowest boundary and its top.

  either side it reads) are all under the chunk's bottom (−FAR) or all over
  its top (FAR) returns after its job (the job's words read again with
  workgroupUniformLoad: the uniformity analysis takes a Job, which holds the
  thread's sample, as non-uniform). Mesh identical (meshcmp: window 209 528
  vertices, band 75 616, the same sums). Riding (in renderprep units, the
  clocks drift): verts 0.274/0.288 → 0.245/0.263, quads 0.166/0.171 →
  0.138/0.135 — ~12 %: most of the work is the field at the samples and the
  eight fields a vertex (its gradient, its share), not the empty height.
  `?idleskip=0` off (for meshcmp).
- Tried: hashing a chunk with nothing owed every third turn, staggered by
  chunk (`hashevery`): the change pass's total didn't move (0.60 → 0.59
  units) — its cost is the passes themselves (two a turn, a workgroup a

- driveprofile's SUMMARY adds the draw, shadow and each rebuild pass in
  renderprep units; meshcmp takes --extra. vegprep.wgsl and fieldmesh.wgsl

## Round 83 — `?ticks=N`: the sim's share of a slow frame (perfopt)

Why: the sim runs at 60 Hz, up to the tier's ticks a frame (low 2). With
`skip=render` the phone runs 60 fps: one tick a frame. Drawing, at 30 fps,
each frame runs two ticks — the sim's GPU work a frame doubles as soon as
the render slows it under 60, and a frame that runs long makes the next
one run two: the render's cost is amplified in the frame time. `?ticks=1`
caps it at one (the sim then runs slower than real time under 60 fps — a
diagnostic, not a setting): on the phone, the difference to the default is
the second tick's share of the frame. Not measurable on the desktop (it
runs 100 fps, under a tick a frame).

- (later) `?cull=1` culls in the shadow pass too: the mesh's faces turned
  from the sun (a shell's sun-facing side casts). Same picture; the desktop
  again no change (its rasteriser drops them as cheaply as it draws them);
  a tile-based GPU bins fewer — the phone to tell.
- Tried `meshh=1.5`: not a lattice the chunks tile (ground missing, holes).
  Only 1 and 2 work.


## Round 83 — the terrain's cached layer: the user's baked tiles, first step (perfopt)

Why: the user's fourth item, "render static terrain to iso tiles … relit per
frame, characters and particles composited over"; with the look deferred,
the terrain was the largest piece of the draw left (G-buffer 0.28 ms +
resolve ~0.2 on the still frame). The simplest form that works with a
moving camera: one layer the size of the screen and a margin, not tiles.

- `?tcache=N` (renderer.ts terrainCacheMode, tcPrepare, encodeTerrainCache;
  tcache.wgsl): every Nth frame the terrain (window and band, the chunks
  near the view) is drawn deferred into a layer 24 render pixels larger
  than the screen each side (its camera the frame's, clip x and y scaled),
  the resolve writing colour, pick and depth (fsMeshResolveC; depth as an
  r32float target). Between, the camera is snapped to the layer's pixels
  (its translation in camData moved by under a pixel, so the shift since
  the layer is whole pixels — everything that frame draws with the snapped
  camera; the CPU's camera is untouched) and a full-screen draw copies the
  layer in, shifted, writing the depth (moved by the camera's along the
  view: the orthographic depth is linear) and the picks; plants, water,
  bodies and particles draw over it as before. Drawn again at once after a
  slide (the picks are the window's cells), a turn or zoom (the matrix's
  rotation and scale must match exactly), a new size, the margin used up,
  the band replaced; off with the cutaway or the free camera.
- Riding at 18 (the drive zooms with speed but mostly holds), 87 % of
  frames reuse it at N=8. Drawbench (still frame): draw 1.89 → 1.25 ms at
  N=4 (the mesh's whole share 0.78; the layer saves 0.64). Riding, in
  renderprep units: draw 7.2–7.3 → 5.6–5.8.
- The cost: what's in the terrain's look that moves — the water film's
  swash and streaks, the wet glint, cloud shadows, the shadows of what
  moves (the bike, bodies) on the ground — updates every Nth frame; the
  camera moves in whole pixels (the render's: at low, two CSS pixels).
  A refresh frame costs what a frame costs now: it lowers the average, not
  the worst frame.
- Next for it: refresh a band of the layer a frame (chunks culled to it)
  instead of the whole every Nth — no refresh frames; tiles keyed to world
  chunks (keep them across slides; bake them at a higher resolution for
  crisper lines); per 90° step for the turning view.


## Round 83 — the simulation's cost: land comes in settled; the layers rewritten in place (perfopt)

Why: the user's directions (DECISIONS round 83). Measured first, riding
(driveprofile now prints `ticks` and every pass's mean a frame; scratch
dps.mjs sums the passes that aren't the render's): the sim is ~2 ms of
GPU a tick on the desktop (6.2–7.9 renderprep units) — at 30 fps the phone
runs two a frame. The largest: edit 0.26 ms a tick, project 0.20, surface
0.20, structure 0.16, sediment-out 0.15, renderfields 0.14, particles 0.13,
sediment 0.11, lava 0.08, agents 0.07. Not timed at all: the full-buffer
copies between passes (copyBufferToBuffer is outside the timed passes) —
the layers are 16 MB in the atlas's window, and the editor's brush (always
on in the sandbox) and the structures each copied them back whole every
tick: 32 MB a tick, ~2 GB/s of a phone's bandwidth at 60 ticks.

- `?settle=0` (sim/sleep.ts `SETTLE`, `settleAll`): land that comes in — a
  slide's new chunks, the window cut again in z, a warp, the first window —
  doesn't wake for 1.5–2 s to settle; it falls asleep at once (drowsy a
  moment: its layers carried through). Awake chunks riding were 48–118 of
  256 (the player's ring plus the settling); the sim a tick 6.24/7.91 →
  5.25/5.38 units (−16 to −32 %). Not yet looked at: whether what comes in
  unsettled looks wrong (the user: fix that in the generator) — rivers
  especially: the flux isn't frozen with a region (keep: false), so a river
  come in asleep has none and its surface is drawn still until something
  wakes it (next: freeze the flux with the region, and a generated river's
  flux from the generator).
- `?inplace=1` (sim/systems.ts `INPLACE`, `columnPass`): the brush, the
  structures and the layer pulls rewrite the layers in place (each thread
  its own column: the brush and the pulls read only it; the structures read
  their neighbours' support — one tick's Gauss–Seidel instead of Jacobi)
  instead of into layersNext copied back whole; and the brush runs only for
  5 s after an edit (a pour lands up to 3.9 s after the press). The timed
  sim a tick 5.30 → 4.6 units with settle=0 (the brush's pass gone), plus
  the two 16 MB copies a tick, untimed. brushtest 5/5, pulltest 6/6,
  buildtest 4/4, worldapitest all ok with inplace=1&settle=0.

- (later) `?settle=0` also gives rivers their flow: a column come in asleep
  with water and no flux takes, while drowsy, the pipes' steady state for its
  levels at once (water_flux.wgsl: f = GAIN (H − Hn) / (1 − FRICTION),
  capped at its depth) — drawn flowing, frozen; and the flux is frozen with
  its region (streamer `keep`), so land that comes back keeps its flow.
  Riding 15 s: wet columns with no flux 17 of 5 148 (default) / 205 of 10 605
  (settle=0). More water stands with settle=0 (10.6 k wet columns against
  5.1 k): the generated water isn't at rest — the default's settling drains
  it. The user's rule applies: fix it in the generator (open).
- `?sleepmore=1` (sim/sleep.ts `SLEEP_MORE`): the surface and render-field
  passes skip sleeping chunks too, but drowsy ones; every chunk is drowsy for
  0.25 s after any slide (the derived textures moved — round 80 kept the
  surface pass awake for exactly that: "levels stay 0 for columns in
  sleeping chunks"). With settle=0&inplace=1: the sim a tick 4.66–4.70 →
  3.75–3.80 units (surface 0.24 → 0.05 ms, render fields 0.15 → 0.05).
  atlasworldtest 6/6 (its "no column top 0 after the slides" included) and
  streamtest 8/8 with sleepmore=1&settle=0&inplace=1.


## Round 83 — the tick rate (`?simhz=30|15`), the flows' own rates (`?flowhz=`), loose ground settled in the generator (perfopt)

Why: the user's directions (DECISIONS round 83): "Simulation can absolutely
be 30 Hz or even 15"; every animated flow cached and drawn moving, its update
rate its own, full rate only where disturbed; streamed land with no floating
pieces. And the phone: "Deferred shading helped a lot" — it stays the default.

- `?simhz=60|30|15` (sim/flow.ts `TICK_HZ`; simulation.ts re-exports it):
  the systems' rates were written per 60 Hz tick (G.dt was 1/60 and almost
  no kernel read it). common.wgsl `simStep()` (G.dt × 60: 1, 2 or 4) and
  `perTick(p)` (a chance over the tick), `relaxTick(k)` (a decay or a
  relaxation over the tick) scale them so the world runs at the same speed in
  its time: moisture, contamination (its transport by the water's flux too),
  fire (burning, and the chances of catching), wilt, ecology, climate (its
  DT_C), the structures' chances (support still relaxes a cell a tick, so a
  collapse spreads at the tick rate), the brush's pours (DT_E), sediment
  (DT_D, slumps, wind smoothing, piping, faces, falls, the shaking's age;
  slumps and smoothing capped at a sixth of the excess a neighbour — more
  over-corrects into a checkerboard), particles (every spawn chance and the
  grains a running stream sheds), the wind field and the sway (their DT).
  The water's, oil's and lava's pipes are stable only at the 60 Hz step:
  tried scaled (the pipes' gain and the flux moved × the step) — a pond
  then over-corrects (6 pipes × twice the gain is over 1) and the sloshing
  water carried soil into a dug hole: the sandbox's dig, −1.71 at 60 Hz,
  filled back to −0.27 at 30 (scratch digtest.mjs). So they run `FLOW_SUB`
  60 Hz substeps a tick instead (cheap passes); the dig then holds at −2.0
  at 30 and 15 Hz. api/water.ts reads the flux as a 60 Hz tick's whatever
  the rate. worldapitest: 16/16 at 30 Hz; at 15 all but "warmup with
  debris" (its warmup counts ticks: 600 are 40 s at 15 Hz).
  Riding (settle=0&inplace=1&sleepmore=1, two runs each; the laptop was
  warm): the sim a frame 1.74/1.93 ms → 1.11/0.93 at 30 Hz → 0.65/0.63 at 15
  (−45 %, −65 %); a tick costs more (the flows' substeps), a frame less.
  At 30 fps the phone ran two ticks a frame; at 30 Hz, one.
- `?flowhz=water:4,oil:4,lava:2,sediment:1` (sim/flow.ts `flowN`,
  common.wgsl `slowTick`, `flowFrozen`): a sleeping chunk's flow is frozen
  (drawn moving from its frozen flux: the default, as round 80 had it); with
  a rate it's updated that many times a second instead, staggered over the
  chunks, at the 60 Hz step (slow motion — which keeps the pipes stable while
  it settles); awake (the player near, an event, a storm), every tick. One
  mechanism for water, oil, lava and sediment, a rate each, for the user to
  tune on the phone. Not measured yet (default off).
- `?settle=0` now also drops a streamed column's loose intervals with air
  under them onto their support (streamer.ts `settleLoose`, in cutRegion:
  the generator's output, before it's cut into the window); solids stay
  (overhangs, arches). Counted in the streamer's stats (`settled`).

- `?windhz=N` (sim/flow.ts `WIND_K`): the wind field and the world API's
  blows and wakes run every TICK_HZ / N ticks, each update the time since
  (DT × the ticks between, the spreading relaxed over them too); the
  player's strokes and a mover's wake wait for the next update — the wake's
  segment then covers everything since (api/wind.ts: its clock and the
  blows' timers by the ticks between). worldapitest 16/16 with windhz=15
  (the first try, with the API's wakes still painted every tick, lost three
  quarters of a wake: "wake trails behind" failed). The field still reacts
  within 1/N s of the player's movement. Storms need nothing: they are
  analytic on the GPU (stormDist) and a few dozen lines of CPU a frame.

- `?fieldhz=N` (sim/flow.ts `fieldPeriod`, `fieldPass`): moisture,
  contamination, climate and ecology run every max(their period,
  TICK_HZ / N) ticks, each update the time since (their kernels' simStep,
  perTick, relaxTick become fieldStep — × K, the ratio to their own period
  — fieldChance, fieldRelax). Wilt and fire stay every tick (one-tick taps
  and lightning). First try wrote K as `${k}.0` (7.5.0 when K wasn't whole:
  the climate kernel didn't compile — and the frame went on, its command
  buffers invalid, no fatal overlay: worth a look on its own). worldapitest
  16/16 with fieldhz=1&simhz=30&windhz=15.
- Riding (two runs each; renderprep 0.33–0.67 ms — the laptop's clocks all
  over): the sim a frame, default 1.14/2.37 ms; settle=0&inplace=1&
  sleepmore=1&simhz=30 0.90/1.06; + windhz=15&fieldhz=1 0.97/0.86. In
  renderprep units a tick 6.08/7.92 → 6.75/5.55 → 5.15/4.91.
- The phone (the user): "The current iteration of perf branch is crushing
  it. About 16ms for p95!" with lite=1&settle=0&inplace=1&sleepmore=1 —
  p95 from 80–100 ms (round 82) to 16, the frame rate's own.

## Round 83 — perfopt merged into places

The user, on the phone: the perf branch "crushing it. About 16ms for p95!"
(deferred, lite, settle=0, inplace=1, sleepmore=1). Merged at 33f4ab5: the
low tier's defaults are the phone set (index.html expands it when q is
absent or low; each flag overridable, `?phone=0` the whole set off).
`Camera.focus` (perfopt's prepass, G-buffer and terrain cache) became the
camera's cut (`cutOn`); the gem look and the sections are in meshShade, so
the deferred resolve has them. Riding at the phone tier (driveprofile, 30 s,
the desktop): p95 10.5 ms, worst 43, no hitch over 50 ms, the GPU 5.4 ms a
frame (15.0 before the merge, rings and all).
- The window's edge open (the user: "whenever I pan it draws the side of
  the current cells even if they are going to be covered by neighbors").
  Off the map the field was air, so the mesh closed the window's edge with
  a wall down to the bedrock (scripts/edgeshot.mjs, the window held, the
  camera by its near edge: a cliff of rock and caves' sections); after a
  slide the chunks by the old edge kept it until they were made again.
  With the atlas's rings drawn past the edge, the edge is open
  (`Renderer.openEdges`, MR.ze.w; fieldmesh.wgsl colDist: an off-map column
  is the edge column, going on) — no wall; the rings cover what's past it.
  Without rings (`?lod=0`, the valley, the noise-streamed level) the wall

## Round 84 — one model of material flow: liquids as runs in the columns, falls that arc, steady state frozen (flow)

The user (DECISIONS round 84): a unified model of material flow, for waterfalls out of underground streams and
lava flows; a fall that arcs out, steady from column to column; "think noita physics … in a compressed column
space and adding in velocity … plausibility and spectacle not realism"; steady flow frozen as an animation and
found again when perturbed, with a tolerance; a frozen region's flux kept proportional to its supply. Behind
`?flow=1`; the design is in ARCHITECTURE "The flow model".

- **Why runs in the gaps, not intervals of the layers.** Water as one depth per column on top of the ground
  can't be in a tunnel or fall through the air. A liquid run now lies on the floor of any gap of a column (the
  air between two solid or granular intervals, or the open air on top), up to four a column. They live in the
  flow module's own buffer, not in the layers: a liquid moving every tick would otherwise be a layer write
  every tick per wet column (sediment, the surface pass, renderprep and every other layer reader would see
  water intervals to skip), and the open run stays exactly the water contract, so the ~15 readers of `water`
  didn't change. The only layer writes are lava setting into basalt (measured: 4–8 columns a tick while the
  vent pours, 0 once it has set; water: none).
- **Why one kernel set with a liquid's numbers.** Water and lava differ by gain, friction, yield, thickness,
  heat and setting (LiquidKind); everything else — the gaps, the targets, the falls, the steady state — is the
  same code, so a fall of lava arcs like water's. Loose ground stays the sediment system's: it is the layers
  (strata, repose, wind) and changes the gaps; a granular kind of the same kernel for *moving* sand (a pour
  off a ledge) is BACKLOG FL4.
- **Why streams move a column a tick.** A stream's state (volume, height, vertical speed, horizontal velocity,
  where it enters the next column) is carried column to column along its exact ballistic path through each
  hexagon, so a steady outflow is a steady parabola and mass is conserved (each tick's packet passes on or
  lands). It goes faster than real time across the arc; the shape is right, and the steady state is what's
  seen. The lip speed is the critical flow's for its discharge, 2 (g q)^(1/3): the pipe model's depth at a lip
  is a grid artefact (it empties each tick), its discharge isn't — the first try (flux / edge / depth) gave
  12 cells/s for everything, the second (sqrt(g d)) a fall that hugged the cliff.
- **Steady state.** Per chunk, net change (runs and bed) against throughput, a window at a time. Throughput
  was first each column's gross outflow: a lava pool sloshing in its crater counted as throughput and the
  pool, filling at 0.1 cells³ a tick, was judged steady and frozen. Now it is the length of each column's net
  flow vector (a river's discharge; a pool's sloshing cancels). Defaults ?steadytol=0.1, ?steadyfloor=1e-3,
  ?steadywin=30: at 0.02 / 2e-4 two chunks under the pool's fall never settled (the landing column changes
  by the stream's packets), and the user's "small residual drift while frozen is fine".
- **Frozen and rescaled.** A frozen column beside an awake chunk checks its balance; its chunk's edge inflow
  and outflow, read back, rescale its flux (and its streams, and the water contract's flux) by in / out for
  one step without simulating (the user's "keep the flow proportional and then zero out when they get too
  low"); zero when it dries; past 4× either way, or something arriving where nothing flowed, it wakes.
- **Measured** (scripts/flowlab.mjs, the flow lab, desktop Intel Xe-LPG at the low tier (the phone's flags),
  GPU ms a frame at ~0.6 ticks a frame): the old water system on the same level 0.032 (water-flux 0.020,
  water-depth 0.012). The flow model awake (the pool pouring, 13–18 chunks awake): water 0.28 (flux 0.08,
  jets 0.03, depth 0.14, publish 0.015, prep 0.036) and lava 0.26 — about 8× the old water each, mostly
  every column's gap scan and the neighbour checks of dry columns (FL3: skip dry chunks, skip lava where
  there is none). Everything frozen (awake chunks 0): the simulation passes aren't dispatched; prep only,
  water 0.03–0.05 + lava 0.03–0.06 ms — and the frozen pool still pours: 2 116 pixels change between the
  frozen pool's GIF frames (2 948 at the tunnel's fall) with no simulation. With the defaults the breached
  pool (its spring on), the trench and the vent (stopped) were all near steady and asleep 35 s after the
  breach; the arc from the side: scripts/flowlab.mjs `pool-side`.
- Found on the way: the prep kernel at 9 storage buffers (the chunk table it doesn't use: dropped from its
  layout); the warmup ends past the 1.5 s settle, so everything fell asleep before the steady state had
  judged it — now everything is judged once after the warmup (Steady.judgeAll) and what's unsteady is kept.
- Encapsulation (the user: "Are you still practicing good encapsulation?"):
  three leaks of this round closed. The field mesh's state layout (CHUNK0,
  CSTRIDE, the built hash's word, its indices', FRESH) is published once in
  shaders/meshstate.wgsl, included before meshregion.wgsl wherever that is
  and before far.wgsl (the rings' meshBuilt read the numbers from their own
  copy). The streamer tells the renderer the window moved (Renderer.
  windowMoved: the meshes, the band's, the shore field) instead of reaching
  into each. The edit ops are one table (sim/edit-ops.ts: OP, STROKE_START,
  editOpOf, CUTS) for the world API, the plants and water modules and the
  integrity system's tap. atlasworldtest 6/6, slideshot, craterbench (p95
  10.2 ms) on it. Pages builds the experiment branches too (ceiling, rivers,
  flow).

Why: the user: "all generators make a steady state so when we arrive nothing
is simulated until the player interacts with it" — they saw water rush in on
arrival. scripts/waterrest.mjs: the atlas level (phone tier: land comes in
asleep), every chunk woken with no edits, the water read before and 5 s after,
classed sea / river (a source) / other / dry.

  by springs (0.0008 a tick along its middle); the pipes' steady state for those
  springs is far thinner on a slope (the outflow cap binds: about the river's
  accumulated spring discharge a tick). Woken: 3 378 of 4 929 river columns
  change by over 0.05 in 5 s, the window's water 3 466 → 3 035 (−12 %), and
  converged (2 048 steps) it's ~2 500 (−27 %). Other water (the coarse world's
  lakes, tubes) moves in 161 columns. One basin fed by springs with no outlet
  rises ~1.3 cells in 5 s: never at rest.
- Fixed: Sleep.settleAll's drowsy window for the first window was counted
  from tick 0, after the level's warmup had run hundreds — the first window
  was never drowsy (532015d).
- Tried, kept as a measuring tool only (`?settleiters=N`, default 0): the new
  land's water settled on arrival — water flux/depth ping-ponged over the
  rect of land just come in (one compute pass, no copies; sim/sleep.ts
  `settling` rects, 64 ticks each). 2 048 steps: river columns moving 3 378 →
  ~700, the moved volume 539 → ~190 — but ~44 ms of GPU in a tick for a whole
  window. Not the generator's fix.
- Tried, `?riverhold=1` (default off): a river's source holds its level
  instead of a spring's constant flow (forms.wgsl RIVER_HOLD writes
  waterSource = −depth; water_depth.wgsl tops a negative-source column up to

  banks at least as high as its level (the generator carving the channel and

### perfopt — lazy caves, step 1 (`?caves=mouths`, default off); the band's back faces culled (`?bandcull=1`, no gain)

- The coordinator's lazy caves, travel first. With `?caves=mouths`, the atlas's columns
  (forms.wgsl colFinish, `LAZY_CAVES`) make a column's caves only where they can
  open to the air: where some neighbour's ground is under the rock kept over the caves
  (`lowN < rockTop - caveDepth`). Inside the hills it makes none, so no cave noise is
  evaluated and no runs are written. Why: the caves nobody can see cost generation, mesh
  and memory in every streamed column.

  generation passes were already small on the ride, so there's no clear win there. The
  G-buffer went 0.26 to 0.20 ms in one pair; a second pair was throttled. Fewer runs
  should help the mesh and the band most where the hills are deep. That isn't measured
  separately yet.

  that showed in the window's cut edge. Elsewhere there were only water-shimmer
  differences (mean diff 1.6). The cost: enclosed caves are gone, so the cutaway and
  digging into a hill find solid rock. Step 2, still to do: carve them in later, near
  the player (or when a dig reaches one).
- `?bandcull=1` (the band's G-buffer draw culls back faces) is still in. On a contended
  GPU, two drawbench runs gave draw/ref 26.3 to 22.5 and 11.3 to 14.0, so no measurable
  gain. It stays off. The band is vertical (above and below the window), so the LOD
  rings never cover it and there are no band draws to skip for them.

## Round 83 (2026-10-26, `dialog`) — dialog, the run, story cameras; `?story=demo`

The user: "get dialogue in and basic cameras so we have a way to communicate what is going on." The GM (branch
`gm`) writes a SessionStory as data offline; these systems play it (docs/SYSTEMS.md systems 10, 11, part of 5),
coded against src/api/contracts only.

- **Dialog** (src/dialog/dialog.ts, `DialogBox implements Dialog`). A panel across the bottom, phone first:
  speaker name, role and a portrait slot (a coloured initial until there are pictures), the line typed at 50
  characters a second (a tap shows it all; prefers-reduced-motion shows it at once), then the answers as
  buttons at least 52 px tall, numbered (1–9 on a keyboard). A scrim over the rest of the screen takes every
  touch, wheel and key while a talk is open, so the game's controls get nothing. It knows nothing of runs:
  a choice's `requires` is asked of a `check` callback; nodes said and choices made go out on `onNode` and
  `onChoice`. A choice's index is its index in the node's `choices`, hidden ones counted, so a `chose`
  condition means the same thing whatever was shown. Styled by custom properties (dialog.css).
- **Run** (src/run/run.ts, `StoryRun implements Run`). Keeps the facts noted (talked, chose, reached,
  killed, event), the flags, the items given, attitudes (each cast member's disposition plus shifts), the
  clock. Each fact re-checks objectives (hidden → shown when `when` holds → done when `done` holds, or
  failed) and happenings until nothing changes (64 passes and it throws: a story that doesn't settle is a
  bug). Outcomes: flags, attitudes, give, unlock (where a tree opens next: `entry(tree)`), spawn (told to
  `onOutcome` for the game), endRun, and AtlasEvents applied to the WorldState at once (the atlas scale
  "when a story event fires"), each with an id, the run number and the cause's ref (the objective or
  `dialog/node`). `end(how)` makes the RunRecord (deeds: objectives done, failed and left undone, what
  was said, faction shifts; the events).
- **Validator** (src/run/validate.ts). A story is checked before it's played: unique ids, every reference
  (cast locations, speakers, next nodes, condition targets, choice indices, unlocks, spawn places, an
  atlas event's `detail.location`) resolves. One StoryError lists every problem, so the GM fixes them in
  one go; nothing is guessed. The GM step (SYSTEMS order 3) can use it as its check.
- **Story cameras** (src/story/camera.ts, `StoryCamera`). On the fixed camera's target and zoom:
  `frame(at)` eases there (the point placed 32% down the screen, over the dialog panel) and holds until
  `release()`; `reveal(at)` eases there, holds (a tap skips), eases back; `look(at)` an opening shot left
  with the player; `follow(get)` a spring after a moving point while no shot runs. Every move starts from
  where the camera is (interruptible without a jump); zoom eases in log space; a reveal set off during a
  talk waits for it, then goes from the speaker, not home first. While a shot holds a point it's kept seen
  through the cutaway: Dither.see, and the Slice cut over it (then let back up); with ?cutaway=1 the
  level's own dither and slice are used, the puck's slice paused while a shot runs.
- **Play** (src/story/play.ts, `StoryPlay`). Wires them over the world API: the cast stand where a Stage
  puts them (a pillar built with terrain.build, a badge over it to tap); the player's position (the
  camera's target, the god's-eye game's) noted `reached` inside a staged location; a done objective gets a
  reveal of where its change is seen (an atlas event's `detail.location`, else the objective's); outcomes'
  atlas events realised at play scale where they can be (overgrow: plants grown and petals, flood: water,
  mark: a cairn), the rest left to the atlas; an end card with the record. The Stage (where locations and

## Round 84 — the game master's pipeline: the world wiki, docs/GM.md, the validator, the first story (gm)

The user (round 83): "have a GM (for now we can use a subagent with GM context and tools) take the world state
wiki and offline create a session story as data that we can use to create the locations, dialogues,
objectives and world effects." This is SYSTEMS.md step 3. Everything here sits behind the GM's adapter
(src/gm/). The contracts in src/api/contracts are unchanged; the changes I'd propose are at the end.

- **Why cache the atlas's facts.** The GM is a subagent with files and a shell, not a GPU, and the atlas is
  built on the GPU. So one headless run (`scripts/worldwiki.mjs --pull`, `?atlas=view`, about a minute)
  exports what the wiki needs (src/gm/atlas-facts.ts) to data/atlas/seed1.json. That's 2.2 MB: 7772
  regions, 140 sites, 166 roads, and the spawn at cell 13716,5536 in region 2341. Everything after runs in
  Node from the cache: the wiki takes about 2 s, the validator well under a second.
- **Why the wiki is a snapshot plus more.** WorldSnapshot holds the regions' names, kinds and states, the
  factions and the history. A GM also needs the land itself (tier, climate, ground heights for flood
  levels, rivers, neighbours) and the settlements and roads, and the snapshot has no place for those yet.
  So the wiki JSON carries a WorldSnapshot (what the validator and FileGM check against) beside those
  tables. The markdown covers the world, the factions, the start, every region within 1400 of the start
  (177) and every settlement within 2600 (14). At about 38 k characters it can be read in one go.
- **Why placeholder factions.** None exist yet, and diplomacy is the user's to design, but a story needs
  someone to turn. So a deterministic table seeds them: each continent's settlements are clustered into
  realms (5 realms on seed 1, because the main continent has 127 of the 140 sites), plus four world
  factions placed by the kind of land. The wiki and ARCHITECTURE mark them as placeholders.
- **Why the validator is strict and simulates.** A subagent's story can fail in ways a type check misses: a
  node nothing leads to, a key no one gives, an objective waiting on one that can't be done, a flood with
  "magnitude 0.5" when the contract means a z level. The validator runs a fixed point over what could
  happen and reports each problem with its path. scripts/gmtest.mjs breaks the first story 18 ways, and
  the validator catches all 18.
- **Being the GM once.** I read data/wiki/seed1.md and wrote data/stories/the-bell-under-kaudru.json near
  the spawn.
  - 3 locations: the Thaurd ford camp, Mebe `s139`, and the Wardens' Barrow in Bethorn Downs (2159).

## Round 83 — the perf ceiling: the heightfield alone (`ceiling`, an experiment)

The user: "Can we see how fast things work if we did a heightmap only renderer
streaming in chunks and just using their top material height and color? I just
want to understand what a ceiling on perf is on the phone here." `?ceiling=1` on
the atlas level: each frame only the drive's camera and one render pass (Renderer
.encodeCeiling: colour + depth, no pick target) of far.ts's rings and far land
(far.wgsl fsCeilLod / fsCeilFar: the column's colour, lambert from the sun, a
little height tint, the fog). No sim, no streaming, no field mesh, no renderprep,
no shadow, no band, no plants or particles, no HUD or audio updates. The rings
are lod.wgsl's lodHeight — the atlas's own `ground()`, a top and a packed colour
a texel, world-anchored in toroidal slots, so a move makes only the new strips —
with a ring a cell apart first (`?near=1`, the default: spacings 1, 2, 4, 8, 16;
`?near=2`: the usual four). LodD holds 5 rings now (LOD_UNI_BYTES 7·16). The
window is still built at the start (the level's set-up needs it); it doesn't
slide — the camera leaves it behind, its target's height following the macro
ground (atlas.hmac). `?ringn=` sets the rings' vertices a side (193 usual). The
lod strips are timed in the profiler now (`lod <spacing>`).

driveprofile.mjs, q=low, 412×915 at dpr 2.6 (render 206×457), drive 18, at
12304,5457, 30 s, this machine's Intel Xe-LPG iGPU (vsync ~100 Hz; other agents
shared the machine but no other headless run was open during these):

| run | p50 | p95 | p99 | worst | hitches >50 | GPU ms/frame |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the game (no ceiling) | 9.9 | 10.9 | 20.1 | 57 | 3 | 8.4 (draw 4.0, gbuffer 0.55, renderprep 0.34, shadow 0.38, the rest mesh/sim) |
| ceiling, near 1 (n 193) | 9.9 | 10.2 | 10.5 | 20 | 0 | 2.5–2.9 (draw 2.77, lod strips 0.04) |
| ceiling, near 2 (n 193) | 9.9 | 10.2 | 10.6 | 22 | 0 | 2.2–2.4 (draw 2.17, strips 0.02) |
| ceiling, near 1, n 97 | 9.9 | 10.2 | 10.6 | 35 | 0 | 1.0–1.2 (draw 1.24) |
| ceiling, near 1, n 65 | 9.9 | 10.2 | 10.6 | 21 | 0 | 0.6–1.1 (draw 1.14) |

(Uncapped, --uncapped: GPU 9.13 game, 2.51 near 1, 2.23 near 2 — the frame
times there are bimodal by pacing and say nothing.) Every capped run sits at the
display's interval: the frame time no longer says what it costs, the GPU does.

What's left in the ceiling: the draw, and in it the vertices. Five rings of
193² is 186k vertices and 1.1M triangles for 94k pixels — each vertex reads
its texel and four neighbours (the normal), and in the melt band at a ring's
edge the next ring's four (or the far land's eight); triangles far smaller than
a pixel. Halving the vertices a side (n 97) halves the draw (2.77 → 1.24 ms);
n 65 barely less again (the far grid, 161², and the fixed cost). The strips
the move makes cost 0.04 ms a frame on average (one dispatch a ring that moved
8 of its spacings; the 1-cell ring every 8 cells). The canvas present isn't in
the GPU's timestamps; at this size it's small, and the frame is the display's.
So the ceiling's floor is a screen-sized grid: about one vertex per few pixels,
which the rings at n 193 overshoot at the low tier's resolution. (The game's
own rings are in its 4.0 ms draw too: n 193 × 4.)


## Round 84 — the hybrid renderer: voxels only where they're needed (`hybrid`, `?hybrid=1`)

The ceiling (round 83) drew the atlas as a heightfield alone at ~2.5 ms of GPU a
frame against ~8.4 for the game; on the phone "the performance was solid and
very usable". Its weakness is the cliffs: a slope between vertices with the
plateau's colour stretched down it, no overhangs, lips, arches or cave mouths.
The user: "Yes I think a hybrid approach makes sense to build." So `?hybrid=1`
on the atlas level (the full game stays the default; docs/ARCHITECTURE.md has
the contract):

- **Each mesh chunk (32 × 32 rows) is voxels or the heightfield's.** Voxels:
  the field mesh and the band built and drawn there, the window's water, plants
  and sheets prepared there. The heightfield's: never built — FieldMesh.
  setWanted keeps it out of the change pass, the rebuild and the draw (one built
  before is emptied: indices 0, hash FRESH) — so far.wgsl's `meshBuilt` is
  false and the LOD rings draw it, a 1-cell ring first (spacings 1–16, as the
  ceiling's near 1). renderprep and vegprep skip it through Globals.hfield (a
  bit a mesh chunk, like the sleep mask): its water is the rings' too (the
  sea's and the river's level, lod.wgsl) — the sim's water drawn over the rings
  stood off them in sheets where the carved bed and the ground differ.
- **What needs voxels** (scenes/hybrid.ts HybridChunks): the land, decided as it
  comes in — Streamer.relief / gapTop / colTop per column (writeNow, editLive,
  the first window; moved with a slide): a form on the ground or cut into it
  (the top off the ground's own by over 0.75) or a gap between runs **open to
  the air** (a neighbour's top under its roof: an overhang's lip, a cave mouth,
  a bridge, a tunnel's portal). The first try counted every gap: 58 of 72
  chunks at the first spawn, because 21% of the window's columns hold buried
  caves (stone over stone, sandstone over sandstone, under the hills). Buried
  ones nobody sees from the sky; only exposed gaps count now: 1 of 72 there, 27
  at a mesa's rim. Then the focus (`?vradius=`, 40 world units round the
  camera's target: ~12 chunks), and what a world event touched (kept while it's
  in the window). Over a 30 s ride the mean is 21.7 chunks voxels of 72, 17.9
  drawn.
- **Seams.** The rings and the columns come from the same `ground()`: over the
  first spawn's ring texels the window's column tops differ from the 1-cell
  ring's by 0.0 on average, 0.10 absolute (more only at river banks, where the
  ring stands at the river's level). A hairline still showed the sky along a
  voxel chunk's edge; the rings draw a skirt there (a 0.9-cell strip inside the
  voxel chunk where its neighbour is the rings'). In the window the rings are
  never pressed under the focus (underFocus made a grey shelf of them), and
  they write the pick target as the columns do, so a tap on a heightfield
  chunk lands (and the event it makes turns the chunk to voxels).
- **The rings' look** (all of them, the game's too): where the surface is
  steeper than ~60° (the vertex normal and the triangle's own, which on the
  1-cell ring is a cell's) the region's rock — lod.wgsl now writes the rock's
  albedo and material beside the top's — in beds (render.wgsl's strata, a
  local copy of the noise), lit by sun, sky and a little bounce. The rings'
  green stops 70 over the sea as colFinish's plants do: at the mesa the
  plateau was green in the rings and bare dirt in the columns.

driveprofile, q=low, 412×915 dpr 2.6, drive 18 at 12304,5457, 30 s, this
machine's iGPU shared with other agents (the clocks drift between runs: the
same build gave a draw of 1.9 and 4.0 ms in two runs):

| run | p50 | p95 | p99 | worst | GPU ms/frame | draw | gbuffer | renderprep | shadow |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| full game | 9.9 | 10.5 | 12.4 | 62 | 5.99 | 2.87 | 0.43 | 0.26 | 0.17 |
