## 2026-10-26 — round 85: things as compositions, diplomacy, settlement grids (contracts)

The user's design (DECISIONS round 85) calls for one recipe system for units, items, vehicles, buildings and
civilizations, with legacy carried between runs. They asked for the data model first. Why it's shaped this way:
- **Tags and slots, not a type per combination.** A slot accepts any thing whose tags fit, so a hover knight
  takes no new code: a hoverbike is a `mount`. Stats come from rules over the composition's tags. A part's tags
  show as `slot:tag`, so a rule can say "a knight whose mount is a vehicle hovers". A hoverbike's power slot
  takes a power cell or a magic stone. The magic stone adds `glows`, which gives the user's "different
  consequences" a place to live.
- **Derived, never stored.** Capabilities are recomputed from the parts. Swapping a mount, wearing armour down
  or dropping a power cell changes the result without any sync.
- **Mastery separate from possession.** A people's knowledge of a recipe is uses, repairs, makes or
  understands. `plan` refuses a craft without `makes`. So a medieval people can ride dug-up hoverbikes but can't
  build them, which the user asked for by name.
- **Provenance on every thing**, and a `Place` that can be `in: 'region'` (buried, scattered, a hoard). What a
  run leaves becomes things a later people can find (R7).
- **Diplomacy as a record**, RimWorld style. Opinions are the faded sum of deeds plus standing agreements, so
  dialog can quote the deeds behind an opinion (`because`, `memories`). Rights and trade are agreements with
  places, resources, shares and flows. Units ask `rights(region, at)` before they mine.
- **Settlements:** overlay grids of several styles, and buildings as things, so a ruin can be adapted. The city
  game edits the same records.
scripts/recipetest.mjs checks all of this: 12 checks, all passing.

With `&hybrid=0` it took 9.07 ms, with 55 chunks drawn; p95 was 10.7 and p99 14.9. atlasworldtest passes 6/6.

## Round 86 — falls at their own pace, drawn as a sheet with spray (flow)

The user tested the flow lab on the phone (DECISIONS round 86): "The waterfalls move way way too fast at 1x and
visually it doesn't look as good as the old approach or the sand particles which look fantastic", then "the
waterfall trajectory looks decent … it's just that the columns have gaps and the rendering isn't great".
places merged in first (the hybrid on the low tier, rivers, contracts; docs by union; Sleep keeps both the
flow's wakeChunk and the hybrid's filter, and wakeChunk honours the filter).

- **Why it was fast.** Not the tick rate, the sim's dt or the render's scroll (the streaks scrolled at
  ~7 cells/s, the old water's speed): a stream's state moved on **one column every 60 Hz step** whatever its
  speed — the path's shape was right (each column's exit time t and z − g t²/2), its timing wasn't. A column
  a stream crosses in 0.1–0.3 s was crossed in 1/60 s, 6–18× fast, and a stream falling inside one column
  landed in the step it arrived. Measured (scripts/fallcompare.mjs, the lab's pool, the plug dug the same
  way): breach to the plain 24 cells below in **0.67 s** of sim time with the flow model, 0.55 s with the old
  water (whose sheet moves a column a tick too) — the free fall alone takes 1.85 s at g = 14.
- **Real time.** A column now holds the volume in flight over it (V) and its path's time across it (tc).
  Nothing passes on before the stream's front has crossed (its age ≥ tc), then V dt / tc a step; in a
  steady state V = rate × tc, the same flux as before, and fronts, changes and the water itself go at the
  path's speed. Mass: what leaves a column is what the next one (or the landing) takes; the depth pass lands
  this step's outflow (j3.z), not the in-flight volume. A fourth jet texture (j3: age, time since the lip,
  outflow, carried). After: **2.55 s** breach to plain (0.5–0.7 s of it the notch filling).
- **The critical flow over a lip.** With water now aloft as long as its fall takes, the pipe model's
  momentum at a lip (it pours the whole depth off each step: 17× the critical discharge for a 2.6-deep pool)
  put ~500 cells³ in the air over a pit at once; it landed together and stood 7 cells over the plateau (the
  dark spikes in the first tries). Capped at √g d^(3/2) a unit of edge — plausible, and a fall that lasts
  (the pool drains in ~18 s, not ~2).
- **Lost water.** A stream arriving over a sleeping chunk was dropped (a frozen column took nothing in, its
  landing went nowhere: the plain stayed dry, plainSum 0 at 9 s, with the pool losing 80 cells³). Now it is
  carried on there (j3.w), what would land held aloft, and the chunk flagged to wake whatever its balance
  (act z bit 2, steady.ts). After: the water reaches the plain and the totals add up (upper 584 + plain 98
  at 9 s, the spring adding).
- **One stream off a lip.** A run falling off two faces sent a stream down each, 60° apart, each at the
  speed of its own face's flux: a fan of thin strands (the "gaps"). Now everything a run sends off its ledge
  leaves with one velocity — its falls' mean direction (if within 60° of the face; round a pit or off a
  ridge, each face's own), the speed for their mean discharge.
- **The look** (render.wgsl streamVertex / shadeStream). A stream over its column is a sheet along its
  parabola, not a box: a curtain across the flow (as wide as a column's water, spreading as it falls, so
  neighbours join) and a band in the arc's plane (the arc side on), three segments each, begun a little
  before the entry and ended past the exit with a cross-fade (a column's entry is the average of where the
  streams it gathered left theirs, so segments meet without gaps). Lit by the path's own normal. Its pattern
  is a function of (time along the path − the sim's time): it rides the water, falls at the fall's speed,
  stretches as it speeds up, stands when the sim is paused, and agrees at any tick rate. Glassy off the lip,
  aerated white lower down, ragged edges, gaps opening as it falls; a trickle faint by its rate.
  Spray: liquid.wgsl prep spawns K_DROP particles along each stream's path with its velocity there (a
  little scatter, more the longer it has fallen); particles.wgsl moves them with the flow model's gravity and
  no drag, so they keep to the arc — the sand grains' look (small motes, streaked along their motion on
  screen); gone where they meet ground or water. At the foot: splash (K_SPLASH) thrown up and out by the
  impact, and mist (smoke state 3: faint, white, swelling). All scaled by the particle ring (the low tier's
  16384: a quarter), none off a trickle.
- **The tick rate.** The particles stepped 1/60 s a tick at any rate (at ?simhz=30 everything flew at half
  speed): DT × simStep() now. The flow model runs FLOW_SUB 60 Hz substeps a tick at ?simhz=30|15 (a
  uniform buffer each) instead of refusing.
- **The lab.** The plug's breach digs three cells (its height) — at four a time it sank a ~20-deep shaft that
  took the pool's first seconds. Scene D: a bank of sand behind a concrete wall on a plateau like the pool's
  (its free sides at repose, so it lies still), for the sand's fall beside the water's.
  scripts/fallcompare.mjs (flow / old water / sand GIFs at 1x, time to the plain), scripts/fallstill.mjs
  (stills at times after the breach; --probe the streams drawn, LiquidSystem.probeStreams; --waterprobe).
- **Measured** (flowlab.mjs pool + freeze, desktop Intel Xe-LPG, low tier, GPU ms a frame). Awake: water
  passes 0.29 (flux 0.076, jets 0.039, depth 0.127, publish 0.012, prep 0.035) against 0.25 on the merged
  build before the change; lava 0.25 vs 0.22; particles-update 0.039 both; draw 0.72 vs 0.55 (the sheets and
  the spray). Freezing: everything asleep after ~3 min (35 s before) — the pool drains slowly now and the

## Round 84 — rivers at the atlas's steady state: held, drawn flowing, no simulation (rivers)

The user: "all generators make a steady state so when we arrive nothing is simulated until the player
interacts with it"; "rivers should flow downstream"; "Find the atlas level rivers and what watersheds
feed them … precompute the flow of those as a function of dryness. Then the actual simulation treats the
unperturbed river basin as a steady state with no actual simulation and flow as strictly a render
artifact computed at the atlas level"; "we can have a tolerance and decide when we are close enough to
steady state to freeze"; "keep the flow proportional and then zero out when they get too low".

Why: a generated river wasn't the pipes' steady state. Springs along its middle fed 0.0008 a step; the
pipes carry a flow set by the level's fall, not by depth, so the deep generated channel drained to a
film within the level's 30 s warmup (the sim's window holds 2,086 cells³ of river where the generator
made 7,378), and woken again it moved on (riverrest, wake all: 1,912 of 2,691 wet columns changed in
5 s, −6 %). The perf agent's hold (sources topped to the generated depth) flooded the banks.

What (`?rivers=table`; `sim`, the default, as before; `hold`, the perf agent's, for comparison):
- **The table, at the atlas** (rivers.ts): each node's discharge is its watershed's — RIVER_RUNOFF
  (0.002) cells³ a step for each texel drained through it (the drainage tree's accumulation, less where
  the latitude is dry) — and its speed that over the channel's wetted section (the carve's parabola
  filled to 0.3 under the level), square-rooted so a brook still moves, up to 2.5× where the level
  falls fast (rapids). Node word 7. Stats on the default atlas: speeds 0.06 / median / 0.8 cells a
  step (riverStats.speed); the pipes' own steady surface slope for that discharge is a small share of
  the level's fall (riverStats.pipeSlope) — the pipes can't carry the river the atlas has at its slope,
  which is why the flow is a render artifact and not the pipes'.
- **Per column, when the land is made** (compose.wgsl riverAt → Ground.rvel, rd → ColG → forms.wgsl
  colFinish → ColOut's spare words → atlas.ts landFrom): the flow along the river's segment and the
  depth, into a new contract texture `riverFlow` (world-gpu.ts: xy flow, z the column's depth, w the
  river's depth at its line), kept with its region by the streamer. No springs. Banks: the ground just
  outside the channel (0.95–1.9 half-widths) raised to the level where it lay up to 12 under it (a
  levee), so the river holds what it carries; where the bed steps down 1.5 or more the way the river
  runs, its water is a 0.2 sheet poured over the step (fast: foam), not a pool to empty down it.
- **Held** (riverheld.wgsl, in water_flux, water_depth, renderfields): a river's column asleep, or at
  the window's edge (where the river comes in from the unsimulated world and goes on out), is the
  table at the rivers' wetness — its depth eased to it (2 % a step), its flux the pipes' steady flux
  for its levels (so what's awake beside it is fed as the river would feed it, and drains into it) —
  and is drawn flowing by the table's flow (renderfields: flow × depth, as the pipes' net flow).
  Woken (an edit, a power, a storm), the pipes run it; with `?riverpull=x` (0.02 by default with the
  table) its column is pulled toward the table x a step: what comes down from past the window keeps
  coming, a breach is fed and the river runs on past it. The renderer draws a woken river's column
  with the table's flow (as deep as it still is) plus the pipes' own.
- **Dryness** (weather/riverwet.ts → Globals ocean.y): 1 is the land as made; the season (wettest at
  the thaw) and the storms raining move it, followed over ~20 s. The frozen pattern scales with it, no
  simulation: at the line the depth × wet^0.6 (the level shifted with it across the channel, at most
  0.28 over), the flow × wet^0.4; under 0.03 a dry bed. `?riverwet=x` holds it.
- **Settled, then frozen** (`?settletol=x`, 0.01 by default with the table): water_depth.wgsl keeps,
  per chunk, the most a column's water changed in a step (`waterChange`, atomicMax of the f32's bits);
  the level reads and clears it twice a second, and a woken chunk whose time is up stays awake while
  it's over the tolerance (60 s at most) — then sleeps, its last flux the animation, the river's
  columns back to the table.
- The atlas level's warmup (1,800 ticks, all awake) doesn't run the water with the table: the land
  comes in at its steady state (the warmup had drained it before anything slept). `?settle` is off by
  default with the table (`?settle=1` to settle land as it comes in).
- Without the field mesh (the phone) the flow's heading reaches the water too: renderfields packs it
  in w (1/1024 turns in the whole part, size/8 in the fraction; render.wgsl flowOf), so the streaks
  and the foam run down the river there as well. With the table, foam goes by the water's speed (flow
  over depth), not its net flow — a deep river carries a lot without being fast.

Measured (scripts/riverrest.mjs: an atlas river found on riverNodes — temperate, 5–8 half-widths, not
at its mouth — the level walked in with settle=0, every chunk asleep, then woken with no edit; wet
columns over the sea, |Δdepth| > 0.05 in 5 s; node at 3884,13288):

| | river held at | wake all: river cols changed, volume | wake an event (r 40): near, window |
|---|---|---|---|
| sim (before) | 2,086 cells³ (drained in warmup) | 1,912 of 2,691, −6.3 % | — |
| table, warmup ran unheld | 18,673 (spilt onto banks) | 16,417 of 18,960, −19.9 % | — |
| table + levees + still warmup | 7,378 | 3,979 of 4,522, −28.9 % (reaches above falls empty) | −6.3 %, −0.65 % |
| table + riverpull 0.02 | 7,378 | 4,121 of 4,542, −13.5 % | −2.0 %, +0.12 % |

The breach (riverrest --breach: a trench dug across the bank): it fills from the river and the river
runs on past it (shots84/pull-breach-*.png). driveprofile at q=low, 20 s: p95 10.7 ms (sim) vs 10.4
(table); water-flux + water-depth ≈ 0.05 ms a frame either way.

Open: a woken reach above a fall still empties down it (the pipes have no weir: flux over a lip is
the head difference, not the critical flow) — the pull holds it; the channel's deep middle shows its
silt bed as a grey stripe through the water; the watershed's discharge doesn't yet reach the sea's
mouths' look; `?settletol` reads `waterChange` per chunk by index, not moved on a slide.

## 2026-10-26 — round 85: the sim isn't dispatched over what sleeps (branch `simcull`)

The user (round 85): "only simulate things that need it and the whole point of the laminar flows (steady state)
and scalar drop is it limits how long we need to simulate and lets us cache simulation results … to avoid
dispatching for dead things I think it makes sense." The hybrid's measurement had ~3.5 ms of the phone's frame in
the rest of the game, the sim's kernels among it: they skipped sleeping chunks but were still dispatched over the
whole streamed window (256 x 256 columns, 256 chunks), every thread reading the mask and returning, and the
ping-pong fields copied their whole buffers back each tick (untimed: copies aren't passes).

- **What changed** (sim/cull.ts): Simulation.step makes, on the CPU from the same Globals.sleep and drowse masks
  the kernels read, the list of chunks live this tick (awake, drowsy, or on a `?flowhz=` flow's slow turn). The
  passes with an asleep branch (structure, edit, water, oil, lava flux and depth, sediment and its outflow,
  contamination, moisture, fire, wilt, ecology, climate; surface with sleepmore) are compiled with a wrapper entry
  that finds its columns from the list, and dispatched over it: four 8 x 8 workgroups a live chunk, nothing at all
  when none is. Their copies back run over the same list. The CPU knows the count when it encodes, so no indirect
  dispatch or GPU compaction was needed (the simplest thing). A sleeping chunk is then exactly what its asleep
  branch made it: the current buffers untouched; only the next buffers, which nothing else reads, go stale.
  Steady-state water still looks flowing: the frozen flux isn't touched, the render reads it as before.
- **Correct, bit for bit:** scripts/culltest.mjs (new). The atlas at rest, a flood and a fire set by the camera
  (26 chunks wake), then all asleep again. Read 4 s apart while asleep, water, flux, fire, veg, moisture, contam,
  lava and oil don't change in a single column; the chunks never woken (nor next to one) hold what they held
  before the flood; the flood's water stays; 3 574 columns still flow. Water's volume after the same flood is
  3648.8 with and without culling. With `flowhz=water:4,lava:2,sediment:1` (the slow-turn lists) both modes drain
  alike (3614.6 vs 3613.3). atlasworldtest 6/6, worldapitest 16/16, craterbench (30 craters, p95 10.2, worst 29)
  pass with it.
- **Measured** (driveprofile, low tier, 412 x 915, desktop iGPU, on places with the hybrid; ride 18/s 15 s, idle
  at rest 12 s; off/on interleaved; before the rivers merge; GPU ms a frame, all passes over the run / frames resolved; the GPU's clocks
  drifted between pairs, so compare within a pair):

| pair | GPU off | GPU on | sim passes off | sim passes on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ride 1 | 8.23 | 7.75 | 1.205 | 0.907 |
| ride 2 | 7.53 | 7.22 | 1.049 | 0.844 |
| idle 1 | 7.08 | 6.30 | 1.069 | 0.740 |
| idle 2 | 7.24 | 6.78 | 1.047 | 0.831 |
| ride (before hybrid) | 4.23 | 3.97 | 0.629 | 0.484 |
| idle (before hybrid) | 3.85 | 3.38 | 0.611 | 0.422 |

  Riding, the culled passes go from ~0.35 ms a frame to ~0.04 (structure 0.055 → 0.019 for the land coming in
  drowsy, water-flux 0.022 → 0.003, lava-depth 0.047 → 0.002, the rest 0 to 0.001); the copies back that are
  left cost 0.004. The frame's GPU span falls more than the passes (0.3–0.8 ms) because the whole-buffer copies
  (seven fields, ~3 MB a tick) are gone too. One pass got dearer: lava-prep 0.012 → 0.03 (it now reads the lava
  buffer cold, no lava-depth before it to warm the cache). On a phone the same work scales with its weaker GPU.
- **Rivers (after merging places with `rivers=table` the default):** a held river's columns are simulated asleep
  (riverheld.wgsl: the depth relaxes to the atlas's table at the rivers' wetness, the flux follows; at the window's
  edge always), so the water can't be culled by the sleep mask alone. Tried: a list of the live chunks plus every
  chunk with a river (39 of 256 on the ride's start), made on the GPU each tick from the riverFlow texture and

## Round 87 — the collapse on a real tower: what held it up (collapse)

Why: the user on the phone (DECISIONS round 87): a tower with its base destroyed stayed standing; "Why do cells
matter here? Shouldn't we care only about columns?" Found by reading the paths, then checked with the regression
scripts/towertest.mjs (below):

- The heat beam bores through rock in lava.wgsl with no edit event: nothing told the integrity system. Now the
  level judges the beam's spot as a cut every 0.25 s while it's held (Integrity.cutAt, at once).
- A spire taller than the window (the atlas's spires reach 120 cells; the window holds 248 with the ground
  mid-way): its top is Streamer.outside, drawn by the band, and never came down. A piece with a run at the
  window's top now takes the runs above it (Streamer.takeAbove, the band repacked: OutsideBand.packColumns),
  falls with them (written clipped to the window) and gives back what's still above the window where it lands
  (putAbove).
- Limits in runs, not cells: a hanging piece reaching MAX_PIECE (4096) runs is held only if something holds it;
  held nowhere it floods on to MAX_FLOOD (65 536 runs) and falls as far as followed. Rock freed under 8 cells
  of volume crumbles to rubble instead of staying where it was (floating). Rock that gives is cut out by its
  runs (fractional ends too), not as integer cells (which left slivers hanging).
- A structure going on past its analysis box was skipped silently (touchesEdge): now the box is looked at
  again twice the size (to 256).
- A bug from round 86's own last change: apply() built the pieces from the cell lists, so once the rock came
  as runs only it would have dropped them — now rock pieces and structure cells are both spawned.
- simcull (merged): a falling piece's chunks are woken every frame (touch), so they're live.

## Round 88 — the sea held over a raised window floor (`seawall`)

The user, on the phone at the atlas level (hybrid, rivers=table, simcull): "I did find what looks like a bug with
sea level where I saw a steep wall of water."

Looked for first (scripts/seawall.mjs: six coasts and river mouths, q=low 412x915, default zoom and 10; the window's
water read back and every wet column standing over a neighbour's level by more than 3 counted,
scripts/seawallprobe.mjs): where the window's floor is at 0 (oz 0, the usual at a coast) the window's sea and the
rings' agree (both world 90; Globals ocean.x = 90 - oz), no sea column stands over its neighbours, and the open
edges show no water face. The candidates in the brief (the seam, the hybrid grid, Renderer.openEdges, shore swell)
were not it.

The wall comes when the window's floor is over 0 by the sea — oz 32 or 64, which a warp picks at a coast with high
land and which the window slides to when the player walks up a mountain (Streamer.slideZ, the ground under the
camera over zMax - 40). Then the sea's floor near the shore lies under the window: those columns have nothing in
the window (sfCount 0). They came in dry (Streamer.cutRegion / reslice / slideZNow and Atlas.window zeroed the
water of any column whose top wasn't inside), and water_depth.wgsl emptied whatever ran into them each step
("what runs in falls on out of the window", round 69). The sea beside them, held at its level by the edge rule,
stood over the dry floor as a cliff of water: at 11600,18213 after one slide up (oz 32 -> 64, seaZ 26), 2404
columns cut off, none wet, 151 wall faces all at the sea's level, 26 tall. And they drained the sea into nothing.

The fix (the cause, both ends):
- layout.ts `waterInWindow(cut, oz, zMax, level)`: what of a column's water lies in the window — over its top
  there, or over the window's floor where its ground is under it, up to the water's level (world z: its ground's
  top plus its depth); nothing where its top is over the window. The four places that cut columns (Atlas.window,
  Streamer.cutRegion, reslice, slideZNow) use it: a column under the sea comes in, or keeps on a slide, the sea
  from the floor up (depth seaZ), and one that comes back inside on a slide down gets its depth over the real
  ground back (it was zeroed then too: wasTop was false for a cut-off column).
- water_depth.wgsl: a column with nothing in it drains what runs in only where there's no sea (Globals ocean.x
  <= 0, the -1e9 of a level without one); under the sea it's the sea's, full below the floor.
  (A hollow on land under the window's floor would hold water too, if the window's floor is under the sea's level
  there — the atlas has no dry land under the sea's level away from the sea, so it isn't seen.)

In the hybrid, a chunk whose land is past the window's floor is the rings' (round 86: the atlas's sea at 90, the
same level); the rest are the grid's, which draws the window's own water — now the sea over the floor where it
drew the dry floor beside the sea's wall.

driveprofile isn't the measure here: no GPU work was added (one comparison a column in water_depth), and the
CPU's cuts already walk every column. The repro (scripts/seawallslide.mjs: the atlas level at 11600,18213, q=low
412x915, the window slid up one tier as walking up the coast's mountain does, oz 32 -> 64):

| | columns cut off under the floor | of them wet | wall faces (> 3 over a neighbour) | the sea's level (window z) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before (places) | 2404 | 0 | 151 (all at 26, the sea's) | 26.04 |
| after | 2404 | 2404 | 0 | 26.04 |

Shots: C:/Projects/shots88/sea/slide-before-z5.png / slide-after-z5.png (the cut-off shore, zoomed in: the ragged
grey faces down the sea's edge are gone), -z2 at the phone's default zoom. The first survey (oz 0 coasts and river
mouths, nothing wrong there): before-*.png.

Perf: no GPU work added (one comparison in water_depth; on the CPU a few operations a column in the cuts, which
already walk every column).

Second wall found, not changed (BACKLOG W2): a rivers=table river held at its filled level over a macro hollow
deeper than the levee holds (RIVER_LEVEE 12): at 1040,13551 a river at 123.6 (the hollow's spill height, the
depression-filled level of findRivers) runs 12 wide over coastal ground at 101-118, its water 17-22 deep with no
banks — 167 wall faces. Either the hollow is filled as a lake to its spill level (needs the per-texel fill on the
GPU; where the fine ground lacks the macro rim it's a wall again) or the river runs on the hollow's floor (its level
the ground's + its depth past the levee's reach). The user's call.

## Round 90 — more of the atlas on the phone, and turning the view (`phonecam`)

The user, on the phone at the atlas level in sandbox mode: "can we increase the range of tiles that load and add a
button or bar to rotate the camera?" — and then "Maybe We can prioritize tiles close to the center of the screen but
load others late? And have a setting for how far out it will build?" (DECISIONS round 90).

**The range.** The streamed window's side (`?win=`, whole regions of 64) is now a setting: scenes/range.ts. `?win=`
wins; else the viewer's own choice (localStorage `reclaimed.atlasRange`, read and written in try/catch); else the
tier's default — 320 on the phone tier, 256 elsewhere. The bottom-left range button steps 256 → 320 → 384 and reloads
(the window's buffers are made with the level). Measured at q=low 412x915 on the desktop iGPU (the phone proxy):
scripts/driveprofile.mjs at 12304,5457 (speed 18, 30 s, the phone flags: hybrid, simcull, rivers=table) and
scripts/rangeprobe.mjs (the world's and the renderer's GPU buffers summed, the JS heap, 8 s after the level):

| win | p50 | p95 | p99 | worst | >50 ms | GPU ms/frame | draw | slide (last, ms) | load (s) | GPU buffers | largest buffer | JS heap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256 | 9.9 | 10.8 | 16.3 | 75 | 4 | 8.94 | 4.91 | 140 | 36 | 312 MB | 67.5 MB | 139 MB |
| 320 | 9.9 | 10.7 | 14.4 | 147 | 1 | 8.94 | 4.79 | 198 | 38 | 453 MB | 103 MB | 190 MB |
| 384 | 9.8 | 10.9 | 16.6 | 100 | 2 | 11.07 | 5.42 | 222 | 43 | 656 MB | 158 MB | 267 MB |

320 is the phone's default: the frame and the GPU's time are 256's (the hybrid draws the added land as heightfield
chunks), 1.56× the land in detail; one frame of 147 ms in the ride against 256's four over 50 (noise on one ride —
the slide itself is spread, a tile a frame). 384 costs 2.1 ms more GPU a frame, 656 MB of buffers, and its largest
buffer (158 MB) is past 128 MB — WebGPU's default maxStorageBufferBindingSize, which many phones' adapters stop at
(the desktop gives 2048): it stays a choice, not the default. The LOD rings and the far land already reach past what
the phone's widest zoom shows (the 16-cell ring is ~3000 cells across), so they're unchanged.

**Nearest first.** A slide brings in a strip of regions (5 at 320); each region's columns are made a tile a frame,
in the order asked (atlas.ts tileGate). The streamer now asks for them — and writes them — nearest the camera's
target first (Streamer.nearFirst, in prefetch and in the slide), so what's under the middle of the screen comes in
first and the strip's ends after, already spread over frames.

**Turning the view.** render/turn.ts `Turn`: steps of a sixth of a turn from the fixed view's π/4 (the hex lattice
looks the same from every one), eased on a critically damped spring (sub-stepped: a slow frame doesn't overshoot),
steps adding up while it eases; held past 0.3 s a button turns on continuously (1.6 rad/s) and stays where it's let
go. It writes `Camera.azimuth` (round 82's Orbit already turned it: the draw, the culling, the pick, the shadow box
(the field mesh's near rect from the view), the far land's press under the focus (`FC.eye`) and the rings were
already the azimuth's, not the fixed view's). The turn goes round the ground under the screen's middle (the target
is put there first: it was 7 over it, and the ground swung ~10 cells). Bottom left, clear of the tool panel (top
right) and the atlas buttons (bottom right): ↺ ↻ (52 px) and the range button; Q / E on a keyboard (not flying —
there they're down and up — nor with the place tool, whose E turns the model). With ?cutaway=1 a step is the Orbit's
goal (it owns the azimuth there). Coming back from the free camera the view faces the way the flyer looked.
scripts/turnshot.mjs (the buttons tapped at phone size, touch): the ground under the middle 119.2,102,117.4 at
45°, 105°, 165°, 225° and after a 1.2 s hold (307°); no errors. Shots: C:/Projects/shots88/phonecam/turn-0..3.png,
turn-held.png (320, the default), turn320-*.png (before the pivot fix).

Not changed: the window's edge still shows where the rings past it are pressed under the focus (P13/W3) — from

## Round 91 — names on the map, a compass, the edge of the land (`phonecam`)

The user, on the phone at the atlas level: "I think the map needs to show you names of place and a directional
compas for the way your are facing. I notice that I easily hit the edge of the loaded ground" (DECISIONS round 91).

**Names.** The map writes the world wiki's names — the ones the GM's stories use — because they're made by the same
code: on the map's first open the level runs gm/atlas-facts.ts `atlasFacts` on the live atlas and gm/wiki.ts
`buildWiki` on that (in Node from data/atlas's cache, the same function: all 7772 region names and the settlements
match data/wiki/seed1.json), and gm/map-names.ts turns the wiki into labels: each continent (at its land nearest the
circular mean of its regions, a torus), every region (seas and lakes their own kinds), every settlement by its size —
7917 labels, made in 59–62 ms on the desktop (14 ms of it the wiki in Node). The map doesn't make names: label
sources are a contract (api/map-labels.ts: a name, a kind, a world point, a weight), and the atlas's own lakes (merged
from `lakes`, named by the wiki since places cdf0d95) are labelled from `wiki.lakes`, shown while 14 px across (N7); the wiki's own lake regions are labelled already. The map styles each kind
(Georgia, cream on a dark halo like the sites' dots; seas and lakes italic blue, regions italic, continents spaced
capitals), shows a kind only in its zooms — metropolises always, cities to 3 texels a pixel, towns to 1.4, villages
to 0.7, regions/seas/lakes while they're 34 px across, continents while 40 px across and not closer than 0.6 — and
places them heaviest first, a label left out where it would overlap one already placed (the continents only avoid
each other: they're under everything), clear of the rose, the buttons and the note. The note says which region
you're in ("Haura Downs · 11916, 15437").

**The map was a mirror image.** The game's view is the world seen from above (screen right is the view's forward
turned clockwise: camera.ts screenDeltaToWorld), but the map drew world x to the right and y down — the world's
mirror: facing north (the map's up), a town on the screen's right was on the map's left. A compass would have made
that plain. The map is now drawn with world +x to the left (north −y the map's up, as before): the image flipped in
x, the hill shading's sun moved to stay in the upper left, pan and tap inverted to match.

**The compass.** ui/compass.ts, over the turn buttons: the needle is the map's north on the screen —
atan2(−cos az, sin az) clockwise from up (north (0, −1) against the view's forward (−cos az, −sin az) and its right
(−sin az, cos az)). Measured (scripts/mapnames.mjs, touch): az 45° → −45°, a ↻ tap → 105° → 15°, the compass tapped →
90° → 0°. A tap faces north (`Turn.face`, the short way round, eased; our call — a map app's habit; a turn step after
it goes back onto the sixths). On the map the player's dot has a wedge the way the view faces and the view's
footprint on the ground (the screen's corners), both turning with the view; a rose in the corner.

**The edge — measured first.** scripts/edgeprobe.mjs at 412×915 q=low, win 320, at 11956,15471: each frame the camera
target's distance to the window's edge, and a 9 × 19 grid over the screen (the ground plane at the target's height)
— how much lies past the window and how much on regions a slide has moved over but not written yet
(`Streamer.unwritten`, added for it). Panning (W held: ~150 cells a second up the screen, a brisk swipe) and the
drive at 40 cells a second (`?drive=40`, the hoverbike's stand-in: it zooms out with speed):

| run | target min to edge | view past the window | view on unwritten | busy | slides | slide ms p50 / max | p95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pan, before | 45 | 52.4% | 3.0% (max 9.4%) | 67% | 62 | 174 / 387 | 18.4 |
| pan, after | **64** | 52.4% | 3.5% (max 9.4%) | 91% | 64 | 280 / 495 | 18.0 |
| pan turned 105°, before | 54 | 59.1% | – | 80% | 57 | 271 / 493 | 14.6 |
| pan turned 105°, after | **88** | 59.0% | 1.6% | 47% | 62 | 117 / 310 | 14.8 |
| drive 40, before | 108 | 65.8% | 0.3% | 7% | 13 | 106 / 207 | 10.5 |
| drive 40, after | 106 | 65.7% | 0.6% | 15% | 13 | 229 / 288 | 10.7 |

("before": the turned row the old build on its own server, the others this build with `&lead=0` before the clamp;
the slide times vary run to run by 2×.) What it says: **the edge is in view all the time, not only when moving.** At
the phone's zoom (2.6) a portrait screen sees ground ~158 cells across and ~700 along the view (the 2:1 view

~3 a second needed): the camera ran to 45 cells of the edge.

**What changed.** (1) The camera is kept a region (64) in from the window's edge (level.ts: the target's clamp was
the window itself): a pan faster than the slides waits for them there, the middle of the screen always on built land
(min 45 → 64; turned, 54 → 88). (2) The streamer follows the camera's motion (`Streamer.vel`, smoothed over a quarter
second): the land where it'll be a second on (`?lead=`, 0 the old way) is asked for ahead — the next strip, and the

drive's winding road it slid 30 times to 13 (back at each bend) for no nearer edge. (3) The rings' ground past the

after p95 10.7, p99 13.7, GPU 9.01 ms (noise). No new GPU buffers; the labels are CPU (~8k small objects).

## Round 88 — no floating rock (`collapse`)

Why: the user on the phone (DECISIONS round 88): "It still fails to make some unsupported structures wake up and fall
though. So worth testing on a wider column and seeing if only parts of it fall"; "first step is fixing the floating
rocks". Test first: scripts/floatsweep.mjs (the atlas level, q=low, hybrid=1, 412×915) writes 31 structures into the
window's columns — towers 3/6/10/16 across × 10/40/100 tall, banded towers (soil, sand, concrete every few cells, as
the atlas's strata), concrete, stone on a concrete plinth, slabs on necks, bridges, an arch, an arm — mostly far from
the camera (heightfield chunks), cuts them partly and fully by the break tool's events, the meteor tool, the world
API's crater (a tank's or hero's shot), take, dig, the player's taps through the pointer, the heat beam and a great
meteor, and at the end counts on a fresh readback of the whole window every run with something solid in it and no
way to the ground (its own flood from the window's floor over overlapping runs). scripts/rockcpu.mjs does the same
for the judge alone on the CPU (random worlds, towers, slabs, bridges, random sphere cuts; `--judge` another
fracture.ts).

Round 87's code, measured: the sweep's subset left 107-381 runs floating (banded towers: only the part under the
first band fell; concrete towers, stone on concrete, a slab: nothing or part); rockcpu failed 3 of 30 worlds. Found:

- Runs were the rock's alone, standing on *whatever* was under them: a band of soil or concrete in a tower held up
  everything above it, though the band itself hung free; the soil on a falling run stayed. Now a run is a column's
  touching intervals of every material (fracture.ts columnRuns); it stands only if it reaches the window's floor;
  runs hold each other sideways through intervals that hold (solid, plants) overlapping by half a cell (`joined`).
  Any hanging run with something solid in it is judged, so structures undercut fall the same way as rock.
- A pass threw (`next.get(...) is not iterable`, seen in the sweep's page errors) when a piece's flood reached runs
  an earlier, held piece had stopped at MAX_PIECE — everything after it in that pass went unjudged, and the runs
  short of it were taken as a piece of their own. A piece joined to one judged held is held now.
- A piece held nowhere stopped at 65 536 runs and fell as far as it was followed: now it's followed to its end.
- The pass reads back only the chunks round its seeds; a wide piece reaching past them was judged on columns
  the CPU's copy last saw long before (and a fall writes those columns back). Now such a piece is left, its
  chunks read and it's judged again at once (Fracture.need / undecided, Integrity.needChunks; `rereads` in stats).
  A read that comes back after a slide doesn't count as a look (the seeds were spent on it).
- The rock pass runs before the structures' boxes, so it takes what hangs free whole first.
- The break tool, the dig and the meteor woke structures into physics bodies, pinned at the foot (towertest's
  concrete tower: 15 taps): now they cut the ground as for stone, and the pieces fall as the columns' own.
- A great meteor's window edit changes columns with no event: they're seeds now (Integrity.cutCols).
- A piece that caught up with one falling under it landed on it mid-air, ground again up there when the lower
  one fell on (the sweep's slab on a one-column neck, split in four): it rides down on it now (ColumnBodies).
- After a meteor, crusts of basalt and films of stone a few hundredths thick floated over slivers of air: the
  sediment pass let loose ground run out sideways (an exposed face, sediment.wgsl spill) from under what lay on
  it. Loose intervals under something solid (through the loose ones between) stay put now; the meteor's rim and
  the beam's bore are also judged once a second while they melt and set (Integrity.watch, 15 s / 6 s).

Measured after (desktop iGPU, D3D11): floatsweep 31/31, 0 floating runs in the window before and after the sweep
(each case settled in 2.6-6.5 s, 17.7 s with a meteor's watch); rockcpu 150 worlds × 60 cuts with none left
floating, the judge's slowest call 6 ms; the slowest pass in the sweep 12-15 ms (a 14-across, 70-tall banded tower
cut through: 178 columns × 10 runs), typical 0.1-5 ms. towertest 5/5 (spire 69 ms, wide 80, concrete *one tap*,
71 ms, meteor 94, tall 59). driveprofile (q=low 412×915, 25 s): p50 9.9 → 9.8 ms, p95 10.6 → 10.6, GPU 7.89 →
8.06 ms a frame (noise: sediment 0.05 → 0.06). GIFs: C:/Projects/shots88/collapse/before-wide-banded.gif (a
12-across, 45-tall tower banded with soil, tapped through at its foot: only the part under the first band falls,
the rest stays in the air) and after-wide-banded.gif (all of it comes down). The heat-beam case didn't bore through
headlessly (nothing cut, nothing floats); its path is towertest's and round 87's. Open: BACKLOG C13 (GPU-made
changes elsewhere — a volcano's flows — aren't judged).

## 2026-10-27 — round 88, `runstory`: a run story played as a hero (`?run=bell`)

Why: the user (round 88): "I would like to try spawning as a character like in hoverbike and talking to people or
going places or fighting things for a run story." The slice: a hero on foot on the atlas level, the GM's Bell
story staged near the spawn, its cast as units, talks, objectives, a fight, death ending the run. Each piece sits
behind a contract, so the hoverbike game's heroes and the settlements' GPU agents can replace the stand-ins.
ARCHITECTURE "A run story as a hero"; docs/HEROES.md is the hoverbike session's handoff.

- **The hero** (contracts/hero.ts `Hero`; hero/walker.ts). It walks the world API's ground at the drawn
  mesh's height. Climbs are judged on the columns' own tops half a cell ahead, because the smooth mesh rounds
  a wall's foot into a ramp a stride at a time could walk up (the first browser run walked over every wall).
  A tap's goal is reached by A* (hero/path.ts): a 1-cell grid of column tops, a step over 2.5 impassable,
  cells beside a wall costing more so the way keeps to the middle of a doorway. The path is then pulled
  straight along lines a body's width clear. Without it a tap across a walled room hung on the wall: the
  browser run stuck in the reeve's hall. Its sword hits every hostile in a 70° arc, turning to the nearest
  first, so a tap on a phone hits without aiming.
- **The controller** (hero/touchpad.ts). A floating stick where the thumb lands, view-relative. A tap is a
  person (walk up and talk, or go and fight one who's hostile) or the ground (walk there). ⚔, a "Talk to …"
  button and the health bar go where a thumb reaches; WASD / Space / E on a desktop. It sits under the rest of
  #ui, so the level's pan, gust and tools never see its pointers. The sandbox editor is hidden during a run.
- **The camera.** StoryCamera.follow on the hero, zoom 14 (it was 8, which made the hero a speck on the phone
  screenshot), and Orbit.prefer behind its heading (35°, firm past 80°) while it walks. A talk frames the
  speaker, as before.
- **Units** (contracts/units.ts, src/units/simple.ts; 2745211) and their figures (units/figures.ts): a few
  voxels each, written from the CPU into a buffer drawn by Renderer.addVoxels, the hurt flash through the
  body glow bits.
- **The stage** (story/stage-gen.ts, D10). Each location goes toward its real spot on the atlas: s139 for
  Mebe, the region centres for the ford (2341, the spawn's own) and the barrow (2159). The distances are
  pulled in from 0, ~700 and ~800 cells to 22–95, so the run is a few minutes on foot. The rooms are laid
  out along the brief's connections, away from the player, all within the window. Walls get doorways (≥ 3
  cells; the first try's 1.4 was too narrow for the path grid); locks plug the far room's door (bone for the
  bone door). Landmarks are matched by keyword: the bell on its post, the mill wheel, stepping stones, a ring
  of logs for the oaks, the carts, the dam, the Teeth of Kaudru as three stone spires behind the barrow. The
  stage's 249 edits land before the run starts (it waits for the queue to drain: the world takes four a tick).
- **StoryPlay** with units: the cast are units, and their badges follow them. `killed` is noted when a unit
  dies; rooms note `reached { location, room }`. A lock opens when the hero comes to it with the key. Only
  the plug's columns are taken (`take`): a `dig` there took the floor too and left a pit too deep to climb
  out of, which stuck the walk back. Spawns appear as units round the speaker or in the place's way in.
- **Story contract (additive):** `Outcome.spawn[].hostile`, and `Outcome.hostile` (the cast members who turn on
  the player). The Bell story's walking dead are `hostile: true`, and the Bellwarden's `n-fight` lists
  `hostile: ["bellwarden"]`. storycheck and validate accept and check both; storycheck: ok.
- **The window is held still during a run** (Streamer.auto off, after the camera has settled at the spawn).
  The first browser run's places were built while the window slid round the spawn (it sat 43 cells off the
  window's middle), and every queued edit landed a region off. A run over the streamed world is BACKLOG RS9.
- **The fight's numbers** (herotest, flat ground): the hero has 20 hp and swings 1 a blow every 0.5 s; the
  walking dead have 2 hp and the Bellwarden 12 (2 a blow); a unit's wind-up is 0.45 s and a blow lands if
  still in reach. Swinging, the Bellwarden and four dead fall in 6.7 s with the hero at 14/20. Standing
  still, the hero falls in 15.3 s. A unit's flinch no longer cancels its wind-up: the hero's swings stunned
  everything and it took 0 damage.

Measurements:
- scripts/runtest.mjs, the atlas level at q=low, 412×915, through taps, the dialog's buttons and the swing.

## Round 90 — the atlas owns its lakes (`lakes`, BACKLOG W2)

The user, on W2 (a rivers=table river held at 123.6 over ground at 101–118 at 1040,13551, 167 wall faces): "For the
rivers why does the river height lie above the dip? Is it because the river exits going higher? If so can we
compute that the region is flooded at the atlas level?" Yes: findRivers's priority flood fills every hollow to the
height it spills out at, and a river's level is that filled level; only the river's own columns were given it, so
its water stood over the rest of the hollow (and the levee, RIVER_LEVEE 12, couldn't raise banks that far).

What changed:
- rivers.ts: from the fill, each 8-connected component of texels whose filled level is over the ground by LAKE_EPS
  (0.25; less is a flat the flood only tilted) is a lake when its water would stand LAKE_DEPTH (2.5) deep and
  LAKE_CATCH (30 dryness-weighted texels) drains into it: level the spill height (its lowest filled level), the
  outlet the rim texel it spills over, rivers in and out, its regions (`AtlasLake`). A river's level in a lake is
  the lake's; in a hollow too shallow or dry for one, the floor's (it follows the floor). Lava stops at a lake.
  Per texel a u16: the lake's id + 1, LAKE_IN set inside, unset on its rim (land texels within LAKE_RING 2 whose
  filled level is near the lake's — not the valley past its outlet; a texel two rims reach is the higher lake's).
  Seed 1: 813 lakes (median 14 texels, the biggest 11115 — 100 texels across), 176 deeper than 10, 327 with a
  river in; +~35 ms to findRivers (435–505 ms in all).
- The table and the ids go after the river nodes in riverBuf (the crater block's words 1 and 2 say where; 0
  none), so no new binding. compose.wgsl `lakeAt`: of the four texels round a point, the lake most of them are
  inside of and how much (bilinear). Over half: `Ground.lkw`, its water may stand there. Less: its rim — the
  ground raised to a bank LAKE_BANK (0.4) to 1.9 over the level, before any river cuts it. The bank is what makes
  a wall impossible: every column next to one where the lake's water may stand is either under that too or at
  least 0.4 over the level. Rivers: none cuts a channel or valley under a lake's water (the trench filled with
  what slid down its sides and the water stood over it); one lower than the lake (past its outlet, to the sea)
  doesn't cut the bank where the lake's water is near.
- colFinish (forms.wgsl): every column with `lkw` under the level gets water to it — form tops and holes too (a
  crystal's top under the water stood dry, a wall round it); no lava-tube skylights under a lake; silt under the
  water, but no loose cover on a steep bed (slope ≥ 0.8: the sediment slid down into the hollows at once and the
  water over them stood a few cells over the lake); sand at the waterline where flat (a beach, slope < 1.2), the
  rock bare where steep. Wet margins (moisture 0.8).
- A lake's water is not a river's: no riverFlow, nothing held to a table — still water, asleep as the land comes
  in (its steady state, settle off with rivers=table), simulated where woken like any other. (Tried first: held
  like a table river, then carried as is where held. A held column feeds what's woken beside it the pipes'
  steady flux for its level and keeps its own water: a woken chunk next to held lake columns stood 20–48 deep
  over the lake's level.)
- The far rings (lod.wgsl), the atlas viewer (view.wgsl) and the atlas map (api/atlas-map.ts) draw lakes; sites
  keep out of a coarse cell more than half in a lake (wet sites 11 → 6 of 140); the wiki names them
  (`WorldWiki.lakes`, "Lake/Mere/Water/Loch <name>", "Tarn/Pool" for small ones, in the land's tongue; the
  markdown lists those near the start); contracts/world.ts `Lake` and `lakeFlood` (a lake as the flood it is:
  its regions, its level — RegionState-compatible). AtlasFacts gets `lakes` (the data/atlas cache needs
  `node scripts/worldwiki.mjs --pull` again to carry them).
- `?lakes=0`: found but not realised (the A/B's before).

Measured (scripts/lakeprobe.mjs: q=low 412x915, the atlas level, 35 s after load; a wall face is a wet column
standing more than 3 over a neighbour's level, wet or dry, not counting a sheet over a fall's lip; the W2 spot,
the 8 biggest lakes at their middle and their outlet):

| spot | before (`lakes=0`) | after |
|---|---|---|

| lake 493 middle (123.25, 21 deep) | 747 | 0 (64409 of 64490 wet columns at its level) |
| lake 220 middle (109.71, 40 deep) | 2005 | 0 |
| lake 669 middle (a dry hollow before: no river through) | 0 | 0 |

## 2026-10-27 — rounds 88–89 (session 5, `settlements`): settlements with agents working round them

Why: the user, round 88: "I would like to see settlements with agents working around them"; round 89: quarry,
felling, hauling and building as the first jobs, farming and houses bringing more people, "vegetation and
settlements should work similarly … fields with intensity and maybe some material", settlements by rivers and
resources, quarries and mines "built into the ground/hills in ways that look cool". Round 83 asked that the
settlements use the city game's data structure; round 85 gave the grids (Townscaper's, Voronoi on contours,
Bulwark's rings).

- **Records** (src/settle/records.ts). The wiki is built live from the atlas (`buildWiki(atlasFacts(atlas))`, the
  same code scripts/worldwiki.mjs runs), so a settlement's id (`s<n>`), name, region and realm are the ones the
  GM's stories use. A civ profile by the realm's era and the site's setting (data/recipes/civs.json); seed 1 has
  only medieval realms, so where the Ashwrights (industrial) work the land a town is a foundry town, and half the
  cliff cities are the keepers of old law's — until the GM's eras say otherwise. A quarter stand over an older
  ruin; raiders camp by some (the region's hostile power when there is one, else outlaws).
- **Grids** (src/settle/grids.ts, R6). Every style makes lots; every lot is cut the same way (a ring of yard
  quads, then the inset polygon centre-to-midpoints), so each district is a `CellGrid` the existing `Town` builds on
  — walls, floors, doors, windows and roofs from the neighbours, unchanged. Yards between lots are the alleys the
  agents walk. `Town` now takes a grid (the interface is TownGrid's own members).
- **Arrival** (Atlas.landHooks, plan.ts). The first region of a settlement's box to be made plans it on the raw
  ground of the whole box, once; each region of the box is stamped from the plan as it comes. So the buildings are
  real matter in the columns from the first frame (water, fire, collapse and the agents' surfaces all see them),
  frozen and thawed with the land, and the same whichever region arrives first (settletest: the same seed plans
  the same columns). Planning all 140 sites on made-up ground: ~21 ms each in Node (the growth field and the
  quarry's search are most of it).
- **The field** (src/settle/field.ts, round 89). A settlement is a growth field over its box: intensity and a kind
  (its style) per 3-unit cell, the ecology pass's shape (grow toward suitability, spread along what suits, colonise
  from strong neighbours, a stronger kind takes over where it suits better). Suitability: flat dry ground, more
  near water, rock and the woods. Grown from the middle for as long as the town has stood (by its size); civic
  buildings at the middle, houses on the lots where it's past 0.35, taller where it's stronger; the next two lots
  are houses still to build, the rest wait for it. In play it steps every 8 s while the grain lasts, and opens the
  strongest free lot when nothing's being built.
- **Quarries.** A terraced pit (benches every 2.2 cells in, a ramp down one side, a crane at the rim) or, where a
  hill rises within 10 cells, an adit: the forecourt cut level, a tunnel 3 wide and 2.9 high under the rock that
  stays over it (ColumnPlan.hole), timber posts at its mouth; a spoil heap of rubble beside either.
- **Units** (src/units/agent-units.ts): the runstory branch's `Units` contract on the GPU agents. Jobs are groups
  and fields; per-unit goals share three goal fields by where. Hostiles hunt what's in their sight (the agents'
  targets), the GPU's swings come back as damage; guards strike on the CPU. The agents needed: 12 fields (the
  rounds want one a leg), 48 seeds, `spawn({ hp })`, a work pose (`workPose`: the figure bent forward, a tool in
  front — the user wanted to see them "look when working"), unseeded fields cleared once instead of rewritten
  every sweep, and an idle pass that does nothing (no units, nothing seeded: no peel, no sweeps — the atlas level
  paid for the peel with nobody on it).
- **Life** (src/settle/life.ts). Each role a round, each leg a field: miners take the quarry's floor exactly and
  heap it, woodcutters fell real trees and heap the logs, builders carry from the heaps to the site where every
  1.2 cells³ a block stands (a `Town` over the site's lot in window coordinates through the town stamp; each
  cell's floor fixed relative to the door's ground, so the grid can be made again when the window slides without
  the house jumping onto its own roof). A finished house is a Building + Instance and four more people. Farmers
  carry sheaves to the granary. A raid: the camp marches on the plaza, workers run home, the guards meet it.
- Tests: scripts/settletest.mjs (the planner through its API, no browser: all four grid styles used, every
  settlement with homes, a hall, a store, fields; ruins adapted with their history; nothing built in a pond; the
  same seed the same plan; `--png` top views), scripts/settlementtest.mjs (in play: the town, its people, the cost,
  the raid; screenshots and GIFs).
- **First run in play** (scripts/settlementtest.mjs, the atlas level at the phone tier: q=low, 412×915, the hybrid
  on; `?town=1` the nearest town to the spawn with a camp — Rudag, s42, river guilds, irregular core + radial
  homes, over a ruin): the records in 58 ms at load, the town planned once in 49 ms on 16 raw tiles, 1,455 columns
  stamped; 36 people out (budget 28 + the camp's 7 raiders). Standing at the town for 15 s: frames p50 9.7 ms,
  p95 11.3 ms; the GPU 5.6 ms a frame, the agents' pass 0.95 ms of it (sweeps 2 on the phone tier). A raid of 7
  against 4 guards: repelled, all 7 raiders dead and 4 of the town's. Fixes it found: `?settle=0` was already the
  phone tier's flag (the streamer's settling; phone-flags.ts), so the system's off switch is `?towns=0`; a sheaf
  can't be a carried load (leaves aren't ground: it's drawn as sand); a river town's site is on its river, so its
  middle moves to the nearest dry level ground beside it; a quarry outside its own region had no rights and the
  miners stood idle — the quarry is now sought in its own region first.
- **Seen working, and the cost** (three more runs, Rudag at the phone tier). Over a run: ~2.7 cells³ quarried,
  3.2 of logs felled, 2.4 heaped, 1.7 brought into the house going up (its first block stood); a raid of 7 against
  4 guards repelled each time (7 raiders and 3–4 of the town dead). The workers were in the shots but hard to
  see: a 1-cell figure in canvas colours at the phone's half resolution is a few pixels against plaster and grass —
  now 1.4 cells tall in a yellow tunic (guards in steel, raiders in brick red), and the close-ups at 6–9× the
  default zoom; a probe (40 spawned at the plaza, with the hybrid and without) confirmed they draw both ways.
  Cost at the town, 36 units: frames p50 9.7–9.9 ms, p95 11.3–11.6 ms, the same as the town with nobody out
  (`?townfolk=0`: 9.8 / 11.5) — the frame is vsync's; the GPU's own sum swings with its clocks (5.4–11.9 ms a
  frame, the agents' pass 0.95–3.5 ms of it, the same scene). The idle town (nobody out) seeded its fields
  anyway, so the agents' pass ran with no one to read it: nothing is seeded now when nobody's out. A new load

  conditions:

  - `reached` → the room or the place;

## Round 93 — the land past the window drawn the window's way (`fardetail`, BACKLOG N6)

The user, on main's option 5 (plants, roads and grass colour on the far land, baked once as 2D maps): "I'm also
curious about number 5 and it seems like that could be fairly cheap and fast and resolve much of the visual pop in on
its own" (DECISIONS round 93; round 91: "I easily hit the edge of the loaded ground").

**Measured first** (scripts/fdshot.mjs, new: q=low 412×915, the phone's zoom, a shot plain and one with the window's
edge drawn over it, and the seam's colour — 5 × 5 pixel means 4 cells either side of the edge, along it — at
11956,15471, the towns at 12176,15632 and 11632,16113, the drive's 12304,5457; straight and turned 105°). What
differed across the edge, biggest first:
1. **The grass.** The window's ground is grass by the plants its columns start with and its sim grows (a quarter
   cell green where its random is under the cover, each a little lighter or darker, flowers), lit by the day's sun and
   sky in linear light; the rings' was a region's top colour mixed 65% with one green, in sRGB, lit by a fixed sun — a
   dull olive blur (window grass ~(130,195,76), the rings' ~(122,126,95) in the shot).
2. **The near side pressed flat** under the focus's height (underFocus): turned, at a town, a white or green floor
   where the land falls away — the seam's |dLuma| 29.5 there.
3. **Ways**: none past the window (the atlas's roads stop at the edge), the window's are brick-paved.
4. **Water**: the rings' sea a saturated blue, the window's grey-teal with ripples and foam.
5. Trees (the window's boxes; none past it), towns (the window's plans; none past it), shadows.

**What changed.** All of it is baked where the rings already bake (lod.wgsl `lodHeight`: once a texel as it comes
into a ring — a camera move of 8 spacings makes only the new strips — and a band of a ring every 0.4 s); nothing new
runs a frame but the light. The slot stays 16 bytes: its last word, the rock's colour, is now the rock's material (its
albedo looked up: `farAlbedo`, a 64-entry uniform), **the plants the window's columns start with** (forms.wgsl
colFinish's rule exactly: the region's veg, the moisture, the woods' noise, its random; 0 under water, snow, an oddity,
set lava, over sea + 70; 1/60 a step) and **the distance to the nearest way** (0..3.2 world units: lod.ts `wayBins`
bins the atlas's 98 533 way points — roads, switchbacks, bridges and the plazas; not tunnels or lifts — into 64-unit
bins, each point in every bin within reach, a word a point; made once, 0.72 MB). The top's material is the window's
where it's wet (sand or silt by the sea, a lake's beach, a river's bed) and snow where it's freezing. The albedos moved
from a storage buffer to a uniform: the kernel was at WebGPU's 8 storage buffers, the ways take the place.
far.wgsl `ringWindowLook` draws it as meshdraw.wgsl meshShade does: the top's albedo in linear light with the window's
large-scale tint (meshTint, per vertex: the same noise and G.org) and its specks a cell; the grass by the plants
(meshShade's colours, its season turn, the painted tufts' shade, flowers), a quarter cell's pattern while a pixel is
under 1.5 cells, its average past that; paved ways (brick, edge antialiased from the distance's fwidth); water by its
depth over its bed (fsWater's colours, ~1.9× for its ripples and foam, a fleck a quarter cell); lit by render.wgsl's
lighting without shadows (the Globals' sun, its colour, the sky, the night: FarP.sun/sunCol/sky, set by the level a
frame — `FarLight`) and its haze, then sRGB. **Trees** where the plants are a wood's (vegplan.wgsl: v ≥ 3.6, 4.5% of
cells — here a 3-unit lattice square in three): no geometry — a crown drawn where it stands on the screen (a point h up
lands h / tan(elevation) further from the eye on the ground: the ground fragments that see it paint it, lit as a ball),
broadleaf or conifer, its shadow on the ground the sun's way; up to 25 lattice squares a pixel, only on a wood's ground.
**The window's sim greens its soil over** (65% reclaimed at the start: the shots' window is grass where its columns
started bare); the rings draw at least `?fdveg=` (1.6) on soil, silt and leaf litter — a judgement call: the window's

## Round 94 — the land past the window baked into a streamed texture, towns and all (`farbake`, BACKLOG FB1–FB6)

The user (DECISIONS round 94): "The draw distance is ok but I don't understand why towns and grass aren't baked into
a texture we can stream so that distant tiles draw correctly further out".

**What each band drew before this round, and from what** (the phone: q=low, hybrid, a 320-cell window):
1. **The window** (320 × 320 cells, ~277 world units a side round the camera): the streamer's columns — the atlas's
   full column build (atlas.ts `columns`: the ground, its forms, caves, the ways stamped, then the landHooks: the
   settlements' plans stamped in) — drawn by the field mesh and the hybrid's grid, with the sim's plants, real trees,
   houses, water, shadows and clouds.
2. **The rings** (lod.ts, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 world units between vertices; out to ±96, ±192, ±384, ±768, ±1536 round
   the camera): a grid each, a vertex baked once as it comes in (lod.wgsl: the atlas's ground function — `ground()`,
   the same one the columns start from, without the forms or caves — its top, colour, the plants the columns would
   start with, the distance to a way). Round 93 drew them the window's way **a fragment at a time** (far.wgsl
   `ringWindowLook`: the grass, the flowers, the paving, water, up to 25 painted tree crowns a pixel, the light).
3. **The far land** (far.ts, a 161² grid 32 units apart, ±2560, fading from ~1400): the atlas's macro heights and a
   colour a 16-unit texel made once on the CPU — the region kind's top colour mixed 65% with one green, white where
   it's freezing, the sea's blue — lit by a fixed sun. None of round 93's look: no ways, no grass shades, no woods,
   no towns.

**Why there were no towns past the window.** A settlement's plan (settle/plan.ts `planSettlement`) is made from
the *raw columns* of its box — atlas.ts `columns` + the ways, the full build the streamer makes, ~13 ms of a
desktop's GPU a 64² region (the DEVLOG's round 80 number) — and the box is 2–4 regions a side (a city's 186 cells:
16 regions, ~200 ms of GPU). So it was made only when the first of its regions arrived (Atlas.landHooks), and what
it builds exists only as columns stamped into that land. Nothing at the atlas scale held a town's shape: the rings and
the far land had nothing to draw it from. Planning every settlement that way up front is ~140 × that GPU work, and
the plan itself is 26–82 ms of CPU (measured below) — a phone's frame several times over, each.

**What changed.**
- **The bake** (atlas/bake.ts `SurfaceBake`, bake.wgsl `bakeSurface`): a clipmap — a level a ring, its texel half
  the ring's spacing (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 world units on the phone; 1, 2, 4, 8 off the hybrid), and one more for the
  far land (16 units) — each 512 × 512 RGBA8 texels round the camera in one 2d-array texture, anchored to the world
  (texel (I, J) at (I, J) · its size, in slot (I mod 512, J mod 512); sampled with `repeat`). A level is re-centred
  when the camera has moved 32 of its texels and only the strips new to it are baked; a band of 512 × 32 texels a
  dispatch, two a frame at most, the finest level's first; a band of a level again every 0.5 s (the coarse world's
  changes, the season). What's drawn of a level is only what's baked (its valid rectangle, far.wgsl `bakeAt`; the
  next level out where it isn't). A texel is **the window's look averaged over it, from the rings' rules**: lod.wgsl's
  per-vertex body is now `surfaceAt` (shared, unchanged), then meshShade's grass by the plants (the season's turn, the
  tufts' shade, the flowers' average; soil and silt at least `?fdveg=`), the ways paved (their cover over up to 4 × 4
  points of the texel), water by its depth, the woods (texels to 2 units: each crown seen from above, its shade round
  it, over the texel's points; coarser: their share), **and the stamps** — the towns' tops (below). Alpha says what it
  is (land with its grass's share, water, lava). The light stays a frame's: fsLod and fsFar light the baked albedo
  with render.wgsl's light and haze (round 93's `gLight`/`gHaze`); fsLod adds only the window's speckle a cell and
  the grass's quarter-cell grain where those are pixels across, and the rock's beds on steep faces (geometry). The
  ring melting into the next one out blends the two levels as it blends their heights. `?fb=0`: round 93's look made
  a fragment at a time (the bake isn't made).
- **Towns** (settle/settlements.ts `farPlans`, plan-worker.ts, raster.ts): every settlement within `?fbr=` (2600)
  world units of the camera is planned once, nearest first, one at a time, on **the atlas's own ground at the
  plan's resolution** — bake.wgsl `roughGround`: `surfaceAt` at each column's middle of its box (its top, the water
  on it, its top's material, the plants it starts with; one dispatch, 1.2 ms of GPU for a city's box) — with the ways
  stamped on it exactly as regionLand stamps them on the raw land (ways.ts `stampWays`; `waysNear` hands the worker
  only the bins it reads). The plan runs in a **worker** (the same planSettlement), rastered there (raster.ts
  `rasterPlan`: its columns' tops from above, a texel a world unit — roofs in the civ's colours, walls, the plaza,
  fields, the quarry's pit darker by its depth — a building's edge darker (its walls and eaves, so it reads from far
  away), the ground beside it a little shaded; and a 4-unit average), and the stamp comes back to be laid in the bake
  (`setStamps`: the ground under a new, changed or lifted stamp baked again). When a town's land arrives the window's
  exact plan is rastered the same way and replaces the far one (and their match is logged, `farStats.match`).
- **The far land** samples the far level (towns, grass, ways, woods, water, lit by the window's light) instead of
  the macro colour: "further out" is drawn the same way as the rings, to the far land's fog.

**How the rough ground matches the raw.** It is the columns' own starting function (compose.wgsl `ground`, the
mesa's lip, what's loose on it, the sea's, lakes' and rivers' levels, the ways stamped) — what it lacks is the atlas's
forms (rocks, arches, the lattice's pieces stood on the ground) and caves. Where a town stands (flat, dry ground by
the plan's own choice) those are rare. Measured on the drive (12304,5457, `&drive=18`, 90 s): the city s55 was far
planned, then its land came in and the window planned it exactly — **IoU 0.976** of their tops' cover (1-unit texels):
the window builds the town the bake drew.

**Measured** (the desktop iGPU; driveprofile q=low 412×915 at 12304,5457, speed 18, 30 s, everything in play):

| | `?fb=0` (round 93) | the bake |
|---|---|---|
| p50 / p95 / p99 / worst (ms) | 9.9 / 10.5 / 13.1 / 73 | 9.8 / 10.5 / 13.7 / 73 |
| draw (ms a frame) | 2.59 | **2.31** |
| GPU (ms a frame) | 4.64 | **4.36** |

## Round 92 — what holds rock up; the meteor-made floaters (`collapse`)

Why: the user (DECISIONS round 92) — a huge pillar top stayed up on a two-column leg after a meteor at its foot (a
hanging piece joined to any standing run was held whatever it weighed; round 83's span rule hardly ever fired),
with a design ("connected components of solid intervals then look at total solid support under an interval …
supports can be vertical or horizontal"), "where it breaks", tipping "now and we can add rotation later"; and
"one of my screenshots the column is actually floating with zero visible support … a bug in when we trigger the
logic". Then: "No it was meteor made floaters"; "I'm guessing it just never really tested with all the systems in
play and it's an oversight"; and a playground ("like the one used for waterfalls").

**The floater (test first).** scripts/meteorpillar.mjs: the atlas at the phone tier (q=low, hybrid=1, 412×915),
natural pillars found from the window's columns (a region of spires, `at=9894,12901`: pillars through the
window's top, the band) or a tower the world API builds; meteors at the foot through the pointer (meteorNow when
the pick can't reach it), several in a row, the camera far (heightfield chunks), CPU throttled 5× over CDP; the
ground truth (floatingRuns) after each and 30 s on, by world cell (the window slides under it); `--slide x|z` slides
the window away and back while what the meteor freed is falling. Without slides nothing floated, 40 s on, with the
rim's lava melting and setting — the magma hypothesis played no part (its one "floater" was the judge's, below).
With a slide, round 88's code left the tower in the air over the molten crater, 27 runs from 133 to 157 over ground
at 114 — the user's screenshot (C:/Projects/shots88/collapse2/before-meteor-slide.gif) — and nothing judged it
again. Every test had turned the streamer off (`stream.auto = false`). Cause: the falling pieces live in window
cells; the GPU's columns hold them mid-air at their offset. A slide in z reads the columns back and cuts them again
(the piece mid-air became ground) and then Integrity.clear() forgot it; a slide along x or y froze a leaving
region with a piece in it, and the pieces kept writing their old cells after the pages moved; the seeds, the rim's
15 s watch and the dirty boxes stayed in old window cells too. Now: Streamer.onBeforeSlide(dx, dy, dz) →
Integrity.settle lands at once every piece in the strip that leaves (all of them for a slide in z or a warp);
Streamer.columnsHeld (only while a slide in z or a warp reads the columns back and writes them again — a slide
along x or y moves them in one synchronous step) holds the integrity system (nothing falls or is judged);
onSlide → Integrity.slid moves the seeds, watches, boxes and the falling pieces (ColumnBodies.shift) with the land.
After: 0 floating either way (after-meteor-slide.gif: the tower lands in the crater); a slide in z holds 106 ms
(578 ms at 5× throttle), settling 1.1 ms; along x nothing waits and the piece falls on across the slide. Natural
spires, 3 meteors each at two pillars, far camera, slides in z, 5× throttle: 0 new floating runs (2 pieces fell,
64 cells crumbled).

**The judge's join rule** (the census of the window as made: 0 floating runs at the spawn, 12 on a mesa, 204 among
the spires, 401 in the highlands, all there from the first frame). The user doubted the generator made any, rightly
for most: 383 of the highlands' were thin tilted strata (under a cell thick) whose runs touch their neighbours by
0.47 < OVERLAP 0.5; and a column's overlapping intervals (the meteor's ejecta laid a hundredth into the soil) were
read as a run of their own, hanging. Now intervals touch when they overlap by half a cell or half the thinner one's
thickness (fracture.ts `touch`), and overlapping intervals are one run. Floating as made after: highlands 23,
spires 83 (mostly half-cell films), mesa 12 — seven of the mesa's are truly detached sandstone slabs 10 thick,
1.5–49 cells over the ground (BACKLOG C18: to trace to the form that made them; not dropped at generation, as the
user asked). The "islands dropped as land is made" try was reverted.

**Support** (fracture.ts ROCK, the material table's `bear` and `density`). A held piece is weighed:
- cross-sections from the far end in (its distance from what holds it): every part k or more steps out weighs
  cells × density against its joints to the runs k − 1 out (and what holds it), each strength × min(BEND h²,
  SHEAR h), h the overlap; BEND 3 (a slab a cell thick reaches 3 columns out: round 83's span), SHEAR 10 (thicker,
  10 whatever its thickness). The part most over gives there and falls (one break a pass: what's left is judged
  again). Summed across the part: the first try (each run handing its load on alone, as the user's "flood fill in
  from the edges") broke a slab's edge row for its own length;
- else the piece above its lowest point zc with the standing runs it's joined to above zc (followed NECK_R 16
  columns; past that, the map's edge, MAX_PIECE or a run an earlier flood found so: keyed into the land, held) on
  the standing columns under it: each bears CRUSH 300 × the least bear down its run (rock 1, concrete 0.8, steel
  0.85, soil 0.3, rubble 0.4, sand 0.15, silt 0.2, ash, litter, drift 0.1, snow, leaf litter 0.05). Heavier, or its
  centre of mass off their hull by more than TIP_GIVE 0.25, it gives: those columns crush to rubble from where it
  would land to zc, and it falls (straight: rotation is C4/C21). This is also the waist cut part way round (the
  core still standing: nothing hung free, nothing was judged);
- only a piece an edit changed is weighed: Integrity.cutSeeds, the columns the edit itself cut (a crater's bowl and
  rim, not its 30-cell ejecta; a landing; what crumbled), so the land as made stands; what floats is judged
  wherever it is. `Fracture.why` counts the reasons.

rockcpu.mjs's new cases (before → after): a big top on a 3-column leg falls (0 → 1512 cells), the same on a 44-column
leg stands, an arm 22 out snaps 1 column from the wall (round 88: the tip crumbled 10 out), one 6 out stands, a top
centred 6 off its leg tips (0 → 432) and centred stands, a waist with 4 columns left falls (0 → 4208), a nick stands,
the same nick over a sand band falls, a cave 20 across keeps its roof when its wall is holed. Round 88's judge fails
5 of them. The window judged whole as made with everything weighed (the worst case — in play only what an edit cut
is): spawn 0; badlands 1 piece (53 cells); a mesa 1 (249); the spires 10 broken by load and 3 tipped (~900 cells:
leaning spires); highlands 2.

**The rock lab** (`level=rocklab`, src/levels/rocklab.ts, scripts/rocklabgif.mjs): a flat plain, nine pieces 22 apart
by the camera (zoom 4.5): a top on a thin leg, the same on a wide leg, an arm off a wall, an arch, an off-centre top,

(two breaks at the leg: round 88 keeps the top up; now it falls).

Measured (desktop iGPU, D3D11): floatsweep 31/31, 0 floating before and after (streamer on; no slide in it);
