### Round 107 (`pages`): PG4 met — the ring computed, the own-page fast path; PG5's readback order

- **The own-page fast path.** A column's page is found once: common.wgsl colPlace keeps the invocation's own chunk
  and its place (the first asked for, or set by the cull wrapper from its list entry — entries now carry the page's
  place, cx | cy << 6 | px << 12 | py << 18), and a neighbour goes through the table only in another page. The draw's
  extra went (+0.29 -> +0.07 ms panning at 512), but the sims stayed slow.
- **Why: the table inside Globals.** scripts/kernelab.mjs (new: every sim kernel's dispatches replayed alone, timed
  in one pass, per workgroup, alternated 3-4 times against places — the frame's noise and its sleep's out of it).
  Weighted over the kernels, per workgroup, against places: the table in Globals (8 KB each way) +60 %; the ring
  computed with that 18 KB Globals +55 %; the table sized to the window (Globals 2.9 KB) +48 %; the ring computed with
  the Globals at their old size -4.5 % (data/bench/pg4-kernelab: logs5 the table and the ring with the 18 KB Globals,
  logs6 the ring with the Globals at their old size — an experiment build, logs7 the sized table, logs8 the ring as
  shipped; A = places). scripts/livecount.mjs (new) showed the awake chunks the same parked (~11-14 both). On this D3D11 iGPU a dynamically indexed array in the Globals slows every
  read of the Globals, and a large Globals costs on its own. So: **the game computes the ring** (`?pages=ring`, the
  default; the dense window's slots are the ring's places) and the Globals keep a vec4 a table (1952 B);
  `?pages=table` stays a test path only, for `?pageperm=`; P2.4's sparse table gets a binding of its own, a uniform
  or a storage buffer, never in Globals (PAGES.md §1 rewritten). M1's phone numbers for "table" carry the Globals
  penalty (PAGES.md M1, BACKLOG PG2).
- **PG5 — a contract fix.** WorldCore.readBuffer returns every per-column buffer in window order, but flux, oilFlux,
  lavaFlux and physCols weren't in COLUMN_BUFS, so they came back in the store's order: page-major since P2.2. culltest
  read flux that way and compared river columns' flux as other columns' (the "36 columns of flux changed in chunks
  never woken"). They're in COLUMN_BUFS now (pagetest's own conversion of them removed). culltest also reads through
  the contracts as they are since P2.3b and P2.2: the sleep bits by slot (core.ring.table), riverFlow through
  readTexture (a page atlas). Its check passes (flux 0); the two failures places has too ("the fire lit", plants
  changing asleep) are left.
- **The gate, ABAB** (framecost, places e8187b0 against pages, 4 alternated runs a cell; data/bench/pg4-abab-ring),

  | window, speed | places | pages | |

  | 256, 60 c/s | 4.88 | 5.00 | +2.4 % |
  | 512, parked | 9.74 | 9.69 | -0.5 % |

    the dying cyclones' dust, the particles' dust set down (`exchange`), litter torn off (wind); `waterOut`

## 2026-10-29 — the rivers' wetness per watershed (round 109, session 5, `watershed`)

- The user: "I want it per water shed please." The held rivers (`?rivers=table`, the atlas level's) rose and fell
  with one wetness for the whole world (weather/riverwet.ts: the season plus every storm's intensity, Globals
  ocean.w), so a storm anywhere raised every river. Now a river's wetness is the climate's (the season, eased, the
  same everywhere: ocean.w) plus its own storm water: the rain on its own catchment and what its reaches upstream
  carry, with lags, so a rise travels down the river (BACKLOG RWS1).
- One concern per structure:
  - atlas/rivers.ts `Catchments` (the data): the drainage tree already gives every texel the one it drains to; each
    texel's first river node down it, sampled every 2 texels (1024² Int32 on the 2048 map, 4 MB; the full-res
    basin is a build-time temporary), each node's own runoff (its samples', the latitude's dryness as `acc`), its
    reference discharge `ref` (own plus everything upstream: the graph accumulated in `order`, upstream first).
    Atlas.riverCatchments.
  - weather/catchwet.ts `CatchmentWet` (the sim): per node two linear stores — the hillside's runoff, eased toward
    RAIN (3) × the storms' rain (Weather.rainAt) on its own samples over LAG_S 20 s (the climate's lag), and the
    reach, eased toward its runoff plus its upstream reaches' outflow over the time the river takes to run to the
    next node (its distance over its reference speed, rivers.ts node word 7; 0.2 s at least). Its storm water is the
    reach's outflow over `ref` (1.5 at most). Storms rain only over the window, so only the nodes in the window and
    128 cells round it are kept (467 at the test spot of the 55 085), re-picked when the window's origin changes;
    the rain is sampled every 0.25 s.
  - weather/wetfield.ts `RiverWetField` (the window's representation): WorldGpu `riverWet`, r32float, a texel every
    8 window cells (65 × 65 at 512), each its nearest kept node's storm water within 32 cells, 0 elsewhere; written
    only while some of it is wet (and once more as it dries).
  - riverheld.wgsl `riverWetAt(cellXY)` (the one GPU reader, window cells — the signature tileparity's tiles call):
    riverWet() (the climate's, ocean.w) + the field, bilinear, 0 past the window (so a far tile's river is the
    climate's). riverHere asks it at the column. The texture is declared in riverheld.wgsl at binding 62 (free in
    every kernel and draw that includes it; the water and renderfields kernels have 8 storage buffers already — a
    texture costs none): every pipeline that calls riverWetAt binds 62 = world.riverWetView.

## 2026-10-29 — simtiers follow-ups: the tiers off the Globals, the player's interactions, cleaning live (round 108, session 5, `simtiers`)

From main's review of the first pass.

- **The tiers moved off the Globals.** The first pass put them in Globals words 480-515, which grew the Globals
  from 1920 to 2064 B, and tierRate looped over four region rects in them. That is the pattern docs/PAGES.md §1
  measured on this iGPU: the Globals' size, and any array in them indexed by a computed index, slow every kernel
  (18 KB: +55 %; a 2.9 KB dynamically indexed table: +48 %). Playground's `Tune` also took word 480. Now the tiers
  are their own texture, `world.tierTex`:
  - one texel a window chunk (rgba32float: rain, wind, vegetation rates);
  - rasterised on the CPU by `Tiers.apply` and written only when it changes;
  - read by `tiers.wgsl` (binding 50, prepended only to the five kernels that ask);
  - one `textureLoad` a call, nothing indexed.

  The Globals are back to places' layout byte for byte. Side effects: regions have no cap (main's SM4 point: the
  4-region throw inside the frame loop is gone), and a region's grain is a chunk (16 columns).
- **The gate**, scripts/kernelab.mjs. Each sim dispatch is replayed alone, win 256, on the combined build (places
  650b5be with playground). Five ABAB pairs (A places, B simtiers), with the source swapped under one Vite;
  shots88/simtiers/kernelab/:
  - total 1.392 → 0.915 ms (-34 %);
  - every kernel is faster or within noise (worst: structure +1.2 %);
  - the kernels the tiers touch, relative to the rest in the same run, are -38 % (A 0.92-1.17, B 0.57-0.77): sediment-out -61 %, sediment -34 %, ecology -73 %, climate -31 %, particles-update -29 %.

  Baked columns don't move, so sediment returns early. The untouched kernels are faster on B too (water and lava
  -20 to -35 %). I didn't run that down: it may be less of the window awake when nothing erodes, or the clocks.
  The runs swing up to 2x from one to the next (a shared GPU), which is why there are five pairs.

## 2026-10-29 — round 108 (`tileparity`): a tile is the window's land minus the simulation (TC18-TC20, TC8)

Why: the user (DECISIONS round 108): "the distant tiles have seems and sometimes miss certain effects like snow ... My
expectation is that the tiles are essentially the visual only version of full tiles so I wouldn't expect them to me
different."

What a render-only tile was, against the window's land (found reading both paths; the conflations):
- Its land came from a second path (Atlas.regionTile): no settlement stamps, no neighbours (its edges open: the grid's
  lattice and normals at the region's edge read nothing past it), and none of the window's render preparation — its
  surface words were the top's height alone (no material, no loose run), its drift texture, moisture and flow zero. So
  loose ground (sand, snow) was drawn as solid tops, wet ground was never darkened, the rivers had no flow.
- The weather was baked: a window region's tile kept the snow and wetness it had when baked; a made one had none.
- A held river's level (the rivers' wetness) was baked too.
- The atlas thrashed at wide zooms: at zoom ~1.3 on the phone tier the screen draws ~94 tiles of 96 slots, and the
  look-ahead's margin evicted tiles the screen had drawn the frame before; they were wanted again and evicted the
  margin's: 2,623 bakes and 1,330 regions made in the first ~45 s parked (scripts/tileparity.mjs, zoom 1.3), ~60 bakes a second; between, the far land's
  flat colour showed in the tiles' places (the dark checkerboard in the sea and the flat squares on land in the
  before shots — likely much of what reads as "seams" at a wide zoom).

What changed:
- TC18, one generation path: `Atlas.regionInto(..., how: MakeHow)` for the window and the tiles alike — `how` says the
  pacing (the tiles' lane first), the stamps ('plan' for the window; 'made' for a tile: the plans already made, none
  started, no ground read back, no worker — DECISIONS 106b) and where the per-column summary goes (a GPU buffer: nothing
  read back). regionTile is gone. TC8: the settlements' stamps come with a tile's land once planned; when a plan lands
  (Atlas.stampsChanged) the render-only tiles over its box are made again (TileCache.forgetMade).
- The window's render preparation on a tile's land (render/tileworld.ts): SurfaceSystem and RenderFieldsSystem — the
  window's own classes, through a narrowed `PrepWorld` — run on a small world whose layers are the scratch slot's pages,
  its kept fields copied in per bake (as the streamer's copyIn). The bake draws through the surface words, drift,
  moisture and flow they make. No simulation steps it.
- TC19, a border: a tile's land is its region and 2 cells of its neighbours' round it (68² made, in the corner of an
  80² slot: FinishTarget.corner), so its edge cells' lattice and normals are its neighbours' real columns, as the
  window's are.
- TC20, the weather live: weather/cover.ts (WeatherCoverSystem, its own contract WorldGpu.coverState / coverView): snow,
  wetness and ice at the atlas's scale (512² texels of 8 cells round the window). The window's texels are measured
  from its land every update (the climate sim's snow in the drift, its moisture, its ice and water); past it the
  storms' snow and rain, the melt, the freeze and the drying back step it; a render-only tile's land seeds what it holds
  nothing of. The bake leaves the weather out (meshdraw.wgsl TILE_BAKE); the draw puts it back from the cover: wet
  ground darkened by its porosity (baked in 2 bits beside the normal), ice on the water. Snow keeps the cell's detail:
  the live plane holds a texel's own snow as baked and the cover's there then, and the draw melts the own snow as the
  cover's has melted since and lays what has fallen since over it (a town's roads the window keeps clear stay clear —
  the first try, the cover alone, blanketed them: shots88/tileparity/v2-straight.png).
- The held rivers live (main's addition to TC20): the bake keeps a held river's texel as its bed and the live plane its
  depth under the river's level at the reference wetness and the river's depth at its line; the draw floods it to the
  level at the wetness now (riverheld.wgsl's rule: the line's depth × wet^0.6, the level shifted across the channel, at
  most 0.28 over, a dry bed under 0.03), the wetness read only through riverheld.wgsl `riverWetAt(cell)` (per watershed:
  branch `watershed`). 8 bits a channel: under the level -1..3 cells (1/64 cell steps), the line's depth 0..4.
- The live plane (tiles live, rgba8): x, y the held river's; z the texel's own snow; w the cover's snow as baked. The
  atlas 27.0 → 36.0 MB at the same 96 slots (+4 B a texel on 12; the slots still counted on A and B's 12 — main:
  "Keep the 96 slots"). An rg8 plane (the river alone, +2 B: 31.5 MB) came first; the snow's pair made it rgba8.
- The atlas never evicts a tile the last frame drew; a land job made for a region no longer wanted lets its slot go
  when the atlas is full. In the first ~45 s parked: 2,623 bakes and 1,330 regions made → 245 and 198 (the rest of the screen past 96 tiles shows the far land: TC21).
- The tufts are painted in the bake (as ?tufts=0 paints them): the tile holds no tuft instances. The snow's look in the
  draw is meshSurf's (MAT_SNOW's colour, the per-voxel variation, the mesh's tint).
- The paced tile's side: a batch a little over whole tiles (68² against the pacer's 32 and the finish's 64) took 9 + 4
  turns instead of 4 + 1 (finish p50 154 ms); now a tile a little bigger in as many turns (atlas.ts paceTile): 49 ms.

## 2026-10-29 — round 110 (`physfix`): the rigid rock's four faults in the playground

The user, after playing the playground (BACKLOG PX1-PX6, the quotes there): the arch's span "just instantly
disappear[s]" when a base goes; a rock freed by digging "pushes up out of the earth before becoming a rigidbody";
"we want meshes to intersect … until they are visibly intersecting for large objects"; "When things come to rest they
turn to dust instead of staying as meshes as we discussed". Then: "a tunable parameter for how much objects can
interpenetrate maybe as a function of mass?" Fixed within the CPU rigid rock (round 106's design; the GPU solver,
AR4, later), at the roots:

- **The arch, and "turn to dust" (PX1, PX4): one root.** The half of the arch that gave was freed as a body (the judge
  is fine: a load break at the span's middle, 258 cells) — it fell 4 cells onto its stub and came to rest in seconds.
  A body at rest was then written back into the columns, each cell dropped down its own column onto what's under it
  there (Integrity.settleRigid, round 95's "a heap settles column by column"): a span over air became, in one frame,
  a low heap on the ground, remeshed as terrain — the user's "instantly disappear" and "turn to dust". The resting
  rock as a mesh (round 99, MI4: its cells claimed as External intervals, its mesh drawn where it lies) existed only
  behind `?meshinst=1`. Now it is on wherever the rigid rock is (the trees stay behind the flag). A resting rock that
  loses its ground (judged hanging free) or is cut wakes as a body where it lies, with its own mesh
  (RockBodies.revive from its cells and transform; MI5) instead of becoming ground that the judge frees as a new
  body, remeshed. Cut (dug, smashed), it loses the cells no longer External where they lay (remeshed behind dust).
  The judge's analysis no longer turns External runs into stone inside what falls (Integrity.takeExternal: they are
  taken out and their owner wakes). Baking into ground happens only when out of room (rigid.restMax, 16, and the rock
  mesh's 72 blocks), when leaving the window, or when asked (Integrity.bakeResting, for between runs: PX5 wires it),
  each behind a burst of dust. Why each bake happened is counted (RockBodies.bakedWhy).
- **The span topples (PX1).** A joint that gives under load (analyseRock's cross-section break) now hinges at its
  lower edge (fracture.ts hingeOf: the joints' middle, at the lowest height they share; the axis horizontal, across
  the line from what held it to the part's centre of mass, turned so it carries the part down). The arch's free half
  turns about the other base and comes down onto its stub, rather than dropping straight.
- **The push-up (PX2): three roots.** (1) The collision points were a cube's corners about each cell, (±0.46, ±0.46),
  0.65 from its centre. A hex cell is 0.5 to its faces, so those corners lie in the next columns over. A body freed in
  place beside ground began with corners inside that ground, and the probe pushed them up (within 0.6 of the run's
  top) at half the overlap each substep. Now the points are the hex prism's 12 corners, inset. (2) A speculative
  contact: a point within 0.5 above the ground already took impulses. Now a contact is met only past its slop. (3)
  The push-out itself was a jump of half the overlap each substep. Now the overlap a body is freed with is allowed
  (RockBody.allow: its deepest overlap at spawn, wake or break, only ever shrinking to what it overlaps now, at most
  1.2). A push-out is never faster than rigid.pushV (0.6 cells/s) and never deeper than the slop plus
  rigid.erodeDepth (0.4). A point deeper than that crumbles the solid ground where it meets the body, up to
  rigid.erodeMax (4) cells a frame, as rubble and dust (round 106: "erode material where the bodies meet, not push
  them apart"). A break's pieces are thrown sideways only, never faster up than the body was going (a break thrown
  up off the ground had jumped pieces 3.5 cells).
- **Overlap by mass (PX3).** A contact allows rigid.slop + min(rigid.slopCap, rigid.slopK · mass^rigid.slopP)
  (0.03 + min(0.8, 0.065 · m^0.35)): 0.23 cells for a 30-cell piece, 0.48 for the 260-cell span, 0.83 for a
  1 500-cell pillar. A pair (a body on a resting rock) meets at the lighter one's allowance: overlap reads as
  intersecting on the smaller thing. A pebble sunk into a boulder by the boulder's allowance would vanish into it,
  while a boulder on a pebble crushes it no deeper than the pebble's allowance. The ground counts as the heaviest
  thing, so against it a body uses its own. The probe (moved to rockbodies.ts columnsGround, shared with the CPU
  harness) now looks two rings of columns out for air and measures up to 2 cells deep. Round 95 called anything past
  the six neighbours 1 deep, so a body allowed that much overlap (a big rock's slop, or what it was freed with) fell
  through the floor; the CPU harness showed pieces resting at z 1.5 on a plain at 10.
- Every new number is in the tuning registry's rigid group: slopK, slopP, slopCap, pushV, erodeDepth, erodeMax,
  restMax.

**Measured** (scripts/physfix.mjs, headless, the phone proxy 412x915 dpr 2.6 q=low, every system in play, 1x; the
same script on the code before, `before-*` vs `after-*` in C:\Projects\shots88\physfix\):

## 2026-10-29 — one water path: the playground on the game's water, authored river tables (round 110, session 5, `playwater`)

The user: "The waterfalls don't use the same system as the main game can you explain why?" Why: the playground (round
108) ran the flow model (`?flow=1`, src/flow/) by default, because the game's waterfalls are held rivers (`rivers=table`:
the riverFlow contract, riverheld.wgsl, settle-then-freeze) and riverFlow came only from the atlas's river graph — a
fixed map had no way to declare a river. So the playground's fall was a second water system. Now there's one water
path (BACKLOG PW1-PW6, DECISIONS round 110):

- **Authored river tables** (world/rivertable.ts; ARCHITECTURE "Authored river tables"). A level declares a river (a
  path upstream first with the water's level at each point, a half-width, a discharge; optionally its catchment) and
  gets the atlas's data from it by the atlas's rules: `riverNodes` makes the atlas's nodes (compose.wgsl RiverNode),
  rated by `riverChannelDepth` / `riverSpeed` — now the one rating, atlas/rivers.ts calls them; `holdRivers` is the
  CPU mirror of compose.wgsl riverAt and its cut, columns.wgsl's levee and forms.wgsl's bed, water and riverFlow
  (sheets RIVER_SHEET deep at twice the speed where the bed steps down RIVER_FALL), writing MapData.riverFlow and the
  water it starts with. RIVER_FALL / RIVER_SHEET / RIVER_LEVEE are defined there once and put in the atlas's kernels by
  atlas.ts parts() (they were WGSL literals). Ground more than half a cell under a channel's bed throws (a river would
  stand over it as a column of water: the first try's ledge did exactly that — 8.8 cells of held water at its foot,
  with the line slanting across the ledge, hence "the line square to a fall" in the declaration's contract).
- **Per watershed, as the atlas's** (round 109's riverWetAt, binding 62): a declared catchment (the playground's: its
  station's rectangle) becomes a weather/catchwet.ts RiverGraph (`riverGraph`: the nodes packed as rivers.ts's table,
  samples 8 units apart each draining to its nearest node, reference discharges summed downstream), carried as
  MapData.riverGraph; LevelScene feeds it to the same CatchmentWet and RiverWetField as the atlas's (its window the
  map). Rain on the station raised the river's storm water to 1.5 (the cap) and the river rose; a river without a
  catchment follows the season alone.
- **The river mode is the level's** (sim/world-gpu.ts): `LevelDef.rivers` (`table` on the atlas and the playground),
  set by `useRivers` in LevelScene.create before the atlas and the world are made; `riverMode()`, `riverPull()`,
  `settleLand()`, `settleTol()` replace the module constants RIVERS, RIVER_PULL, SETTLE, SETTLE_TOL (read when a world's
  kernels are made; `riverHeld()` in systems.ts, used by the tiles' draw too). It was `?level=atlas` in the URL — so the
  atlas opened from the title screen ran its rivers unheld (`sim`), and no other level could hold one. (The world API's
  atlas games keep the URL's rule as before.)
- **The playground** (levels/playground.ts): no flow model; its river station is a ramp, a ledge with a 4-column chute
  (9 cells down: each column a fall, as the atlas's falls run down their cliff's slope) and a run out off the map's
  edge, the river declared as a table (half-width 4, discharge 0.3 — the atlas's smallest river) and carved by it. A
  fixed map on `table` gets the atlas level's sleep and wake (what's still sleeps; events wake; ?settletol keeps a
  woken chunk awake while its water changes, then it freezes back to the table) and its water isn't run in the warmup.
  Surge: a spring at the head for 8 s, then none (no spring of its own to go back to). `?flow=1` now runs only in the
  flow lab (elsewhere it throws).

**Headless** (scripts/playwater.mjs; the phone proxy 412x915 dpr 2.6 q=low, 1x, every system in play; debugging aid
scripts/playwater-dump.mjs: the GPU's water beside the table, column by column):

## 2026-10-29 — round 111: the noise lab (branch `noiselab`, BACKLOG TG1–TG7)

The user (DECISIONS round 111): "a noise playground would be a cool way to showcase existing biomes as well as a
general pattern for generating new ones. I like what we have now though so don't break it". So this is a level
beside the game's generators, not a change to them: `?skipmenu=1&level=noiselab`, or "Noise lab" on the title
screen (next to Playground). docs/ARCHITECTURE.md "The noise lab" has the contract.

**The atlas is untouched.** `git diff origin/places -- src/atlas` is empty. The lab includes atlas/noise.wgsl
as it is (pnoise, pworley, the hashes), so a lab layer samples the atlas's own noise. Its octave loops repeat
pfbm's and pridged's sums and seeds, but take a period for each axis, which the radial transform needs. Since
nothing in the atlas was refactored, there was no output to hash before and after.

**A recipe is a tuning preset.** The stack is a second `Registry` (src/noiselab/params.ts): eight layer slots
of 35 numbers each, plus the lab's own group. The tuning panel is the editor (GE1's shell), so the lab got its
sliders, presets, JSON export and import, `?lab=` links and resets for free. The panel now takes a registry, a
store key, a link parameter, built-ins, a top element (the preview) and a visibility rule: a layer shows only
the numbers its generator, shape, op and mask use. A choice (generator, op, …) is a list (`ParamSpec.choices`).
The physics panel is unchanged at its defaults.
- The other option was a free-form JSON layer list with its own editor. That would mean a second editor shell
  and a second preset format. Fixed slots keep one format: a recipe is the values that differ from the
  defaults, so a copied link stays short.

**Live, with the game's look.** Every change runs the stack on the GPU (lab.wgsl). The preview, drawn from
above in the panel, follows every run. The world is rewritten when a slider is let go, when a list or number
changes, or 0.6 s after a drag stops. `world follows: live` rewrites it on every run instead. The record
becomes the game's own columns (noiselab/columns.ts): rock, a cave as a gap in the column (the atlas's caves
are gaps too, atlas/columns.wgsl caveVoids), strata, and the cover. The sea is water depth, with `globals.seaZ`
holding it at the edges. They go in through `WorldCore.replaceWindow`, the same buffers `restoreChunks` puts
back, then `fieldMesh.urgent` over the whole map. So the renderer draws it as it draws any level: cliffs, the
sea, materials, shadows. The level is a sandbox, so rain, the dig and the break tools work on what it makes
(TG2's ravines are for flash floods).

**Presets.** "atlas: range", "atlas: mesa cliffs" and "atlas: hills, terraces, caves" use the regions'
numbers (regions.ts) and compose.wgsl's methods. These are rebuilds, not the atlas's output. The mesa cliffs
use mesaEdge's tiers (up to six walls, each wall's share and ledge set by noise along the edge) on the signed
distance into grouped Voronoi cells, quantized to cells 10 apart (the shelves). They add butte spires off the
foot and fbm-band ravines cut to the plain. The experiments: TG2 mesas from grouped cells with a third of
their outer edges as ramps and ridge-noise ravines cut to the floor; TG3 a coast with mesas and caves where an
fbm lies between two thresholds, their floor 14 under the surface inland, blended by the JFA distance to the
coastline to half a cell under the sea at the coast; TG4 a sheer plateau with two breaks (a smooth ramp, a
stepped one) where a disc mask lerps in a soft-edged copy; TG5 a massif to 79 cells (the lab's window is 128
high); TG6 a 30° grain (fbm stretched 6×) beside radial ridge noise (24 spokes); TG7 spurs of ridge noise
sampled at the nearest point of a plateau's edge, stretched 10× along the distance, so they run straight out
across the isolines. Shots: C:\Projects\shots88\noiselab\ (each recipe, world and panel; tg3-…-caves.png the
cave mouths at the waterline; phone-*.png at 412 × 915).

**Measured** (scripts/noiselab.mjs, desktop iGPU, 1280 × 800, q=medium; 256 × 256 columns):

| recipe | GPU run (submit → read) | passes | columns (CPU) | world write | most runs a column |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| blank | 4.4 ms | 2 | 10.2 ms | 1.5 ms | 2 |
| atlas: range | 5.0 | 2 | 7.7 | 1.4 | 2 |
| atlas: mesa cliffs | 8.1 | 2 | 12.4 | 1.7 | 14 |
| atlas: hills, terraces, caves | 7.1 | 2 | 8.8 | 1.3 | 3 |
| TG2 | 4.6 | 2 | 11.6 | 1.4 | 14 |
| TG3 (one JFA) | 6.1 | 15 | 15.5 | 1.5 | 14 |
| TG4 | 2.5 | 2 | 16.8 | 1.5 | 10 |
| TG5 | 5.4 | 2 | 7.0 | 1.6 | 2 |
| TG6 | 4.3 | 2 | 8.3 | 1.4 | 2 |
| TG7 (two JFAs) | 5.8 | 28 | 13.1 | 1.5 | 2 |

A regenerate costs about 10–25 ms of CPU and GPU, plus the mesh remade over the next frames. The frames in the
2 s after a write: mean 9.7–9.9 ms, worst 10.5–10.8 ms. No hitch showed, because the mesh rebuilds within
`urgent`'s frames. The first version of the column packing took 59 ms (a closure and arrays for every column).
Flat reused arrays cut it to 7–17 ms. At q=low on the phone proxy (412 × 915, dpr 2.6) mesa cliffs measured GPU
9.9, columns 14.0, write 1.7 ms. The slider test: the preview changed while the slider moved, the world was
written 0 times during the move and once on release. No GPU validation errors and no page errors in any run.

**Bringing a recipe into the atlas later (a proposal, not done):**
- Periodic noise on the torus. Lab layers use a period of 65536 (no wrap on the map). In the atlas, each
  lattice needs `perOf(scale)` round the world, which fbmL already takes.
- A region kind gets a recipe in place of `regionHeight`'s fixed sum: a layer buffer bound in compose.wgsl,
  evaluated per column with `p` in world units.
- Field layers (slope, JFA) can't run per streamed tile. They need the macro grid's JFA (the atlas already
  floods borders and coasts there: distR), or analytic distances.
- Caves map onto `caveVoids`, materials onto forms.wgsl colFinish.
- Each existing biome rebuilt as a recipe is checked bit-identical against today's output before it replaces
  the code (hash a region's columns before and after).
- Each tile's cost stays within the streamer's budget.

**Open problems.**
- The sea doesn't enter a cave whose floor is under its level. Water is depth over a column's top, so a sea
  cave's floor is dry ground under the waterline.
- At the farthest zoom, part of the map wasn't drawn in one headless shot. I didn't investigate it; the
  preview always shows the whole recipe.
- Field generators are capped by the eight slots: each JFA layer is one slot and 11 passes.
- The preview's heights aren't to scale with the world's (it shades by slope).
## 2026-10-29 — round 112 (`physfix2`): the playground's physics, played on the phone

The user (DECISIONS round 112, BACKLOG PF1-PF6): the concrete "immediately vanished when any blocks are deleted", "The
bridge on the arch also just vanished when I damaged one side and the other broke instantly", "The tower just settled at
a leaning angle", "The thin stone protrusion survived a fall and collision", "Is sand expected to always fall from the
mountains". Reproduced on places' code (36ff5fe) headless, the phone proxy (412x915 dpr 2.6 q=low, every system in
play, 1x: scripts/physfix2.mjs, `before-*` vs `after-*` in C:\Projects\shots88\physfix2\), and on the CPU
(scripts/physfix2-cpu.mjs: both judges, the rigid bodies and the columns' pieces on the playground's map, as
Integrity.pass and apply run them). Causes and fixes:

- **The concrete, and the bridge (PF1, PF2): an empty mesh.** physfix's guess was the columns' pieces (colbodies.ts);
  it isn't: with the rigid rock on, the rock judge runs first and takes what hangs free whatever it's made of, so the
  build station's concrete and brick become rigid bodies (the CPU harness: "break bases" frees a 195-cell concrete
  tower, a 250-cell brick chimney, the board, the deck as rigid bodies; the structures' judge never fires). A rigid
  body is drawn by the rock mesh, which is the field mesh's mesher — and the field mesh draws no built material
  (meshregion.wgsl fieldMat: what's built is drawn as prisms). The body got a slot (so no cubes either) holding nothing:
  invisible while it fell, and at rest its External cells were drawn by no one. On places, "break bases" left the
  station's census at concrete 608 → 136, brick 760 → 399, with 760 cells resting and nothing on screen
  (before-concrete-end.png: the tower, chimney, board and bridge gone); one pillar smashed took the deck and the other
  pillar (before-bridge-end.png). Now the rock mesh is made of the cells the field mesh draws (Integrity.allocRock); a
  body's other cells are drawn as its voxels (RockBodies.packInto by cell; the body-voxel draw, cubes), moving and at
  rest (each resting entry keeps its voxels at its rest transform: rockbodies.ts restingVoxels); a body with no mesh
  at all rests too, as its voxels, instead of being written back column by column as a heap. After: the same buttons
  leave the pieces lying where they fell (after-concrete-end.png, after-bridge.gif). One rule for "what the field mesh
  draws" on the CPU: world/materials.ts fieldMeshed (api/terrain.ts had its own copy, missing flesh, coral, obsidian,
  quartz and bedrock).
- **The rock station's arch (PF2) did not vanish on places** — physfix's fix holds. Smashing a foot frees the leg with
  half the span: the span snaps at its middle under the hanging leg (the judge's load break — right: a 12-cell rock
  cantilever 3 cells thick doesn't carry a 230-cell leg), and the leg drops the hole's height (4.5 cells) and stands on
  its own (the "two stubs" of the user's screenshot are this). But it struck the ground at 9.2 cells/s, over its
  break speed (8.7), and stayed whole: a tipping piece had a second's grace from breaking (round 96: so a lean didn't
  shatter on its own stub). Now the grace ends once the body has been off the ground 0.15 s (RockBody.airborne): it
  covers the contact it was freed in, not what it falls onto. The CPU: the leg breaks on landing into 193 + 63 cells,
  the hook shatters (17 cells/s).
- **The leaning tower (PF3): damping, not overlap.** The pillar (1 519 cells) cut on one side tips about its foot's
  edge; the contacts' ground damping (rigid.contactDamp, 1.5/s) took its spin out each substep while it pivoted, so the
  topple crawled — 2° to 30° in 10 s, its spin 0.02-0.04 rad/s and its speed 0.6 cells/s — and a slower one (under
  rest speed 0.3 and rest spin 0.15 for 0.6 s) was at rest, leaning. The mass-scaled overlap doesn't prop it: sunk in,
  its support is the footprint it sank with. Now RockBody.balanced: its centre of mass over the convex hull of its
  contact points (seen from above, within rigid.balanceGive 0.1); unbalanced, the ground doesn't damp it and it isn't
  at rest. Page: before 6° at 3.6 s, 30° at 11.9 s, 57° at 20 s; after 10° at 3.6 s, 30° at 5.7 s (it then leans a
  moment on the neighbouring top's cap — a real support — and goes on over, 56° at 11.9 s, and breaks). CPU: 30° in
  4.0 s instead of 10.5 s.
- **The thin protrusion (PF4): necks.** A break was judged against the whole body (RB.breakSpeed × √strength ×
  (cells/200)^−sizeK) and split it round random seeds, so a thin part never snapped on its own. The user: "find thin
  points with a quick JFA based medial axis to find thin areas where mass on either side is large". RockBodies
  findNecks, once a body is made: the distance transform of its cells (breadth-first from the skin on the lattice —
  exactly what a JFA gives; on the CPU because the bodies are, the GPU solver (AR4) is where a JFA belongs), its
  medial axis (a cell shallower-bounded on both sides along one of the lattice's four axes: up-down and the hex's
  three; even thicknesses through a neighbour as deep), and every thin axis cell (half-thickness ≤ rigid.neckDepth 3)
  tried, the thinnest first: a ball of its thickness taken out, does the rest fall in two sides of rigid.neckMin (12)
  cells or more? A hit then snaps the worst neck when (the mass beyond it from the point hit) × speed / (its
  cross-section, π r²) passes rigid.neckStrength (70) × strength: the side struck stops and the side beyond's momentum
  goes through the neck. It snaps in two (no rubble), each side going on as the body moved. Under the whole-body
  break speed only — over it, the old shatter. The CPU: a 6³ block with a rod 10 long (77 cells, a neck r 1.5) dropped
  3 cells lands at 8.2 cells/s, under the block's 8.5: the rod snaps off (dropped 1 cell, 5.5 cells/s, it holds); the
  station's concrete tower snaps at necks on landing at 6.9 and 5.6. fracture.ts NECK_R ("neck reach", the registry's
  `fracture.neck`) is not a thinness test — it's how far the judge follows a piece above a cut before calling it keyed
  into the land; the standing rock's thin sections are the judge's joints (BEND h², SHEAR h) and its buckle test. Two
  tests of thinness now (the judge's on the standing columns, the bodies' necks) on two representations; one is not
  built on the other (flagged).
  Cost: the search at a body's spawn is bounded by NECK_WORK (15 000 cell visits): measured warm on the desktop 0.16
  ms for 148 cells, 0.5 ms for 296, 1.6-1.8 ms for the 1 519-cell pillar; the page's worst over a run 1.5-2.3 ms (a
  spawn frame). The neck test at a hit is a loop over a body's few necks.
- **The sand (PF5): a frozen animation.** The peaks a Range stroke raises are stone with a skin of the plain's soil,
  which the wind can't lift (the air texture's lift summed 0 over the window). What fell were the sliding grains: the
  particles stream grains off each column the sediment says is sliding (sediment.wgsl airOut, "the flow the particles
  show"). A chunk falls asleep 8 s after its event; asleep, the sediment returns before writing airOut, so the last
  tick's slide stays in it. Measured on places: the stroke's chunks asleep (0/4 awake), the ground moved 0.00 cells in
  90 s, and 1 340 columns still showed sliding (before-sand-80s.gif: grains streaming off the peaks). Now nothing streams
  off a sleeping column (particles.wgsl: `asleep`), and the wind's dust follows the user's read: where nothing is lifted
  (the column asleep, or the wind's work baked — simtiers) the emitter shows dust by the wind's strength over the loose
  material there (its lift threshold, its airborne share, smoothstep over the lift), at dust.shown (0.12 a column a
  second at most), carrying nothing; none on ground the wind can't lift. Before, baked, the sediment worked out the
  lift every tick and the particles showed it at full strength over ground that never changed (simtiers' "litter
  throwing scrap endlessly"); the sediment no longer works out a lift it won't take (baked, windOut isn't called).
  Open (PF6): a slope asleep mid-slump stays as it froze until something wakes it — sleep holds a chunk awake only while
  its water changes; its loose ground moving should hold it too.
- Every new number is in the tuning registry: rigid.balanceGive, neckStrength, neckDepth, neckMin; dust.shown (GPU,
  in struct Tune, a pad taken).

**Measured** (the phone proxy, desktop iGPU, vsync 120 Hz; cost runs back to back on the two builds, the same script):
idle p50 8.3 / p95 8.8 ms on both; while the rock station's two buttons fall p50 8.3 / p95 9.0 both; the rigid step's

## Round 112 (2026-10-29, session 5, `tilefast`) — a tile's land in a few frames, the atlas's slots at wide zoom

The user's goal (round 104): "steady 60fps on the phone with no hiccups and no pop in". The Pixel 9a pan bench on
`places` with tileparity (data/bench/pixel9a-pan-tileparity.json) had three problems: a tile's land took ~130 ms and
wanted-to-drawn ~150 ms at every speed and zoom; at zoom 5 and wider every run failed at 20 cells/s on pop-in (8-19%
of the screen); and land from disk had 33-50 ms frames.

**Causes.**
- *The ~150 ms.* The bench's per-step breakdown puts nearly all of it in `land`. A render-only tile's bordered 68²
  batch is paced on the tiles' lane: 4 column tiles (paceTile(68, 32) = 34², 2 x 2), then 4 finish tiles on a phone
  (`FINISH_TILE` 32 there, 64 on a desktop: 1). That's 8 turns. Each turn awaited a fresh `requestAnimationFrame` of
  the pacer, because a region's next tile is asked for a microtask after its last submit, after the frame's turns were
  handed out. So it took 8 frames, about 133 ms, whatever the GPU cost. The phone's timestamps put the whole region at
  ~4 ms (colHeight 0.5, formSeed 0.7, colFinish 1.1, regionFinish 1.5: pixel9a-2026-10-28-v4). The desktop's 1 finish
  turn is why tileparity measured 49 ms there. Also, with 6 regions in flight, the lane was FIFO, a turn each in
  rotation, so all 6 finished late together.
- *The pop-in at wide zoom.* The bench's `missMax` showed it all "behind" the pan. A new measure (`TileCache.whyMissing`,
  the bench's `missWhy`) splits it:
  - Zoom 3.5 and wider: **the atlas was full.** All 96 slots were used and all 96 drawn, so tiles waited as
    `queued` / `making` / `made` (noSlot 446 in a 5 s step at zoom 2.2). TC21's limit arrives at 2.2 on the phone
    proxy, not only at 1.3. A wide zoom's tile needs 98 x 57 texels of a 128 x 192 slot.
  - Window regions' tiles were the first evicted. The window draws its own land, so their tiles were never marked
    used, and the look-ahead's tiles took their slots. The tile was then missing the frame the region left the window.
  - At zoom 5, a different cause: the **eye-side skip**. A tall window-baked tile just past the window's trailing edge,
    on the eye's side (top 215 against a cap of 138), is left out so it doesn't rise into the line to the focus. The
    rings draw it flat. That's the 12.5% "behind" at zoom 5. It's a design rule, not a fault: open as TF5.
- *The disk hitch.* Disk is the one source that uploads: one region's 1.7 MB record in a single writeBuffer a frame
  (`UPLOAD_BYTES` 2 MB). The phone's long frames on the disk path were gpu-held and gpu-busy at 10 cells/s, where
  generated land had none. The phone's own io bench shows writeBuffer completions up to 39 ms (upload 8 MB p95). The
  desktop proxy can't reproduce Mali's stall: there every source shows the same 42-66 ms throttled frames.

**What changed.**
- **The pacer (atlas.ts TilePacer).** The tiles' lane is ordered by `MakeHow.order` (TileLandGpu counts the regions it
  asks for, the camera's way), so the first asked finishes first. The lane's share of a frame's turns is half while
  the streamer waits, else all. What its queue doesn't take, plus what the streamer leaves, is the frame's **credit**:
  a tiles'-lane request made in that frame's task (a region's next tile) runs at once, until a `setTimeout(0)` ends the
  task. The guard's turn count still bounds the frame. `?tilechain=0` turns the credit off.
- **The atlas's parts (TC21).** A slot holds one whole tile (128 x 192), two halves (128 x 96) or four quarters
  (64 x 96). A tile takes the least part that holds it at the view's own scale (`?tilefit=` 1: no resolution lost), so
  96 slots hold up to 384 tiles in the same 36 MB. Render-only tiles choose their part from the region's flat extent
  plus 48 units of height, and the GPU camera fits them to it. When the atlas had no place lately, drawn render-only
  tiles bigger than the view needs (a close zoom's whole slots, still on screen after zooming out) are made again at
  the view's size, into where they were.
- A window region's tile is marked used while the region is in the window.
- The eye-side skip applies only to a tile whose image covers the focus on the screen (a tighter test; it doesn't
  change the zoom-5 case above).
- The streamer's pool uploads are split across frames: `UPLOAD_BYTES` a frame in all, 0.5 MB on a phone, so a 1.7 MB
  record takes 4 frames. **The phone has to confirm this one.**
- The pan bench: `missWhy`, `slots` (used, drawn, evicted, noSlot), `pacer` (perFrame, turns a frame, chained),
  `landFrames` (the renderer's frames from a tile's start to its land made); `?benchzooms=14_2.2` runs only some
  zooms. New script: scripts/tilefast.mjs, the same measures in a short headless pan per zoom and speed.

**Measurements.** The desktop proxy for the phone: q=low, 412 x 915, dpr 2.6, window 256, the bench page's phone
flags, `Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate` 4, `&finishtile=32` (the phone's 8 turns). Before: places 36ff5fe; after: this
branch. Runs vary ±30% under throttling. Files: C:/Projects/shots88/tilefast/probe-before.json, probe-after*.json,
probe-final.json, bench-after-desktop-throttle4.json.

| case | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| zoom 5, 20 c/s: land p50 / p95 | (no tiles needed) | 23 / 56 ms, **2 / 3 frames** |
| zoom 5, 80 c/s: land p50 / p95 | 162 / 225 ms | 60 / 137 ms (4 / 9 frames) |
| zoom 5, 80 c/s: wanted to drawn p50 / p95 | 194 / 250 ms | 75 / 165 ms |
| zoom 2.2, 20 c/s: screen out of detail behind | 9.7% | 0% |
| zoom 2.2, 80 c/s: out of detail (worst frame) | 12.5% behind, 1.4% ahead | 0-0.7% |
| zoom 2.2: tiles the atlas held (36 MB) | 96 (full; noSlot 446 in 5 s) | 122-153 |
| zoom 1.3, 80 c/s: out of detail ahead / behind | 31% / 31% | 12.5% / 2% |
| zoom 1.3: tiles held | 96 | 195-228 |

The GIFs, zoom 2.2 panning at 60 c/s: C:/Projects/shots88/tilefast/before-z2.2-pan60.gif has grey (flat far-land) holes where
tiles couldn't get a slot; after-z2.2-pan60.gif has none (stills: before/after-z2.2-panning.png).

**Open.**
- At zoom 14 and 80 c/s the land still takes ~7 frames. The streamer's lane is busy there, so the tiles get half the
  turns and little credit. At 2.2 and 80 c/s it's 24 frames: 6 regions in flight queue behind each other, and they
  wait for places while remakes free them.
- After a zoom-out, noSlot persists for seconds (the screen's old whole tiles are drawn and can't be evicted). The
  remakes free them a region at a time on the land lane.
- The eye-side skip at zoom 5 (TF5).
- The disk hitch on the phone (TF4).

## Round 112 (2026-10-29, session 5, `tilefix`) — the terrain past the window drawn on every screen, and a gate for it

The user opened the atlas on the deployed `places` build on their PC and the tiles were broken
(C:/Users/cshel/Pictures/Screenshots/TilesLoadingWeirdly.png): the window's land floated over grey void, a few
scattered tiles were drawn, and most of the screen showed the flat far land. The user: "The most basic thing is that
all the tiles visible on screen load visually and our framerate doesn't dip below our thresholds." And: "Honestly I
think that behavior has been in there since early on ... Regardless, we should fix it and get the terrain drawing
reliably."

**The causes.** Three faults combined. They're old (rounds 103-108), not one of the day's merges. The new gate fails
places 27f0ffa at every wide zoom; main's headless shots of 9e7779b (before tileparity) and c06d52f show the same.
1. **The atlas was sized for the phone's screen.** It was a fixed 24 MB, 96 slots. A desktop's 1600 x 900 at zoom 2
   shows ~220 regions; with the look-ahead's margin it wants 300-1000 tiles. The atlas filled with the first 96, and
   everything else stayed the far land's flat colour. On the phone it was enough down to about zoom 2.2.
2. **Off-screen render-only tiles were never culled, so they were never evicted.** Since round 105 a render-only
   tile's box is known only on the GPU (TP), so `TileCache.prepare` drew every one within the mask's reach (32
   regions, 2048 cells) and marked each one used. Since round 108 (tileparity) a tile drawn last frame is never
   evicted, which stopped the thrash at wide zooms. Together: once full, the atlas could never let a tile go. That's
   the user's scattered tiles: they stay wherever they were first made. Before round 108 the atlas thrashed instead.
3. **The look-ahead sampled the screen on a 16 x 16 grid.** At a wide zoom on a desktop that's fewer than one point a
   region, so whole regions were never asked for (the gate's `none`).

The grey void under the window's eye side is the far land pressed down there (far.wgsl underFocus: nothing rises
into the line to the focus). It's meant to have tiles over it, so it's covered once they draw.

**What changed.**
- The atlas's budget is the phone's 24 MB scaled by the screen's css area (411 x 785 is 1), up to 128 MB
  (`?tilemb=` still sets it). Desktop 1600 x 900: 384 slots, 144 MB including the live plane. The user's 2046 x 672:
  the same. Phone proxy 412 x 915: 104 slots, 39 MB. With `tilefast`'s halves and quarters, 384 slots hold up to
  1536 tiles. The gate saw up to ~1000 in use at zoom 1.3, 600-700 drawn.
- **A CPU bound for each render-only tile, with no readback** (TileLandGpu.boundOf). The bound is the region's
  footprint plus its height range from what the CPU knows at bake time (Atlas.zRange: the macro ground over a 9 x 9
  grid, the sea's level, any giants reaching in), padded by 128 above and 64 below. `prepare` culls the tile on this
  bound, so only tiles on the screen count as used and the rest can be evicted.
  - *The pad's calibration:* against the GPU's exact boxes (the prep kernel's, read back once for this and then
    removed), 2210 tiles at three spots. The true top was at most 119 over the macro's highest, and the true bottom at
    most 53 under its lowest.
  - *Why no GPU cull pass:* the user asked "Can we not simply do that on the GPU? Culling should be dirt cheap", and
    the CPU has to know what's visible to evict anyway. After the CPU cull the draw is at most ~600 quads (1200
    triangles), and the rasteriser clips the rest. A cull pass plus drawIndirect would save nothing measurable and add a
    storage buffer to a vertex stage near its limit of 8. (main agreed; skipped.)
  - The 8-byte box readback tried first is gone (DECISIONS round 106b: no readback for what's only seen).
- The look-ahead's grid is dense enough for two points across every region on the screen (16 to 64 a side).
- `tilefast` merged in: the pacer's credit, the halves and quarters, window tiles kept, the bench's why.

**The gate: scripts/tilegate.mjs** (main runs it before every merge into places).
- Screens: desktop 1600 x 900 at dpr 1, at the page's own tier (as the user's PC runs it); the phone proxy
  412 x 915 at dpr 2.6, q=low; and `wide`, 2046 x 672 (the user's report), on request.
- The atlas at a fixed spot, world, time of day and season, nothing saved. For each zoom (14, 8, 5, 3.5, 2.2, 1.3):

## 2026-10-29 — round 112 (`testspeed`): tests faster — where a check's minute goes, a shared runner, a contract tier, warm snapshots

The user, verbatim: "Please put some effort into making tests faster as they are the biggest bottleneck to iteration
right now." and "Part of the reason for encapsulation and code deduplication is to minimize the test surface area and
speed up tests, improve coverage and reliability." (BACKLOG TS1-TS12.)

**Where the time goes** (the atlas level, `?skipmenu=1&level=atlas&q=low`, 412×915, desktop iGPU, D3D11; the boot
marks src/perf/boot-marks.ts — `window.__boot` — and WorldCore.warmStats; scripts/run.mjs boot, scripts/warmprobe.mjs):

| stage | Vite dev `--force`, fresh profile | build, fresh profile | build, kept profile | build, kept-up Chrome (2nd page) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| server up | 0.2 s | 0.5 s (vite build, 1st time) / 0 (cached) | 0 | 0 |
| module load (HTML → main.ts runs) | 0.8 s (250 requests, 9.4 MB) | 0.1 s (6 requests, 2.1 MB) | 0.1 s | 0.05 s |
| WebGPU device | 0.3 s | 1.0 s | 1.0 s | 0.1 s |
| atlas build (4–6 s of it its pipelines) | 7.2 s | 6.4 s | 8.6 s | 6.6 s |
| first window | 0.2 s | 0.2 s | 0.2 s | 0.2 s |
| the level made | 0.1 s | 0.1 s | 0.1 s | 0.1 s |
| warmup: its loop of 1 800 steps | 30.7 s | 30.5 s | 34.8 s | 27.0 s |
| warmup: the GPU's tail after it | 6.4 s | 12.0 s | 14.8 s | 7.6 s |
| level-ready (attach, the streamer) | 2.0 s | 2.1 s | 2.5 s | 2.0 s |
| **to a level a check can use** | **47.8 s** | **52.5 s** | **62.3 s** | **43.7 s** |

(Run-to-run spread on this shared iGPU is ±15 %.) So the dev server isn't the cost: Vite 8 serves the 250 modules in
under a second. **The warmup is 75–80 % of every atlas check's start**, and the user's own boot pays it too.

The warmup's loop isn't CPU: its 1 800 steps encode in 73 ms in all (windfield 17, particles 9, oil 8 …); one step
blocks for 18–20 s mid-loop (step ~1 330) — the GPU's queue full, the wire waiting. Started from a snapshot (below)
with no ticks at all, the first big queue write blocks the same ~28 s, and an `onSubmittedWorkDone` queued right
after `new LevelScene` resolves only then: **~28 s of GPU-process work queued by the level's constructors, before any
tick; the 1 800 ticks themselves are ~8 s**. That work isn't cached by a kept-up Chrome: the second page in one Chrome
pays it again (27.8 vs 28.8 s; the playground 31.4 vs 32.1 s), though it makes exactly the same 125 shader modules
(identical hashes) — 9.56 MB of WGSL (common.wgsl, layers, materials prepended whole to each kernel, ~76 KB a
module), 114 sync + 24 async compute pipelines, 18 sync + 11 async render pipelines. The contract tier's tiny world
(the same sim and renderer kernels) does get cached across pages (10 s → 0.27 s), so the atlas's is either kernels
whose cache never hits or per-page work that scales with the world.

**The trace settles it** (scripts/bootrace.mjs, a Chrome trace of one atlas boot with the GPU categories): Dawn runs
on D3D12 and compiles every pipeline with DXC, and the sync pipelines compile one after another on the GPU process's
main thread — CompileShaderDXC 17.5 s for the compute pipelines, 13.1 s in the 15 sync render pipelines — while the
page waits 32 s in `CommandBufferProxyImpl::WaitForToken`; DXC runs again every boot (no cache hit, page or launch).
Two experiments, A/B on the same build:
- `?wgslstrip=1`, each module cut to what its entry points reach (a pure transform, 2.73 MB → 0.96 MB of WGSL over
  the 47 shader files' kernels): DXC 17.5 → 16.4 s, the boot 50.8 → 47.8 s — Tint already drops what isn't reached
  before DXC sees it. Dropped (not kept as code).
- `?pipeasync=1`, the compute pipelines asked for async, all at once, the level waiting for them before its first
  tick: Dawn's worker pool compiles them in parallel — the boot 50.8 → 36.7 s; then the 15 render pipelines too
  (`renderPipe`): **48–52 → 28.5 s**, the pipelines stage 6.9 s. The warmed world is hash-identical to the sync
  build's (every buffer but particles: the same md5 over 42 buffers), and tilegate's desktop z5 golden image against
  the places baselines passes (0.76 % changed, under its 1 %; 103 fps). Now the default, no switch:
  gpu/pipeline.ts `beginPipelineBatch` … `await endPipelineBatch()` round the level's making in LevelScene.create
  (and round a contract world); outside a batch (the menu, lazily, mid-game) pipelines are made synchronously as
  before, and a kernel used before its batch ends throws.

**The user's boot** (the deployed build; the atlas level on this desktop, cold Chrome): 48–52 s before → **28.5 s**
the first visit (async pipelines) → **19.0 s** the second (the warm cache: the warmup's 1 800 ticks skipped — on by
default, `?warmcache=0` off, keyed by `__BUILD_HASH__`, a content hash of src/ and data/ made by vite.config.ts, so a
new build never starts from an old world). The phone's share of each is still to measure (BACKLOG TS7).

**What changed**
- `scripts/lib/runner.mjs` — one place for the server, the browser, the page and the GPU's schedule:
  - the server: a production build (`vite build`, 0.5–1.4 s, cached by the content of every build input — the whole
    worktree top but docs/, scripts/, node_modules — so a source or data change rebuilds and nothing stale is served;
    the runner's self-check found data/ missing from the first hash) on this worktree's own port (same origin every run),
    hashed assets `immutable`, pages `no-cache`; `--dev` for checks that import /src/… in the page; `--server URL` for
    one already up;
  - the browser: Chrome on a profile kept per worktree and slot (`.testcache/chrome-<n>`), the origin's storage cleared
    before every page (a fresh world store, as a fresh profile gave); `node scripts/run.mjs daemon` keeps one Chrome up
    and checks connect to it (the in-memory pipeline cache: the contract tier's 10 s compile → 0.27 s);
  - the GPU's schedule: a check says its kind — `behaviour` (states, sim-time speeds, coverage, pixels) shares the GPU
    with up to 2 others, `timing` (frame cost) takes it alone and holds new behaviour checks back while it waits;
    leases are files in the OS temp dir, across worktrees; `node scripts/run.mjs status` lists them;
  - the page: waits for the boot marks (`level-ready`, the store open), not a fixed sleep; `R.ticks(p, n)` /
    `R.simSeconds` wait in sim time, so a check sees the same simulation on a shared GPU as alone; console and page
    errors and the fatal overlay reported; behaviour checks default to 412×915 at dpr 1;
  - warm snapshots: `R.level(params, { snapshot: true })` / `--snap` — below.
- `scripts/run.mjs` — `status | build | serve | daemon | boot | selfcheck [--gpu]`. The self-check: every asset
  content-hashed, the pages no-cache, a WGSL edit (a kernel's own constant and common.wgsl's ROW_H, prepended to every
  kernel) changes the build and its asset names; on the GPU, the edited kernel's constants come back new on the same
  kept profile and origin — in the same browser and in a relaunched one — and the old build's come back old (the
  user: "For the kept shaders in the profile just make sure we replace ones that update"). Passes.
- Ported: shot.mjs, tileprobe.mjs, playwater.mjs, tilegate.mjs (their flags as before; `--url` is a server for the
  last three, a path for shot). playwater's waits are sim time now (`--settle` sim seconds after each level is up,
  where it slept 35–40 s of wall time; `settled()` polls in ticks); `--skip cost` makes it a behaviour check.
- **The contract tier** (`contract.html`, src/test/contract.ts, scripts/contract.mjs): a system or a few on a tiny
  world — a playground station's chunks cut out (src/test/crop.ts), the real WorldCore, its kernels, Simulation.step —
  its contract inputs set and its outputs read back. `breach` (the pool held by its plug keeps its water within 2 %;
  dug through as the station's button does, it pours into the basin: 0 → 576 cells³ in 1 800 ticks), `river` (the held
  river wet down its whole length; awake, it drifts 0.07–0.26 off its table at the ramp, foot and run — the level's is
  asleep once settled, where playwater checks it steady), `pool` (water on bare stone kept within 1 %: 512 → 510.3),
  `stamp` (the self-check's kernel). Bitwise the same numbers run to run. 2.2 s for the four on a kept-up Chrome
  (35–43 s cold, nearly all of it the kernels' compile), against a 45 s atlas boot before a check can start.
- **Warm snapshots** (src/sim/snapshot.ts): every buffer and texture of the WorldGpu (the contract — every system's
  state) and the sim's tick, captured in queue order at the warmup's end and put back by `WorldCore.warmFrom` (the
  warmup's other work — the deferred pipelines, the tiers' rates, the primed derived buffers — done the same way).
  Left out by design: uniform buffers (the Globals, re-uploaded) and what can't be copied back (a tick's outputs for
  the CPU, editResult). `?warmsnap=<key>`: the runner's store (`/__snap/<key>`, `.testcache/snap/`), keyed by the
  build's hash and the level's URL; `?warmcache=1`: the player's, IndexedDB (src/sim/warm-cache.ts), keyed by the
  main chunk's content-hashed URL and the settings — the same capture and restore. 132 MB for the atlas window.
  **Proof** (scripts/warmprobe.mjs --snap): the snapshot start's world equals the fresh warmup's, every world buffer
  hashed (FNV-1a) at the boot mark 'warmup', particles too (restored); the sim goes on from it (1 799 → 1 919 ticks,
  no errors). Two fresh warmups also agree on every buffer but `particles` (alone or three at once).
  It saves the ticks' ~8 s of GPU (the warmup stage 38.4 → 31.8 s); the ~28 s above remains until its cause is fixed.
- Boot marks (src/perf/boot-marks.ts) and WorldCore.warmStats: read-only; a test's hook (`window.__bootHook`) sees
  the world at 'warmup' (the runner's stateHook hashes it there).

**Before / after, per script** (wall time, the same checks, one at a time on the iGPU):

| check | before (Vite dev `--force` + old script) | after (runner) |
|---|---|---|
| shot.mjs, an atlas picture | 62 s (`--wait 60000`, the wait a guess that must overshoot) | 52 s (waits for the level, then 2 s) |
| tileprobe.mjs `--seconds 10` | 92 s | 91 s (its 30 s settle and sampling kept) |
| playwater.mjs `--skip atlas` | 348 s | 321 s (sim-time waits; same results) |
| contract tier (breach, river, pool) | — (an atlas boot, 45 s, before a check can start) | 2.2 s warm Chrome, 35–43 s cold |
| atlas boot (async pipelines, round 112's default) | 48–52 s | 28.5 s cold |
| atlas boot from the warm snapshot / the player's warm cache | 48–52 s | 19.0 s |

**Concurrency** (scripts/warmprobe.mjs, three at once in three Chromes): all three finished in 85 s against ~48 s
each alone (1.7× the throughput), and their warmed worlds hash the same as the solo run's, every buffer but
particles. Sharing the GPU doesn't change what a behaviour check sees — provided it waits in sim time (R.ticks), not
wall time: with the GPU shared a wall-time wait sees fewer ticks.

## Round 112 (2026-10-29, session 5, `tilefix2`) — the hero's grey screen, a gate that doesn't depend on the machine, the eye side cut

**The hero's grey screen** (the user's Pixel 9a, `?run=bell`: grey round the hero, the window's own land not drawn; and a
grey corner in the sandbox).
- *Cause, older than the tiles:* `HybridChunks.clear()`, called on the streamer's `onWarp`, wiped every chunk's land
  flags and readiness (`land = 0`, `readyAt = Infinity`). But a warp writes all its regions first, and each write calls
  `landBox`, which sets exactly those. So after any warp every chunk was neither the grid's nor voxels, and never ready,
  and the window drew nothing. The rings don't draw deep inside the window, so the screen was grey.
- *Where it happens:* the run's "window made again" after its stage stamp is a warp, and so is a save's `restore()` on
  load. The default page saves (worldsave on); the gate ran with worldsave=0, so it never saw this.
- *Measured* (phone proxy, run=bell): before, 0 of 110 chunks drawn for over 35 s; after, 12 meshed and 98 grid. Places
  2fe8588, before tilefix, has the same bug.
- *Fix:* `clear()` resets only the place's history (edited, touched). Shots: C:/Projects/shots88/tilegate/run-pre.png,
  run-fixed.png.

**The gate doesn't depend on the machine** (the 3080 runner: headless Chrome there was held to 29 Hz with the monitor
off, and fills that pass at 120 Hz in 8 s failed).
- Chrome runs without vsync (`--chromeargs` overrides), and the page's `requestAnimationFrame` is held to 60 Hz ticks
  by the script. Every rAF sees the same rate: the game's and the tile pacer's.
- The load is counted in frames: `--loadframes` 180 (3 s at 60). After the load budget each view reports `fillFrames`,
  the frames until the screen was all in detail (checked every 30, up to 3 x the budget). Over the budget fails.
- The page's rate under the cap is measured first. Under 55 fps the frame criteria aren't judged, and the gate says so.
  This laptop's iGPU really draws 1600 x 900 and the phone proxy at ~52 fps once Chrome presents every frame; the
  earlier headless "120 fps" were vsync'd headless frames that weren't really presented.
- Baselines are kept per adapter (`data/baselines/tilegate/<vendor>-<architecture>/`), written on an adapter's first
  run. Vendors differ by 1.5-12% of a frame.
- The phone screen runs with a Pixel's user agent, so the page takes its phone paths (finish tiles, pacing, uploads).
- New views: `run` (`?run=bell`, zooms 14/8/5, desktop and phone) and `w384` (the atlas at window 384, the user's phone
  setting).
- A new reason, `window-undrawn`: a window chunk neither meshed nor the grid's, and no tile. It's counted only while the
  CPU's built-chunk mirror is the current slide's.

**Tiles a frame off the phone.** When the tiles' lane has 3 or more turns waiting, the pacer's guard may climb to
`TILE_MAX_FILL` (16), one more turn per on-time frame and halved by a long one. Off a phone: 12 regions in flight and 8
bakes a frame (a phone keeps 4 turns, 6 in flight, 4 bakes).

| fillFrames (budget 180) | before (`&tilemaxfill=4&tilelandn=6&tilebakes=4`) | after |
|---|---|---|
| desktop 1600 x 900, z2.2 | 420 | 240 |
| desktop, z1.3 | over 540 (24% still out) | 180 |
| phone proxy (phone paths, unchanged), z1.3 | over 540 (1% out) | 270 |

**TF5, the eye side** (the user's option (a)). A tile on the eye's side is no longer left out whole. `fsTile` discards
what of it rises into the line from the eye to the focus: the rings' rule (far.wgsl `underFocus`, 0.85 of the line's
height, from 12 world units on). What's behind it shows through, the focus with it. The focus is in TileU.focus.

**The pan bench's disk rows were mostly generated land.** On the phone each disk ramp brought 6-7 regions from disk and
made the rest (z14: 242 made, 6 loaded). The fill pan stopped once it had been asked to go the line's length, but it
had waited at the window's edge for its slides, so it saved a line a third as long as the ramp then went. The fill now
runs until the camera has gone the length (up to 180 s), and `came` reports `storeMiss`, `mismatched`, `loadFailed` and
the store's size. Desktop, z14 disk ramp: 187 loaded, 430 made, store 568. So TF4 (the disk hitch) can't be judged from
the phone runs so far.

**Disk to RAM ahead** (the user: "Is there any way we can cache from disk to the GPU or RAM proactively to speed this
up?"). What exists: the streamer prefetches regions ahead of the motion (`Streamer.prefetch`, up to AHEAD_MAX strips at
the camera's speed). That `bring`s each one: the store's get, read off the thread in its worker, then the record decoded
on the main thread (`decodeRecord`, slices), then uploaded into a pool slot. So land made ahead from disk arrives as a
pool hit. Nothing is added yet: the phone's disk rows have to stream from disk first (above) to show what's slow.

**Open.**
- The phone path's fill at z1.3 takes 270 frames, over the 180 budget. More turns a frame on the phone when the lane is
  backed up is the lever; the phone bench should decide it.
- A grey sliver at a region's edge in one panning frame (desktop z3.5).

### Round 112, `tilefix2` (2): the 3080's premerge gate run (29 failures), read

The run is on origin/runner/tilegate-premerge, runner-results/tilegate-premerge/.

- **"window-undrawn" on every pan** (z14 59-63%, z8 29-36%) was a false positive. The pan shots are drawn whole. The
  check reads the CPU's mirror of the built chunks, which is read back every 60th frame, and the hybrid's grid, and the
  two move at different moments around a slide. It isn't the clear() change: a slide goes through hybrid.shift, not
  clear. Main asked to keep judging pans. While the gate runs, the mirror is read back every frame (`FieldMesh.statPeriod`
  1; 60 in play), and a chunk counts once it has been read undrawn for 5 frames running, keyed by its place in the
  world. A readback is a frame or two behind, so a flash of an undrawn chunk longer than that is still caught.
- **The slow wide fills** (desktop z1.3 43% out after 540 frames, "none" 212) were mostly the gate's own 60 Hz cap. After
  a late tick it caught up, so the next frame was ~7 ms. That pulled the tile pacer's low envelope (`base`) to 8-11 ms.
  Every 17 ms frame then counted as long, and the guard sat at one turn.
  - *Shown on the laptop with `--throttle 3`:* base 7.8-11.7 ms, guard 1.
  - *Fix:* each tick a whole period after the last, less a ms, with no catching up; base then read 15-18 ms.
  - *What's left is real:* at 3x CPU throttle the page is CPU-bound at 38-45 fps, so the guard rightly holds one turn,
    and a 1.3 screenful can't fill in 180 frames there.
- I tried a guard averaged over four frames while filling. Under 3x throttle it made no difference, so it's removed.
- **The gate:**
  - one frame threshold, the criterion itself (58 fps), for every view (w384 was judged at 55.5 while others weren't);
  - "frames not judged" is a note, not a failure;
  - `--throttle N` (CDP);
  - each row records the tile pipeline: the pacer's perFrame, guard and base, the land's made, baked, inFlight and noSlot.

## Round 112 (2026-10-29, session 5, `tilefix3`) — the zoom held to what the device's tiles can fill; lava in the tiles

The user, verbatim: "Hero is still not loading tiles for the on the phone. The atlas has pop in of details like magma
that pop in and some tiles just never load. Can you just limit the zoom to max supported tile size for the device then
if any are missing we know it's a bug for sure?" And, after `&world=new`: "Same issue with the new world tag. The tiles
load in very slowly over multiple seconds and still don't fill the whole screen so I think the zoom is too far for the
phone."

**The zoom floor.**
- `Camera.zoom` is an accessor that never goes under `Camera.zoomFloor`, whoever sets it: every mode's input, the
  director, scripts.
- The renderer's TileCache sets the floor every 30 frames (`TileCache.zoomFloor`). It's the widest zoom at which the
  screen's regions fit, counted with the look-ahead's margin (MARGIN² of the screen's ground, plus a region's ring):
  - each in the part of a slot it takes at that zoom (whole, half or quarter), within 80% of the atlas's slots;
  - and no more of them than the land makes in 300 frames at the path's rate: 0.3 tiles a frame on a phone (the gate's
    phone-path fill, ~81 tiles in 270 frames at z1.3), 2 elsewhere. `?tilerate=` and `?floorframes=` set them;
    `?zoomfloor=0` turns the floor off.
- A level without a streamed window (the playground, the noise lab) has no tiles and so no floor.
- Inside the floor every view should be all detail: a miss there is a bug. The gate's rows report `zoom` and
  `zoomFloor`.

**Lava in the tiles.** The window draws lava as its own sheet of instances. A tile's bake draws only the mesh and grid,
so a tile showed the rock under the lava, and the magma "popped in" as a region came into the window.
- `renderfields.wgsl` now writes a column under molten rock deeper than 0.15 as z = 2 + its heat. The bake
  (`tiles.wgsl` `tileBake`) paints it with the window's look (render.wgsl): hot orange to yellow-white by heat, and a
  crust with glowing seams as it cools. It lies flat, with no porosity.
- The only other reader of z, the firelight (render.wgsl `lighting`), decodes it with `glowOf`.
- The tile's own world runs RenderFieldsSystem on its land, so render-only tiles carry it too.
- *Open:* a tile's lava isn't lit by its own light at night (no emissive bit left in the atlas), and a frozen tile keeps
  its lava as baked.

**The hero's grey screen with a saved world** (the user: `&world=new` draws it, their saved world doesn't). Under
investigation with scripts/herorepro.mjs: a saved world kept in a Chrome profile between launches, an older build's
saved by one, loaded by another. The lead is the relief (colTop), which is restored from the record, not rebuilt; the
hybrid judges a chunk out of the window's z from it.

**Measured (tilefix3, the laptop's iGPU, the gate at window 320 and 384).**
- The floor: desktop 1600 x 900 holds at zoom 2.57; the phone proxy (a Pixel's UA, the phone's paths) at 2.78, at
  window 384 too.
- Inside it, every zoom from 14 down to the floor was 0% out of detail, parked and panning, and filled within 180
  frames. One exception: desktop z14 while panning, 2.3% "window-undrawn" in one frame at a slide (TX5's slide, or the
  filter's 5 frames short of it).
- The saved world: a run=bell world saved by places 4ce9840 (window 384, a Pixel's UA, 36 regions touched and saved)
  and loaded by tilefix3 on the same origin restored all 36 regions. The window drew 92% of its chunks (8 meshed, 147
  grid, the rest voxel chunks still meshing), the hero on grass (C:/Projects/shots88/tilegate/hero-new-load.png). So a
  world saved by today's builds restores; the relief theory isn't confirmed. Left to rule out on the user's phone: a
  stale cached bundle, a much older world, their run's own saved progress (their quest arrow said 3030 m, ours 120 m).

## 2026-10-29 — round 112 (bgcheck): the background colour caught on the GPU, in the pan bench and the tile gate

The user: "Can we do a pan test for the phone that fails if any bg color shows?" then "Or flags it anyway".

**What it measures.** `?bgcheck=1` (render/bgcheck.ts). The world pass keeps its depth and pick targets (stored, not
discarded; TEXTURE_BINDING added) and after it one compute pass samples them on a coarse grid, 64 x 128 on a portrait
screen (128 x 64 landscape), 8192 samples: depth still the clear 1.0 → **background** (the clear colour: no geometry,
tile or far land wrote there); else pick (0, 0xfa000000) → **far land** (far.wgsl fsFar now writes that tag; x 0 is
"nothing" to Renderer.pick so picking is unchanged; tiles write (0, 0), so the far land is told apart from a tile
cheaply — the rings' fsLod and the quartz giants aren't tagged). Workgroup atomics, one global add a workgroup, a
1-thread pass folds the frame into running totals (frames, frames with any, summed, worst frame — for both); a
readback (mapAsync) 4 times a second zeroes them. No swapchain read. Without the flag nothing is made and the world
pass's store ops are as before (play pays nothing). Checked: the pinholes it found are exactly the clear colour
(screenshot pixels 101,110,119 = light.clear 0.397,0.432,0.466).

**Cost** (scripts/lib/runner timing check, phone proxy 412x915 dpr 2.6 q=low, atlas parked at zoom 5, desktop iGPU,
A B A B, 150-180 GPU frames each): the bgcheck pass 0.024 ms p50 / 0.028 mean. The world pass with the stores on
2.69 / 2.36 ms p50 against 2.11 / 2.81 off — inside the run-to-run noise. On a tiled phone GPU the two stores (12

The user, after the stable build's phone bench (data/bench/pixel9a-pan-stable.json: background on 14-58% of the screen

cover it? It seems cheap though and I don't buy your theory." Main's theory (untested): the screen is inside the live
window at close zoom, fast panning outruns the window's slide and mesh rebuild, the look-ahead doesn't scale with
speed, and since the pool (in-memory) runs were worst it isn't generation. The streaming design the user approved
(https://claude.ai/artifact/UnqDENhSKGH1abe7pxWiNh: layers 0 stand-in, 1 tile, 2 height grid, 3 full window) makes
this its migration step 1: measure the chain, add the geometric check, show it agrees with the pixel check.

**The tools.** scripts/holediag.mjs: pans on the phone proxy (412x915, dpr 2.6, q=low, a Pixel's UA, window 256, the
pan bench's flags; `--throttle 4` slows the CPU four times, the phone's main thread) and for each frame the pixel check
(render/bgcheck.ts snapshot) samples, classifies every background sample by what the CPU knew that frame, the sample's
view ray marched down to the first chunk whose highest column top it passes under (a first version put the point on the
ground at the camera's height — 25-50 cells off on this land, and misattributed half the holes). scripts/chaintime.mjs:
per region that comes into the window during the pan, the time of each link from wanted to drawn.

**The chain, timed** (z14, window 256, phone proxy with the CPU at 1/4, ms from the slide; data: shots88/tilesfirst/
chain-before.json):

| link | 40 c/s line | 80 c/s line | 80 c/s pool |
|---|---|---|---|
| land asked (prefetch) | −634 | −697 | −670 |
| land made (in the pool) | −241 | −993 (one −17) | −907 |
| slid → written into the window | 27 (max 81) | 18-27 (max 72) | 17 (max 32) |
| written → the grid draws it (READY_TICKS, 3-6 sim ticks) | **199** (max 232) | **99-101** (max 152) | **98** (max 132) |
| a tile of it drawn inside the window | only while none of its 4 chunks is drawn | same | same |

The land is made 0.2-1 s before the slide needs it, the slide writes it in 1-2 frames: **neither generation nor the
slide is the slow link**. The slowest is the hand-off to drawing: the hybrid grid waits READY_TICKS (3) sim ticks after
the write, and the sim doesn't tick while the slide is busy writing the rest of its strip — 100-230 ms in which the
region is in the window, written, and drawn by nothing: with the tiles on (the default) there are no LOD rings
(level.ts `lod = tilesOn ? null`), and the window region's tile (TC9) draws only while **none** of the region's four
chunks is drawn (and only when the CPU's mirror of the mesh is in step with the slides). A region whose chunks come in
one by one, or that has a chunk neither the grid's nor voxels (outZ: its land under the window's floor), has no cover.

**Where the holes were** (holediag, same proxy, `standin=0`; shares of the background samples): the region's tile was
**in the atlas and not drawn** (`+held`) in 77-100% of them; by chunk state: the grid not ready yet 35-85% (the
READY_TICKS wait), the window's mirror saying drawn — the voxel mesh built and in view, or the grid's first frames —
15-61%, voxel mesh not built 4-23%, slid in but not written 0-29% (pool 80, one frame), chunk culled on the CPU with
stale tops ~26% of one run. Never: a region that was never asked for. So main's theory was half right: the holes are in
the window, at close zoom, worse from the pool — but not because the slide or the mesh can't keep up with the camera
(the land was made a second early); because nothing covers a region between its land being written and its drawing
being ready, and a made tile was held back. The look-ahead not growing with speed didn't cause these (2 strips ahead
were enough at 80 c/s); it would at the bike's speeds with the pull-back.

**The old "out of detail" metric** (bench.ts writtenShare / missingWhere, the gate's measure) counted a point inside the
window as detailed once its region was **written**, not drawn — exactly the 100-230 ms these holes live in — and put the
point on the ground at the focus's height. **The geometric check** (render/coverage.ts, TileCache.coverCheck,
Renderer.windowDrawn): the camera's orthographic view against each window chunk's box (its lowest to highest column top:
the hybrid's) and each region past the window (its heights as the CPU knows them, Atlas.zRange); each seen piece is
drawn if the window draws it this frame (the grid's and in the grid's view, or the voxel mesh's built and in view) or a
tile of its region is drawn; the undrawn pieces' footprint quads at their middle height, clipped to the screen, are the
share. CPU only, a few hundred boxes, run every frame by the bench and the gate. **It agrees with the pixel check**: in

**The bench and the gate.** The pan bench's step has `geo` (max, mean, frames with any, chunks and regions undrawn) and

## 2026-10-30 — round 113 (`tilesfirst`, step 3): tiles as cover — a window region's tile draws wherever the window doesn't

The user's "load the fast tiles first and then something is always there and swap only when the slow one is ready".

  uniform written by a compute pass (the buffer UNIFORM | STORAGE). TC9's `arriving` is gone.
- **Tiles asked for inside the window.** TileCache.wanted no longer skips the window: a point whose chunk the window
  doesn't draw for sure asks for its region's tile (the render-only land, made from the atlas as past the window).
- **Grow with speed (the tiles' part).** The look-ahead's seconds are TileCache.tileLatency (the 90th percentile of the
