## 2026-10-30 — round 113 (`tilesfirst`, step 4): the planner — reach by speed × measured latency, holes first, rendering before simulation

The user: "It's really dumb not to grow with speed" and "Prioritize rendering over simulation too".
- **scenes/planner.ts `StreamPlanner`**, once a frame from level.ts (`planFrame`, before the streamer's update): reads
  the camera's motion, the geometric coverage (the footprint), and three measured latencies — land (Streamer.landLatency:
  asked to made, p90 of the last 24), window (slid in to every chunk drawn by the window, measured by the planner, p90),
  tiles (TileCache.tileLatency) — and gives each consumer its reach in cells along the motion: speed × latency + 96
  (a region and a half). Consumers, each through one field: Streamer.reach (`land`: the strips asked ahead,
  AHEAD..AHEAD_MAX; `slide`: the slide judges where the camera will be in the window's latency, at most a region, along
  the motion only), FieldMesh.lead (the chunks where the view will be are near: rebuilt first), TileCache.reach (the
  tiles' look-ahead), TilePacer.holes and WorldCore.simCap.
- **Holes first, rendering before simulation.** While the footprint has undrawn land (now or within 30 frames): the tile
  pacer gives its lane every turn it asks for and the frame's whole room (else 0.33-0.8 of it by speed); the sim's ticks
  a frame are cut to 1, its time kept up to half a second and caught up after (WorldCore.advance).
- **SF7, step 1's slowest link.** Land written into the window is prepared for drawing at once: WorldCore.prepareArrived
  runs the surface and render-field passes over every column (SurfaceSystem / RenderFieldsSystem `all`: no sleep skip —
  the new strip's drowse bits may not be in the Globals yet) and the hybrid's landBox marks it ready now (no
  READY_TICKS): written → the grid draws it 85-230 ms → 0-40 ms (chaintime, phone proxy, CPU 1/4: chain-after.json;
  0-2 sim ticks). `?arriveprep=0` as before.
- `?planner=0` no planner; `?planoff=slide,tile,mesh,sim,pacer` one consumer left as before (the A/B).
- **The coverage check's cost.** The first step-4 gate ran 3 fps under step 3 in every view, parked too: the coverage
  check, now run by the planner every frame as well as by the gate, cost 1.3 ms of CPU — Atlas.zRange (10 µs a call)
  for every region of a 6-region reach. Now only the regions under the screen's corners' footprint at the land's lowest
  and highest are looked at, and TileLandGpu caches each region's heights: 0.03 ms. The gate's pages ran 50-52.5 fps
  under the 60 Hz cap (step 3: 47-50), p99 21-30 ms. The stand-in's grid has half the far land's vertices a side.

**Measured.** Repeated A/B (holediag, phone proxy, z14 and z8 at 80 and 160 c/s from the gate's spot, three runs each,
worst-frame geometric / pixel-hole %): planner on — z14/160 0.0 / 1.4-1.5, z8/80 0.3-0.5 / 0-0.5, z8/160 0-0.1 /

them, which the hitch recorder can only call "browser" or "gpu-busy". The user: the hero run "framerate feels bad";
the goal a steady 60. It was the same on the stable build, so not the streaming redesign.

What the phone's reports already say (data/bench, bench v4 2026-10-28, win256 parked): GPU frame span (timestamp
first pass begin to last end) p50 12.2, p95 18.4, max 22.5 ms; the span grows with the window (320: 15.9, 384: 30.9,
448: 40.2, 512: 53.9 p50) while the canvas is tiny — the phone's low tier renders at 205x393 (dpr capped at 1, render
scale 0.5; canvas bgra8unorm, opaque). So the frame is GPU work that scales with what's drawn and simulated, not with
pixels, and at 256 its tail crosses 16.7 ms. The phone has timestamp-query; Mali's timestamps are sane within a pass,
not summed across passes (round 102), so the span is the number to trust, the per-pass ones only roughly.

**The probe** (src/perf/framepace.ts, `?hitch=1` — every bench page — or `?framepace=1`): per rendered frame the rAF
interval, the lag from the rAF timestamp to its callback, the callback's CPU, rAF to the frame's last submit, last
submit to onSubmittedWorkDone, the frames still on the GPU when it began (main.ts holds a rAF at 2), the rAFs held, the
GPU span, the gap between this frame's GPU begin and the last one's end (≈0: the GPU never idles), its passes, the sim
ticks it ran and the slow-period systems due, and which counters moved (the coarse world's step parts, the streamer's
work). `report()` sets the slow frames (over 1.25 vsync) against the rest and against the frame before each.
Profiler got `listen()` (a listener list) so the probe hears the GPU without taking the hitch recorder's `onFrame`.

**The pan bench (v6)** runs it parked at each zoom before the ramps, 4 s a phase: `timed` (timestamps read back),
`untimed` (as the game plays), and at the first zoom `inFlight1`, `inFlight3` (main.ts's pacing limit) and `simOff`
(every sim system's encode a no-op). `summary.pace` has a line per zoom; `pan256.zooms[].pace` the whole. The phone's
next run (https://csheldondante.github.io/Reclaimed/framepace/?bench=pan&panwin=256&benchzooms=14_8_5) says which:
the GPU span over 16.7 ms on the slow frames (and which passes), done latency holding rAFs (held > 0, inFlight 2), the
sim's ticks (`slowFramesByTicks`), or none of ours (lag or interval long with the GPU idle: the browser).

**Desktop proxy** (scripts/paceprobe.mjs, headless iGPU at the phone's shape, q=low, window 256, zoom 14, parked; the
headless display runs ~100 Hz, so its 9.6 ms frame against ~7-9 ms of GPU is about the phone's 16.7 against 12):
- GPU span p50 6.7 ms; `draw` 3.6 of it — geometry, not pixels at 206x457: skipping the field mesh saves 1.4 ms,
  the grid 1.0, the far land (the stand-in under the whole view, SF2) 0.9, plants 0.5; then renderprep 0.3-0.6,
  fieldmesh-hash 0.3, gbuffer 0.24, shadow 0.23. The sim off changes nothing measurable (ticks 0-1 a frame at 100 Hz).
- submit to done p50 9.5 ms against a 6.7 ms span: half the frames begin with the last one still on the GPU (inFlight
  1); `inFlight1` halves the rate (60 → ~51 uncapped, 101 → 61 at vsync): the pacing limit of 2 is needed, 3 changes
  nothing parked.
- **the coarse world's step** (atlas/coarse.ts: flux, depth over 512x512 cells and an 8 MB copy back; every 4th frame,
  untimed till now) is the largest spike: those frames' span 11.5 ms against 6.7 (flux 0.9, depth 2.2, the copy the
  rest). In the bench's pan page 96% of the slow frames ran it against ~75% of the others.

**The change**: Coarse.stepPart — the step's three parts (flux, depth, copy) on three frames of four, the same step at
the same rate (the cells everyone reads are the step's before till the copy; an event or a whole `step()` finishes a
step under way first). ?coarseparts=0 the whole step every 4th frame, to compare. Both steps' passes timed now
(`coarse-flux`, `coarse-depth`). Desktop, uncapped: GPU span p95 11.2 → 9.9, p99 12.3 → 10.8 ms (p50 6.7 → 7.3: the
work moved, not removed); at vsync, two runs each: p95 10.4 / 10.4 → 9.35 / 9.36, submit-to-done p95 12.1 / 11.3 →
10.9 / 10.9. The headless desktop drops almost no frames either way (0-2 in 625), so the phone's run is the judge.
The per-cell look is untouched.

Not changed, for the phone's numbers to decide (BACKLOG FP4, FP5): the draw's geometry (the far stand-in drawn inside
the window too), 2-tick sim frames ("Prioritize rendering over simulation too": a frame-locked tick when the rate
is the display's), the pacing limit.

## 2026-10-30 — round 114 (`framepace`, FP4): the frame-locked tick

Why: the Pixel 9a's bench v6 run on `framepace` (scratchpad pixel9a-pan-framepace.json; the user: "Subjectively this
one looked really good with very little pop in and pretty smooth"). Parked, GPU span p50 6.2-6.6 ms, p95 10-11 (of
16.7); slow frames 2-8 of ~245, and they ran 1.5-2 sim ticks on average against 0.8 for the rest. With the sim off,
or three frames in flight, none of 249 was slow; with one in flight 20. 20% of frames ran no tick at all (zoom 14
timed: 45 frames 0 ticks, 200 one, 2 two). So the drops left are the sim's 2-tick frames: the fixed-step accumulator
against a 60 Hz display at the 60 Hz tick rate drifts in phase, and the rAF's jitter puts it either side of a tick
boundary — 0, 1 or 2 ticks a frame. (The slow frames also began late: rAF lag 5-7 ms, the last submit 10 ms in.)

The change: sim/tickclock.ts, behind `WorldCore.clock.take(simDt, speed, maxTicks, keep)`:
- 'locked' (the default): when the display's median rAF interval over the last 31 frames is within 12% of the tick
  (and speed 1), a frame runs exactly one tick — rendering first.
- Drift: what's owed (or run ahead) stays in `acc` as the accumulator's did. Past two ticks owed it runs one extra tick,
  past one ahead it skips one, never two corrections within 20 frames (4 once it's past 100 ms owed — a planner's cut,
  a stall). Past 0.5 s owed it's dropped, as the accumulator dropped time rather than spiral. Sim time stays true over
  the long run (below: within 30 ms over 2 minutes).
- Any other display rate (90/120 Hz: 0/1 a frame; 30 Hz: 2), speed, or `?tick=accum`: the accumulator as before.
- Counters `clock.stats` (frames, locked frames, ticks, extra, skipped, dropped); the bench's parked pace records them
  each phase (`tickClock`), and bench v7 adds a `tickAccum` phase (the accumulator) at the first zoom beside untimed
  (locked), inFlight1/3 and simOff — the phone's next run compares directly.

scripts/tickclock-sim.ts (made-up displays, 120 s each; ticks a frame 0 / 1 / 2, sim time less real):
| display | accumulator | locked |
|---|---|---|
| 60 Hz, 1 ms jitter | 117 / 6974 / 113, -9 ms | 4 / 7199 / 1, +7 ms |
| 60 Hz, 3 ms jitter | 336 / 6550 / 325, -9 ms | 19 / 7184 / 8, -9 ms |
| 59.94 Hz | 118 / 6958 / 121, -12 ms | 1 / 7192 / 4, -12 ms |
| 60.5 Hz | 135 / 7060 / 70, -16 ms | 65 / 7199 / 1, +1 ms |
| 60 Hz, a vsync missed every 40 frames | 114 / 6630 / 285 (each miss followed by a 2-tick frame) | 1 / 6857 / 171 (paid back 20+ frames later), -29 ms |
| 60 Hz, the planner cuts 30 frames | -476 ms (dropped once the cut lifted) | +7 ms (paid back) |
| 120 / 90 / 30 Hz | 0/1, 0/1, 2 | the same (not locked) |

Desktop: the headless (and headful) Chrome here presents at ~100 Hz, and its rAF can't be held to 60 Hz on a whole
vsync grid (scripts/paceprobe.mjs --hz with --uncapped gives ~19 ms frames), so the clock never locks there — rightly:
it measured a 10 ms (and 19 ms) display and ran the accumulator, the ticks a frame identical to `tickAccum` (0: 340,
1: 490 of 830 at 100 Hz; 1: 358, 2: 66 at 52 Hz). The locked path is checked by scripts/tickclock-sim.ts above; the
phone's v7 run (`untimed` locked against `tickAccum`, `tickClock` per phase: lockedFrames, extra, skipped) is the
measure. Bench v7 ran end to end headless (pan page, zoom 14, no errors).
## 2026-10-30 — round 114 (`covercheck`): why the geometric check missed the stand-in — the tiles' eye-side cut (SF13)

**The disagreement.** On the user's Pixel 9a pan bench (places) the geometric coverage check read no pop-in up to
640 c/s at zooms 14, 8, 5 on the disk and pool rows while the pixel check's far share was 4-10% of a frame at 160 c/s
(z8, z5), 30-75% at 320-480 and 100% at 640. And the user, on the phone (world=new, window 384): "sometimes there is a
screenspace band of low detail that never loads even as I pan around" (user-band-1.png, user-band-2.png).

**Found, not assumed.** scripts/covshot.mjs (new) pans, and for every frame the pixel check samples it takes the
geometric check of that same frame (bgcheck's encode hook), the classes split (render/bgcheck.ts's snapshot now tells
the stand-in, class 2, from the far land drawn nearer, class 3), and a screenshot with the classes over it; `--stopat`
stops the pan on the first frame with that much far and lists each far sample's region (in the window or not, its
tile drawn or not). What it showed:
- The far samples past the window were regions with a tile drawn this frame (holediag: `far:out+tile`), baked long
  before (600 frames) — not missing, not stale. The far region was a horizontal band across the whole screen, tiles
  drawn above and below it (shots88/covercheck/dbg-desktop-z14-v640.png, tiles tinted).
- Tinting instead of discarding what fsTile's eye-side cut (TF5, round 112) takes (a temporary shader edit): the band
  was the cut (cutdbg2-desktop-z14-v640.png, cyan). With the cut tinted, not discarded, desktop z5/z8 at 40 c/s went
  from 2-4% stand-in a frame to 0.03-0.06%.
- Two faults in the cut. Its focus was the camera's target, whose z stays where the window placed it while the camera
  pans (only a slide's tier shift moves it): over land higher than that, everything on the eye's side over the line
  was cut. And its rule is the rings' wedge (far.wgsl underFocus): a point is cut by its distance toward the eye and its
  height, wherever it is across the screen — the eye's direction is the screen's vertical, so it's a band the screen's
  whole width, not the line from the eye to the focus (a point on the screen). The rings press their land down, so
  their wedge only flattens it; a tile's discard leaves a hole, and behind a tile's own land there's only the stand-in.
- The geometric check counts a region with a drawn tile as covered, so it never saw the holes. The pixel side wasn't
  the wrong one: the far pick is written by far.wgsl fsFar and the stand-in only, and class 3 (fsFar nearer) was
  under 0.3% of a frame throughout.
- Not what showed here: every far sample the stop-frame probe placed past the window was in a region with a tile drawn
  that frame, so neither the check's reach (6 regions past the window) nor a missing or late tile; the sea (on the
  straight route the far share over open sea is the stand-in's sea under the water: SF8/SF11 as before — the comparison
  route below stays inland).

**The fix.** (1) `Camera.focus`: the ground the screen's centre shows — down the view's ray through the target, the
first point at or under `Camera.ground` (api/atlas-world.ts: the window's own column tops, none past it or in a region
not written yet); null where none, and then no cut and no pressing (TileU.focus w 0, FarLand.focus null). The rings get
the same focus. (2) fsTile cuts a point only when it is (a) over the line to the focus (the rule as was), (b) within
FOCUS_HOLE (0.2 of the screen's shorter side) of the focus on the screen — only that can hide the focus — and (c) where
the view's ray behind it runs into the window's footprint before the window's floor (hidesWindow): what the hole opens
is the window's land. The hole's size is a judgement call for the user (TF5's "not hiding the focus"). No change to
the geometric check: with the holes gone it agrees.

**Measured** (desktop 1600 x 900, the gate's spot 15024,14337, back and forth over 400 cells up the screen so every run
sees the same land, 3 s a run, every system on; the stand-in's share of a frame, mean / worst frame, against the

## 2026-10-30 — round 114 (`worldstore`): a saved world from another generator; the generator's version a hash of its sources; a run's places made fresh

The user (DECISIONS round 114): "Without the flag my world seems to me glitched … I think the intention was to have
places regenerated from the atlas data the first time you visit each run (as long as it can be deterministic from
seed)". (The flag: `?world=new`.)

**The cause, reproduced.** `GEN_VERSION` (world/region-record.ts) was a hand-bumped number. `git log -S GEN_VERSION`
shows only round 100 adding it as 1 and gpugen touching it. It never moved through rivers, the vertical datum, lava,
caves and the rest. So a region saved by an older build loaded next to land made by the new generator. The test
(scripts/worldstale.mjs) uses one browser profile and one origin (IndexedDB is per origin), with each build served on
port 5291 in turn. First d26891c (10-29, record format 2 like places) touched and saved all 25 regions of the
window. Then places 3604bc2 opened the same profile: "25 saved regions of atlas:1 restored", mismatched 0. Its shot
(shots88/worldstore/2-places-saved-world.png) differs from `?world=new` (3-places-world-new.png): the lake at the top
is gone, the rivers are reshaped, and the snow field has straight region-edged seams.

**The fix: the generator's version is derived, never bumped.** scripts/lib/gen-sources.mjs walks the value imports
from four entries: atlas/atlas.ts, world/streamgen.ts, settle/settlements.ts and story/stage-land.ts (the generator,
the noise land and the two stamp hooks). It includes their `?raw` WGSL and JSON data. Type-only imports are erased
by the compiler, so it skips them. It doesn't descend into gpu, sim, tune, weather, grids, gm, units, render, ui or
scenes: the generator calls into those (riverMode from sim/world-gpu, the pipeline helpers), but their code doesn't
decide what land is made. The result is 41 files (`node scripts/lib/gen-sources.mjs` lists them). The version is the
first 16 hex digits of a SHA-1 over each file's path and LF-normalised text, so a Windows checkout and the Pages
build agree. vite.config.ts defines it as `__GEN_HASH__`, and `GEN_VERSION` is that string (71eeb082ad1625e3 here).
A comment added to atlas/sites.ts gives 26adacb1217bbab5. A render or UI edit doesn't change it. The hash is
deliberately wide: a stale region beside fresh land is a visible bug, while a dropped save is only lost changes.

**Stale saves handled once, as the store opens.** The store's meta rows now carry `gen`. A new worker op, `prune`,
reads the meta rows of every world in one transaction and drops three kinds of record:
- this world's records of another generator;
- every record with no `gen` (rounds 100-113, any world: no build from now on can use them);
- when a run opens, this seed's earlier runs' records.

It logs one console line. Other worlds' records stay: every branch's Pages build shares the origin, so they share
the database, and another branch may still use them. A world opened under a different generator keeps only that
generator's records. The header check in `Streamer.load` stays as a backstop.
- With the old d26891c save under the fix's build: "[worldsave] dropped 25 saved regions made by another land
  generator (this build's is 71eeb082ad1625e3): made again from the seed — atlas:1: 25". The store is left empty and
  the window matches `?world=new` (4-fix-old-save-dropped.png against 3).
- Saved with the fix's build and opened again by the same build: 25 restored, 0 mismatched.
- Opened by the build with the edited generator: dropped 25, "this build's is 26adacb1217bbab5".

**The world id carries the options.** `atlas:<seed>~<fnv>` hashes the atlas's other parameters (`?a.*`), the river
mode and whether land comes in settled. Before, a world made with other options loaded this one's records.

**Runs.** `?run=` was a story id, so `atlas:1:run=bell` persisted across reloads. Yet a reload restarts the run: the
story's objectives are fresh, `runWorld` restores no snapshot, and the world's run number is always 0. So a new run
saw the last one's land. Now a run is its own world, `:run=<story>@<instance>`, with a new instance each page load
(`?runinst=` names one, for tests or a future resume). Its places are made from the seed the first time they're
visited and keep their changes for the run. Earlier runs' records on this seed are dropped as it opens.
worldsavetest `--run` (`--onlyrun`, dev server, all ok):
- `&runinst=wst` reload: the opened door's land comes back (plug 0).
- A load without it is a new run: the door is shut (plug 47, as before it was opened), and "dropped 1 regions of
  earlier runs".

Without `?run=`, nothing changes: the plain atlas world persists across reloads until `?world=new`. The user is to
say whether it should be fresh each load (BACKLOG WV4).

**Deterministic from the seed: yes, for the four regions tried.** scripts/gendeterm.mjs uses `Streamer.genHash`, which
makes a region with regionInto and WINDOW_MAKE into a spare pool slot and hashes its columns (world z) and every byte.
It ran on the dev server at q=low 412x915 with every system on. The regions were E (the window's corner), A (the
middle), G (by the spawn's settlement) and F (20 regions east), visited four ways:
1. in order;
2. reversed;
3. after a warp 40 regions away;
4. on a second page spawned at F, reversed.

Every region gave 1 column hash and 1 byte hash in all four. No order or history dependence was found, settlements'
stamps included.

**Disk to RAM to GPU (TY7, WV5).** This is a note and a design, not built here. A saved region reaches the GPU in
three steps:
1. The store's worker runs one op at a time: an IndexedDB get, inflate, unshuffle.
2. The main thread runs `decodeRecord`, copying out each section.
3. `pump` uploads the record's raw body into a pool slot at UPLOAD_BYTES a frame: 0.5 MB on a phone, 2 MB on the
   desktop.

The sizes, measured:
- A body is 1.64 MB (1.8 MB with its CPU parts), 145 KB compressed: 25 regions were 45.2 MB raw, 3.6 MB packed.
- Only 7.8% of a generated region's slot words are non-zero (region A: 33,412 of 430,080). The rest is empty slots
  and planes.

So on a phone each disk region takes about 4 frames of the upload budget. That caps arrival near 60 × 0.5 / 1.8 ≈ 16
regions a second, which is the ~15 a second the Pixel 9a bench showed. Generated land doesn't pay this cost:
finish.wgsl writes it straight into its slot. The worker's time per get looked small next to that (single-digit ms
on the desktop, but measured while the GPU was shared, so not a timing).

The proposal, for the streaming planner (covercheck / tilesfirst's files):
- (a) A RAM tier in the worker. The store's index already says which regions near the camera are saved, without a
  read, so their compressed records can be read into the worker's memory well past the pool's reach (~145 KB each,
  so 100 regions ≈ 15 MB).
- (b) Decode in the worker, and hand the main thread transferred typed arrays.
- (c) A sparse upload: only the non-zero words with a run table, expanded into the slot by a compute pass. At 7.8%
  non-zero that is ~10x fewer bytes a region, in the same per-frame budget.
- (d) In the planner's reach, ask for disk regions before generated ones, since they arrive slower.
- (e) Size the pool against window + ahead + the disk prefetch.

Also noted (WV6): tiles are made from the generator, never from a record, so a region that play changed shows its
generated land in the tiles until the window holds it.

The shots were taken while the GPU was shared with another agent's run: visual and correctness only, no timings.
Shots are in C:\Projects\shots88\worldstore\ (1-old-build-saved, 2-places-saved-world, 3-places-world-new,
4-fix-old-save-dropped, 5-fix2-other-gen-dropped).

## 2026-10-30 — round 114 (main): the test runner served an empty build without saying so

Merging covercheck and worldstore, the tile gate's first page never booted (no boot marks in 240 s). Both branches passed
alone. The cause was the runner, not the merge: in the agent's sandboxed Bash shell every directory rename inside
.testcache fails EPERM, and `build()` took a failed rename for another run having built the same sources, deleted its
build and served the missing directory. It now throws when the rename fails and no other build is there. Runner-based
scripts were run from PowerShell, where the rename works.

## 2026-10-30 — round 115 (`tilecal`): the tiles calibrated to the device and the screen (the user's wide monitor)

The user, verbatim (DECISIONS round 115): "the desktop version on my wide monitor does not load all the tiles (and I
assume it is considerably more powerful than the phone) which seems like it is an issue with the implementation
because I don't think the PC streaming should be that slow if it is just a heightmap. ... Worth spawning one subagent
to investigate on the PC and see if it is an issue with settings and if so make the runtime calibrate to the hardware."

**Reproduction** (this laptop's Intel Xe iGPU, D3D11; the tile gate at 1600 x 900 and three ultrawides at dpr 1 —
2560 x 1080, 3440 x 1440, 5120 x 1440, new `--screens uw2560,uw3440,uw5120` — parked at zooms 14-1.3 and panning at
20 and 80 c/s; places 3c850b9). Parked, every size loaded whole: 0 out of detail, 0 background (one transient 0.61% at
5120 z5, 9 of 97 frames). What changed with the screen was the **zoom floor**: 2.57 at 1600 x 900, 3.12, 4.27, 5.2 at
5120 x 1440 — the camera couldn't zoom out past it, and the wider the screen the closer it held. The pans showed the
stand-in at the arriving edge on every size, 1600 x 900 too (far land 1-3% of a frame at 20-80 c/s, the SF13/SF14
family); at 5120 z5.2 80 c/s 1.9-5.9% geometric undrawn and 7-18% far land.

**The cause: two constants that don't see the hardware or the screen.**
- The atlas budget: the phone's 24 MB scaled by the screen's css area, *capped at 128 MB* — every screen past
  ~2000 x 1000 got the same 459 slots. The floor was then the atlas's: a wide screen's regions in 80% of a fixed
  atlas.
- The fill rate: `FILL_RATE` 2 tiles a frame off a phone, 0.3 on one (`FLOOR_FRAMES` 300). Measured here
  (scripts/fillprobe.mjs: the view turned a quarter at the floor, so no tile is drawn, then frames till the
  geometric check reads 0 for 10 frames): **~1.1-1.2 tiles a frame from nothing** — 100-112 tiles/s at the headless
  ~90 fps, 45-65/s under the gate's 60 Hz cap at ~50 fps. The constant was 1.7 times this iGPU's; the old count of
  the screen's regions (a square of its area, MARGIN² of it) over-counted by about as much, so it held by luck, and
  for a 3080 it's the same 2 tiles a frame whatever the card does.
- The screen's regions were counted as a square of its area: a 32:9 screen's ring of regions is ~1.2 times a
  square's.
So on this machine nothing failed to load inside the floor: the wide screen's limit was the floor, and the floor was
the constants'. A parked view that doesn't fill on the user's PC isn't reproduced here at any of the four sizes; a
device whose real rate is under 2 tiles a frame (a page under 60 fps — the 3080's headless runner ran 29 Hz with the
monitor off) gets a floor it can't fill in 5 s, which the calibration below now measures instead of assuming.

**What changed** (render/tilecalib.ts, `TileCache.cal`; ARCHITECTURE "The tiles' calibration"):
- **The rate measured.** TileLandGpu.step tells the calibration each frame's bakes and whether the land was the
  bottleneck (a region wanted with no scratch slot free, or the bakes at their cap; not the atlas full), with the
  camera at rest and the planner's holes on (the pacer's turns all the tiles' then — a screenful filling, the floor's
  own case; a frame whose turns the streamer's strips share isn't the fill's rate). A second of such frames is a
  block; each block moves the estimate 30% of the way, from the tier's prior (120/s, 18/s on a phone). Tiles a second,
  at whatever frame rate the device runs. `?tilerate=` (tiles a frame at 60 Hz) fixes it.
- **The floor**: the screen's own regions (area and perimeter, without the margin — the look-ahead asks for them
  first) no more than the rate makes in the fill budget (5 s, round 112's 300 frames: the gate's 3 s budget was tried
  and narrowed every device's floor, the phone's 2.78 to 3.8, so it isn't kept); the screen with the margin in 80% of
  the atlas. `stats.floorBound` says which held it (`rate` / `room`), `floorTiles` the screen's regions.
- **The atlas grows.** It's made as before (24 MB by the css area, 128 MB at most) but as wide as its budget allows,
  so a growth adds rows and every slot keeps its place: TileCache.grow copies the three planes and the slots' params
  into the taller ones, remakes the instances' buffer and the groups, and retires the old a frame on. It grows when
  the floor is the atlas's (`room`), the rate is measured, and the rate's own floor would take 10% more slots than it
  has — to those slots, within the budget: 512 MB off a phone, 128 MB on one (WebGPU says nothing of a device's
  memory, so it's a budget, not the adapter's; `?tilemb=` fixes the atlas, no growth). Grown once or twice per page.
- Reported: TileCache.stats (`zoomFloor`, `floorBound`, `floorTiles`, `slotsMost`, `grown`, `slots`, `mb`),
  `TileCache.cal.stats` (`rate`, `prior`, `measuredS`, `source`, `fillS`, `blocks`), the tile gate's rows (`tiles`,
  `cal`) and the pan bench's `tiles.slots`.

### Round 115 (`tilecal`, 2): no memory caps — the atlas bounded by the hardware; unit tests

The user on the budget (BACKLOG CAL3), verbatim: "Why limit to 512 and 128MB both should use as much as we need that
the hardware supports."
- No policy caps, the phone the same rule. The atlas starts where it did (24 MB by the css area, at most 128 — a
  start) and grows to the slots the measured rate's floor needs. Its bounds are the hardware's: it's as wide as the
  device's widest texture and grows to that texture's height (device.ts now asks for the adapter's
  maxTextureDimension2D, as it already did its buffer limits; the slots' params and instances are KB, far under
  maxBufferSize / maxStorageBufferBindingSize), and its allocations succeed: a growth's planes and buffers are made in
  an 'out-of-memory' error scope; out of memory, they're destroyed, the atlas stays, and the bytes are the ceiling
  (`cal.stats.ceilingBytes`) — no growth at or over it is asked for again. Validation errors stay outside the scope,
  fatal as ever. The copy into the new atlas runs the frame after the scope resolves (TileCache.finishGrow).
- The floor's search is a pure function (tilecalib.ts `floorSearch`), and the estimator takes its clock
  (`landFrame(baked, bottleneck, now)`): **unit tests without a browser** — vitest (added: `npm test`,
  vitest.config.ts, node only), src/render/tilecalib.test.ts, 11 tests: the prior, a block's 30% step, convergence,
  frames left out (not the bottleneck, stalls, no holes), the ceiling; the square's (side + 2)² count, the rate's test,
  the room's test and the slots the atlas grows to, a wide screen's closer floor, a faster device's wider floor. 0.4 s.
- One browser smoke (fillprobe, shared GPU — growth's correctness only, no timings): 1600 x 900 grew to 512 slots /
  192 MB (floor 1.32), 5120 x 1440 to 1024 / 384 MB, the phone proxy to 256 / 96 MB; no out-of-memory, no errors.
  The atlas now starts as whole rows of the widest texture (64 slots a row at 8192), so its first size rounds up a row.

## 2026-10-30 — round 117 (`testkit`) — the test pyramid: unit and GPU tests in Node, a smoke test

**Why.** The user (DECISIONS round 117): "TDD make some unit tests so you can stop hogging my browser so much. Do complete
integration tests after unit tests work and do quick smoke tests to find failures early." Until now every test needed the
shared browser and GPU: ~180 headless scripts and the 4-test contract tier (contract.html). docs/TESTING.md has the
pyramid, how to write a test at each tier, and when to use the browser.

**Tier 1, unit (vitest 4 in Node).** I picked vitest over node:test because it reads vite.config.ts. That gives the same
`?raw` WGSL imports and defines (`__GEN_HASH__`) as the build, TypeScript with no build step, and projects with an order.
tilecal's vitest@3 config on places (round 115, src/**/*.test.ts) folded into the unit project, and its 11 tests pass
under vitest 4. 79 tests in ~2 s wall. Tested so far: the tick clock (locked one tick a frame under ±2 ms timestamp
jitter; drift paid a tick at a time, never two fixes within 20 frames; a missed vsync, a cut tick and a paused frame
not owed; the accumulator at 120 Hz and speed 2), the world state (every event kind, clamps, listeners, history,
snapshot/restore), the region record (layout alignment, encode/decode round trip, mismatch reasons, columnsHash the
same at any window height, stepped equals whole), the generator hash (GEN_VERSION is this checkout's genHash; a fake
checkout shows boundary, type-only and CRLF edits don't count), the External registry, and buried things un-buried.

**Tier 2, gpu (real Dawn in Node).** The npm `webgpu` package (Dawn's node bindings, D3D12 here) gives navigator.gpu
and the WebGPU globals in Node. gpu/device.ts is split so tests ask for the device the game's way: `requestGpu(gpu)` is
the adapter, limits and features with no canvas, and `initGpu` adds the canvas and the fatal overlay's handlers.
test/gpu/world.ts `tinyWorld` makes the real WorldCore (its WorldGpu buffers, every kernel, the Simulation) from a map
and steps it the way the contract tier does. The modules WorldCore pulls in read `location` and the viewport at load,
so the setup defines a page with no query and the phone proxy's 412 x 915. Measured: the first tiny WorldCore takes
10.6 s (its ~100 async pipelines on DXC: the renderer's and the sims', particles/blended/rain/water-flat the slowest at
~9 s each, compiled in parallel), and 600 water ticks take 0.5 s. A second WorldCore on the same device takes 84 ms,
because Dawn keeps what it compiled. So the gpu files run in one worker, not isolated, on one device: 3 files and
5 tests in ~15 s. Backends: D3D11 (FXC) took over 4 minutes for the same pipelines, and Vulkan has no vulkan-1.dll
here, so D3D12 it is (`DAWN_FLAGS` passes Dawn options). Two full `npm test` runs at once both passed in 19 s wall, so
agents can run them in parallel.

**Tier 3, smoke.** scripts/smoke.mjs runs on the shared runner (lease, build server, kept Chrome). It boots the built
atlas from its warm snapshot (sim/snapshot.ts), checks there's no fatal and no console or page error, and that the sim
runs a second of ticks. 42 s wall uncontended (ready in 25.7 s: pipelines 12.6 s from Chrome's cache). `--levels` adds
more, at ~25-50 s each on a shared GPU: two levels didn't fit 60 s with three other checks on it (playground's
requestDevice took 29.8 s), so the default is the atlas alone. First found: the fourth level booted in one tab lost its
device (TK7), so it now opens a page per level.

**Findings.**
- Buried statues (the user: "Unburying something should not make it suddenly launch into the air. It should maybe
  topple or slide and tumble and maybe stay up depending on support"). The tests were written before they were run.
  test/support/rockworld.ts runs the production External registry, rock judge (analyseRock), WorldVox and
  RockBodies/columnsGround on packed CPU columns, and mirrors only Integrity's glue. No launch in any case: the
  centre's rise is 0 and the fastest upward speed is 0.23 cells/s (the drop's bounce).
  - Dug round to its foot: it stays (not woken).
  - Undercut past its centre of mass: it wakes, tilts 26°, moves 2.9 east and drops 1.4 into the hole.
  - Freed entirely: it drops 9 to 4.65 (onto the floor, its slop).
  - Leaning 35° on its foot: it topples to 82° and rests.
  - Lying under the ground with a cave dug beneath: held by the stone beside it, it stays.
  - In soil: it stays.
  - At 25° the tilted foot spans enough rows that the centre of mass sits 0.14 past it, inside the judge's 0.25 tip
    give, so it stands. With the NW/SW cells left, the hex cells' own width reaches the centre, so it stands too.
- TK4: a thing with air under it and only ground on top hangs from that ground. The judge reads the column's External
  cells and the stone on them as one run, keyed into the land through the roof (`test.fails` until fixed).
- TK9: MemoryWorldState.snapshot() shared the live factions and settlements, so a saved snapshot changed when a faction's
  attitude moved later. Now copies (structuredClone; a few factions, not hot).
- Conflations that widen the test surface: Integrity's glue inside its 2000-line GPU-owning class (TK5), and WorldCore
  always making a Renderer (TK6).

vite.config.ts: `__dirname` → `import.meta.dirname`, which vitest's config loader asks for. Same value.

planned fling, pull, force push, the storm). Left in GameplayGM for now: the knight, gorilla, tank and mech; the
lich's spellbook and its physics-body/rock throws (no world API for bodies yet); hero select and saving.

**The capability profile (why derived, not written).** The user: "parameterize it so we can reason about it during
generation and make not only obstacles but fun ones." Each controller is data (ParamSpec list + defaults,
controllers/*.ts) plus a small module (heroes/*.ts), and `profile(params)` derives what generators need — speed,
turn radius, climb, jump height/gap (and whether it needs a ramp), fly ceiling, water, vegetation, bridge,
destruction, encounter weights — from the same numbers the controller runs on. Tune the bike's launch cap and its
ramps' clearable gap grows; the generators can't drift from the controller. `crossCost(profile, crossing)` (1 open
ground, Infinity can't) and `fun(profile)` (ramps, straights, slaloms, packs, breakables, climbs, delves, with sizes)
are pure functions in the contract so terrain, flora and runplan agree on one answer.

**A new ability: the slam** (the lich's wrecking ball). A tap on the lich (or 💥): the world API's crater under it, a
ring that shoves and throws (Units.strike with lift and stun), the air slammed out. The GameplayGM lich broke nothing
of the ground itself; "a floating wrecking ball power fantasy" asked for it. Its health is 30 (12 for the slice's):
the raiders wore it down in seconds in the first browser run, not a power fantasy.

**A drive fix: `carry`.** Ported as-is, the bike rode a kicker with vz pinned at 0 (the ground clamp zeroed it every
step on a climb faster than the cushion lifts), so it went over a ramp's lip with no upward speed — "launching off
ramps" only happened where the ground fell away. Now, held down on a climb, it keeps `carry` of the ground's rise
speed (the slope over a cell either side, times its speed, at most launchMax): a 0.6 kicker throws it ~13 cells/s up
and it clears a 10-cell gap to a landing at the same height (heroes.test.ts). `carry: 0` is the slice's drive again —
a slider in the tune panel, so the user can compare.

**Why the controllers run on the CPU (the D-r101 ruling said the GPU).** One hero, a few hundred flops a frame, and it
must answer the thumb in the same frame; a GPU kernel adds a readback (1-2 frames) for no throughput win. Measured:
the whole play layer (input, hero, its voxels written) costs 0.12 ms of main thread a frame on the phone proxy
(scripts/perf/play.mjs). Kept GPU-ready: Params are flat number records and the drives are pure functions of (state,
stick, dt, height), so many riders (race rivals, AI bikes) can move to a kernel when there are many (PL9).

**Units contract tweak (for main to consolidate).** Optional `strike(AreaHit, by)`, `hold(id, at)`, `release(id, vel)`,
`maxHeld` on Units — a hero's blows shove and throw, telekinesis holds — implemented in AgentUnits by forwarding to
Agents.hit/hold/launch (its private goal `release` renamed `releaseGoal`). The play world requires them (a clear error
otherwise, no silent fallback).

**The sandbox** (`?skipmenu=1&level=atlas&play=hoverbike|lich`, `&tune=1` opens the panel): the atlas level as
deployed, every system on. Hero chips top left (switch in place), ⚙ tune (a slider per parameter, grouped, live; the
profile it gives shown above; reset; copy as JSON; kept per hero in localStorage), 👹 raiders spawned ahead, ⟲ back up.
Controls phone first: a floating stick where the left thumb lands (the bottom-left zone), everything else the hero's
gestures, thumb-sized buttons bottom right with gauges (the boost tank, the slam's cooldown). The camera follows at a
fixed angle, leads along the way and pulls back with speed (D-r80). The level's own camera buttons, turn and score bar
are hidden while it runs (they sat under the thumbs: the first browser run's screenshot).

**Measured** (Intel Xe-LPG iGPU, phone proxy 412x915 dpr 2.6 q=low, data/perf/play-intel-xe-lpg.json): riding flat

## 2026-10-30 — round 117 (`terrain`): rivers off the texel grid with banks; the region graph; the basin flood; the terrain viewer

The user, verbatim (DECISIONS round 117): "Generally speaking we want our terrain to be striking to look at and
interesting to explore." "Rivers look bad right now. They have serious isotropy issues and they have no banks. Use SDF.
Have them carve into the ground. Make their banks look eroded. Add reeds. Have rocks and rapids. Have waterfalls. So many
waterfalls." "Waterfalls and flow are what look pretty good." "We want to partition our map … we should know by
character controller what they can and can't pass easily. I would make regions recursive with open fully connected
spaces 1-3 screens big and that are part of larger terrain features." "Terrain makes the barriers initially but the run
manager should be able to get. The graph and request obstacles or otherwise request a certain number of exits." "A GPU
algorithm we use for generative tools. I want to be able to flood a basin and bury things".

**Rivers (terrain/rivershape.ts on the CPU, terrain/river.wgsl on the GPU).** Why they looked bad: the river graph is a
drainage tree over the macro texels (8 cells, 8 neighbours), so every reach ran at 0, 45 or 90 degrees, and the water
stood at the filled ground's level, flush with the plain it crossed — no bank could show. The fixes, each for one of
those causes:
- The course: the nodes relaxed along their main stems (6 Laplacian passes, at most 7 cells each so a node stays near its
  texel — the GPU finds a river by the nodes nearest a point's texels), and the GPU's lookup warped by a slow noise (7
  world units, period 150: its gradient well under 1, so the line never folds) — bends at every angle. riverAt now tests
  the two segments from each nearby node, so the joints are continuous once nodes leave their texels.
- The level: incised under the filled ground by 0.8 + 0.35 × the half-width (1.2-4.5 cells), ramped in over 4 nodes from
  the river's end and never under the still water it runs into (a channel below the lake beside it would drain it
  backwards); steep reaches (0.6 cells a node or more) made a staircase of 3.5-cell steps — still pools and falls. The
  level still only falls downstream (unit-tested: every consumer, the held rivers and the pipes, relies on it). A step
  of 2.9-8.5 cells drops at its segment's middle within about a cell, so the bed steps and forms.wgsl pours a sheet over
  it (a step over RIVER_FALL): a waterfall, not a chute. The cliffs' big falls keep their interpolation (the ones that
  looked good).
- The cross-section (riverCut): the channel's parabola; a bank whose steepness varies along the river (cut banks steep,
  slumps gentle), broken into slumped blocks by Voronoi cells ~6 across — the cliffs' treatment the user praised
  ("voronoi plus noise plus sdf to make steps") — benches (a floodplain the river left, a little over the water) on some
  stretches; gravel bars just over the water on one side; boulders in rapids, round plunge pools and a few on every
  bank (bare rock: forms.wgsl now lets a cap stand in a channel where it is over the water); a deeper pool under each
  fall.
Pictures (the same spots before/after, the atlas level at 1x, q=high): C:/Projects/shots88/terrain/base-*.png and
r1-*.png. The fall spot (a plateau's river, 6108,14009): before a 45-degree zigzag flush with the sand; after a
winding channel between brown banks with bars and rocks. The wide lowland river (12916,4435): banks now line it; its
45-degree kinks are softer but still there (TR3).
Cost (scripts/perf/terrain.mjs, the desktop iGPU, the least of 3 for each of 24 64² regions on river nodes, wall
including the readback): Atlas.columns median 28.3 ms vs places 28.5 ms — a wash. The rivers' CPU pass 627 vs 599 ms
(+28 ms shaping), "ground with rivers" (the macro pass) 149 vs 64 ms, once per atlas. The phone's frame isn't touched
by this (the columns are made as land streams; their GPU passes on the phone are TR9's driveprofile).
Not done: reeds (flora's contract, TR6), rivers into holes and out of caves (TR4), the wide rivers' kinks (TR3). The
authored rivers' CPU mirror (world/rivertable.ts, the playground's) keeps the plain profile (B-TS13: the rule is
duplicated already; the new cross-section uses the atlas's noise).

**The region graph (api/contracts/terrain.ts; terrain/sample.ts → terrain/partition.ts).** Why this shape:
- Features are what the walker reaches without crossing anything it can't (union-find over passable sample edges), so by
  construction every barrier lies between features. Rooms split a feature: seeds deepest first a room apart, grown
  together by a weighted geodesic distance whose step costs more near the feature's edge (1 + 6 / (1 + distance)) — on
  open land a Voronoi of the seeds (bounded rooms), where it narrows the crossing is dear so two rooms meet in the
  narrows (the door). (A plain watershed on the distance gave one 16-screen room on a plain: it has one maximum.) Then
  rooms under a screen merge into their best neighbour, and neighbours across a long shared edge (no narrows) merge
  while they stay within 3 screens. A slot (no clear disc 2 samples across: a ravine's floor, a ledge) is no room.
- Borders keep measures, not verdicts: the least climb, drop, depth, vegetation, the narrowest water and gap, each by a
  bottleneck (or least-count) search across a band round the border. What a controller crosses is reckoned when asked:
  a Dijkstra over the two rooms' band by its PassCaps (step, slope, drop, deep, lava, veg, gap, fly), cached per caps.id
  — the user's "parameterize it so we can reason about it during generation". A body over water it can't touch bottom
  in rides the surface (a hovering bike). Soft barriers (hostiles, storms, distance) are laid on a border and add to its
  cost.
- Controllers: PassCaps is a stand-in until the `play` track's controller contract (herosandbox's Mobility is a subset);
  CAPS_PRESETS walker, bike, lich.
- The samples are taken on the GPU from the atlas's own ground() (the heights, rivers, lakes and coarse world the
  columns are made of: the graph and what's drawn agree), read back once; the graph's search work is on the CPU (graph
  search, a few hundred thousand samples, at planning time). 512² samples (2048 world units at 4): sample 32 ms,
  partition 374 ms in the page (Node: 350-500 ms; the borders' searches were 275 ms of it before they were banded, 21
  after).
- Vegetation density in the samples is forms.wgsl's woods formula, a stand-in until flora supplies the plants' density.
Tests: src/terrain/partition.test.ts (plain, dumbbell narrows, cliff, one-way drop, river, ford, vegetation, ravine and
the bike's jump, soft barriers, a 512² noisy valley), src/terrain/terrain.test.ts.

**Requests (terrain/terrain.ts).** `exits` opens the cheapest barriers out of a room for a controller — a ramp up a cliff
long enough for its slope (stamped: the column made exactly that high, solid 40 cells under it), a ford (the bed raised
to 0.4 under the water, rubble), a bridge, vegetation cleared (needs: structures, flora) — or closes the easiest doors
with a wall 9 high (the walker and bike stop, the lich floats over). `obstacle` and `open` act on one border. Edits are
stamp hooks (atlas stampHooks: the same operations the GPU and CPU paths make), so land made after a request has it;
land already in the window isn't remade (a run plans first; TR17).

**The flood (terrain/flood.wgsl, flood.ts).** The depression-filled surface by Planchon-Darboux passes on the GPU (W =
max(h, min(W, neighbours' W)); the window's edge and the standing sea are the outlets), the seed's W its basin's spill
height; then the basin marked by a dilation from the seed under that level (or a level given). The standing sea walls
the mark (a flood stops at its shore). Applied as a row of the lakes' table (Atlas.addBasin; FLOOD_SPARE 64 rows
reserved, the row's second word the fluid): the river graph's lakes are already basins filled with water at their spill
height, so a flood is the same thing with any level and fluid, and the land is made from it as from a lake
(compose.wgsl lakeAt) — no new binding in kernels at the 8-storage-buffer limit (formSeed uses all 8). Sand and ash
bury: loose ground to the level; magma: lava to it. The GPU result equals the CPU reference texel for texel
(test/gpu/terrain-flood.test.ts on Dawn, and in the page). Not yet: the global sea replaced everywhere it's read (forms'
sea water, the renderer's sea plane, the shore, the tiles: DZ1's design, TR7); a sand flood buries the ground, not what
settlements stamp on it later (TR8).

**The viewer: `?terrain=view`.** The atlas viewer (seed and sliders, layers 1-9, pan and zoom, double-click walks in)
with the region graph over it (rooms, borders by kind, doors and passes, edits, masks), a controller picker, a room's
exits and reach, the exit requests, and the flood (water, sand, magma; a depth over the tap, 0 the spill height).
Smoke: scripts/terrain/viewer.mjs (graph, a ford made, GPU flood = CPU). Pictures: C:/Projects/shots88/terrain/viewer-*.png.

Shared-system tweaks for consolidation: atlas.ts (river.wgsl in parts(); FLOOD_SPARE rows and addBasin;
riverStats.shaped), compose.wgsl (River/riverAt moved to terrain/river.wgsl; the carve calls riverCut; LakeHere.fluid and
the buried/molten basins), forms.wgsl (a cap may stand in a channel over the water), rivers.ts (the course and levels
shaped before the table), atlas-view.ts (viewport(), worldAt public, onPick), main.ts (?terrain=view), level.ts
(reclaimed.terrain).

**Follow-up (main's review of the first pictures).** (1) The road at the fall spot wasn't carved away: the sites and roads
are planned on the macro ground with the rivers in it, so the channels moved them (TR18). (2) The "trench along the cliff

## 2026-10-30 — round 117 (`terrain`): caves at cliffs' feet (the user's recipe), gorges in the plateaus, buried props placed

**Caves at the foot of cliffs (terrain/cave.wgsl).** The user: "Cliffs would be even better with rocks around the base
and caves that open (often at their base)" / "Caves should have ground level openings and be wide enough to traverse".
The method is the user's own recipe, verbatim in the file's head ("Take a simplex fractal noise in 2d and set a
threshold so that they are windy … make noise lower on the floor so it is walkable"), with TG3's numbers from
noiselab2-r (revive made it work at a visible scale: passages ~12 wide, roof = base + min(0.35 d², 12) + noise, floor =
base − 0.5 + a quarter of the noise, the base a cell over the sea at a sea cliff). noiselab2-r isn't merged: the lab is
its own scene; the recipe is folded into the atlas's cliffs. Per cell, no JFA: the passages are a band of a 2D fbm, the
distance in from a passage's edge its margin × CAVE_MID (the fbm's gradient made d from the margin over the period give
4-cell vaults, measured on Dawn: test/gpu/terrain-diag.test.ts prints the open runs and the made columns round a point).
The base runs from the foot (over the talus heaped against a mesa's wall: a mouth behind the heap was buried; a cell
over the sea where the foot is under it — the sea doesn't enter a gap yet, TG16) up to a share of the cliff's height
inside it, over 70 cells: a passage climbs through the cliff, a way up an impassable wall ("An impassible mountain can
have a cave through it"). Grottos (round chambers ~45 cells apart, 6-10 across) near the foot are cut by the face, so the
base has mouths often, not only where a passage happens to reach it. Where a roof comes within 2 cells of the ground
the ground opens to the floor (a collapse letting light down). Applied in ground(): plateau edges (EDGE_MESA, beside the
lips and undercuts) and EDGE_CLIFF/EDGE_SEACLIFF, as the overhang's open run (columns.wgsl takes it as a cavern).
Pictures: C:/Projects/shots88/terrain/cave*-cliff1.png (a mouth at a plateau's foot), cave*-sea0.png. Honest state:
the open runs are in the made columns (the Dawn probe: 92-99 under a 145 top, round 16234,4213), but the mouths seen in the
fixed view are few; whether the sea-cliff mouths face away from the camera or the draw hides thin gaps at a face is
TR21.

**Gorges (terrain/gorge.wgsl).** The user: "Traversvlable gorges (both at the bottom and above)". The zero lines of a slow
noise wind across a plateau's top; across one, its distance (|n| / threshold) is an SDF: a flat floor over its middle
half (the corridor at the bottom), walls in three tiers whose edges each Voronoi cell moves (the cliffs' blocks), rims at
the plateau's height (walkable above); 14-44 deep, shallowing to nothing at its heads, never deeper than the low ground

**Follow-up: lakes kept, gorges readable, the sea only where it reaches, the gpu tier isolated.**
- TR22: the gorges drained two plateau lakes and moved rivers and roads, because the rivers and lakes are found on the

  lake touches a reservoir and still shift the rivers. The macro pass now has no gorges (AtlasP.macroPass, PARAM_BYTES
  144 → 160); per cell a gorge stops at a lake's rim (g.lk) and under rivers (g.rx).

## 2026-10-30 — round 117 (`structures`): buildings, districts and cities — tile systems, WFC façades, warped modules, a viewer

The user: "I want beautiful structures, sprawling fantastic cities"; megastructures as "various procedural building
assets for various tile systems plus some WFC and mega tile features (features multiple tiles big)"; "bake paths into
the tiles we generate so agents can interact with them". ARCHITECTURE "Structures" has the contract and the pipeline.

**Why meshes for the look and columns for the sims (both, by use).** The settlements' buildings were column intervals
(build/town.ts, settle/raster.ts): a 1 m column can't hold a window frame, an eave or a sharp corner, and the user found
bevelled structures ugly (round 39). Warped module instances give Townscaper's look on irregular tiles at 64 bytes a
piece, a module stored once. The sims never needed rooms, only "solid here": one External span a column (columns.ts),
converted at that boundary only. Agents need paths (round 104): the nav graph is baked from the plan, not from either.

**Why the roof is a height rule.** h = the least distance to the roof's free sides and free corners. Two tiles in a row
continue a ridge, an L gets a valley, a 2 × 2 block a pyramid — none of it tabled. Its creases fall on a 3 × 3 grid with
centre diagonals, so 8 triangles are exact (unit-tested: ridges and the inside of an L meet across tiles).

**Finding (fixed): walls through roofs.** White slivers on the slopes near the eaves. A numeric check (now a unit test)
found three causes, each fixed at its root: square wall ends stuck out past the next wall at obtuse corners (walls are
mitred now); eaves overhung into a neighbour's wall as tall (eaves only over what is lower, corners clipped where a tile
as tall touches diagonally); a warped tile's roof is flat between its warped corners, not the bilinear surface, up to
0.13 m off on skewed tiles (the roof lifted 0.14 m, hidden in the eave's thickness). Worst poke 3.08 m → 0.

## 2026-10-30 — round 117 (`structures`): the city on real terrain (STR9)

`?skipmenu=1&level=atlas&city=irregular` (or contour-voronoi, radial, orthogonal; `&cstyle=`, `&cseed=`, `&cr=`): the
town or city nearest the start is handed to the structures track — its own buildings aren't stamped
(`Settlements.handedOff`) — and src/structures/host.ts `CityHost` plans a city there on the window's ground (the
atlas's window ground and water as made: nothing built or paved under more than 0.3 m of water), draws its pieces with
the game's renderer and claims each building's columns as one External instance (`OWNER_STRUCT`).

**Why the game's renderer draws them (not an overlay).** The pieces must be lit, shadowed, hazed and cut away exactly as
the land round them, and picked like it: `Renderer.enableStructures` makes a pipeline from render.wgsl + structmesh.wgsl
+ structgame.wgsl (the trees' way, meshinst.wgsl), the pieces' buffer at the draw group's binding 3, drawn in the world
pass and the sun's shadow pass. One shared module file (structmesh.wgsl) for the viewer and the game: the look is the
same in both.

**Why External columns, and why they stop a metre under the roof.** The sims treat External as rock that never gives:
rain runs off, sand piles, fire and water go round, the terrain's draws leave room. The first run showed grass tufts
and moss poking through the roofs: what grows on an External top grew on the solid's top, which reached mid-roof. The
solid now stops a metre under the walls' tops, inside the top storey.

**What the sims do to it.** A building whose cells are cut (dug, smashed, melted) or found hanging free is let go to
rubble where it stood, its pieces taken away behind dust (round 106: hide every swap behind a burst of dust). Before a
slide, buildings whose columns would leave the window let go of them (to air); after it, the plan moves with the land
and they claim again once all back. Collapse into bodies is later (with the physics track).

**Shared tweaks (for main to consolidate):** renderer.ts `enableStructures` + two draws (world, shadow) and `drawPl`;
integrity.ts `ensureCopy()` (the CPU copy of the layers read once if none yet: claims at the level's start needed it —
"Invalid typed array length" before); external.ts `OWNER_STRUCT = 2`; settlements.ts `handedOff`; level.ts the
`?city=` site, the host, its slide hooks, `reclaimed.city()`.

**Measured** (scripts/perf/structcity.mjs, data/perf/structcity-intel-xe-lpg.json; phone proxy 412×915 dpr 2.6 q=low,
every system on, parked over a 281-building irregular city, 5191 pieces, ~500k triangles): the world pass ("draw")
2.66 → 3.53 ms at the start's zoom, 2.77 → 3.81 ms at ×3 zoom — about 1 ms of GPU. Back faces culled (the modules are
wound outward, every frame counter-clockwise; checked in the viewer with `?cull=0` to compare): before culling the ×3
zoom cost 2.3 ms. The frame's total GPU time moved ±1 ms between runs on the shared desktop (other agents), so the pass
times are the measure.

## 2026-10-30 — round 117 (`structures`): linear features — roads, viaducts, town walls (STR11)

The user: "linear tile features we can use for bridges, roads, railroads and extrude along splines". src/structures/linear.ts.

**Why the same warped modules.** A segment of a road between two spline samples is a frame like a tile's (its right and
left edges at either end, each end's across-direction its own tangent's normal, so consecutive segments share edges
with no gap), so roads, rails, walls and viaducts are more modules (road, rail, wallseg, wallwalk, deck, archspan) in
the same library, drawn by the same pieces path — no renderer of their own, the look shared with the buildings.

**Roads and bridges.** A road out of the town samples the ground every 2 m and makes its profile: forward and backward
passes that only raise, so it's never steeper than a 14% grade — valleys and water are filled by the deck. Where the
deck stands more than 2.6 m over the ground (or over water, 3 m up) it's a bridge: deck pieces (slab, paving, parapets;
their foot the deck's underside at each end, so the deck follows its grade) and arch pieces under them (their foot the
ground at each corner, their top the deck): spans about as long as the bridge is high (5-12 m), so a tall viaduct gets
Roman proportions and a shallow crossing a low segment — the module scales, the height decides. Roads inside the town
turn the tiles under them into street before the massing. `CitySpec.roads` (viewer slider; the game `&croads=`, 2).

**Town walls.** `CitySpec.walls` on a non-radial town: a loop at 1.06 R following the ground, the walk 8 m over it (the
body's top a height over its foot, so the walk follows the ground), crenellated parapets both sides, round towers with
spires every 28 m and at each run's open end — gaps where the roads go out (the gates' flanks), none over water.

**Nav and columns.** A node every 4 m along roads (street), bridges (bridge) and wall walks (rampart); a road's first
node joins the town's nearest open ground, runs join where they meet, a wall run's ends come down by stairs. Walls
(foot to walk) and bridge decks (their arches open underneath) are each their own External instance.

**Found in the game: the ground stretched up over the buildings.** The hybrid renderer draws most chunks as a lattice
through the columns' tops; a building's External top is a column top, so the lattice rose to it — dark mottled
pillars under the houses. The host now tells the hybrid each claim's box (`touched` → `HybridChunks.edit`, as the
resting rock's do): those chunks are the field mesh's, which leaves External out.

**Measured** (scripts/perf/structcity.mjs, phone proxy, q=low, every system on): the world pass 2.69 → 4.57 ms at the
start's zoom, 2.84 → 5.10 ms at ×3 with two roads and the voxel chunks (the frame's total moved by other agents' load).
About 2 ms on the desktop iGPU at the phone's resolution: STR10 (a LOD for distant pieces, fewer roof masks) before
bigger cities.

Unit tests (30): the profile never steeper than its grade, a bridge in a valley's middle; roads out of a town in a gorge
cross it on arched bridges and their far ends reach the plaza; a walled town has wall runs, parapets, and its rampart is

## 2026-10-30 — round 119 (`structures`): the settlements on the structures contract; density drives what's built (STR15)

The user (DECISIONS round 119): "Let's move the old settlement code over and have them actually use the new structures.
Can we get farms and smaller huts for lower population density? Is it density driven+grid based now?"

**The question, answered.**
- *Before*: grid based, barely density driven. A settlement's districts were overlay grids (settle/grids.ts: the four
  styles → lots → quads), a fields lattice round it. The growth field (field.ts) picked *which* lots got houses (built
  where its intensity passed `BUILT_V` 0.35) and nudged storeys up where it was strong; every building was the same kind
  of house in the civ's materials, stamped into the columns as voxels (build/town.ts), and the fields a ring of furrowed
  lots. The structures track's cities (round 117) were grid based with radial fall-offs, no density input at all.
- *Now*: grid based **and** density driven, as two separate concerns. The grid (the tile system: irregular,
  contour-voronoi, radial or orthogonal for the town; Voronoi plots for the farmland) says *where tiles are*. The density
  (`DensityFn`, a settlement's from its growth field) says *what's built on each*: built or a yard; a town house (dense:
  storeys rising with the density) or a thatched hut (thin); out in the farmland a farmstead (a farmhouse and a barn) or
  crop strips, an orchard or a pasture (thinnest). Size scales the density (a hamlet's middle reaches huts, a city's town
  houses), the field is smooth, so the kinds blend: houses and huts mix where they meet, farmsteads string along roads.

**Why one concern each.** settle/plan.ts plans (its town via `planCity` + the record's buildings, spots, jobs, sites);
settle/view.ts shows and claims (pieces drawn, External columns); life.ts lives (builders raise a site storey by storey:
`LifeIO.raise`, no voxels stamped). The buildings aren't stamped into the land any more (they were build/town.ts voxel
columns: the round-117 representation argument — pieces for the look, External spans for the sims). The far land's
raster is told where the roofs are (`rasterColumns`) since the columns no longer hold them.

**What changes for other systems (contracts unchanged, data changed):**
- `Settlement` records: the same fields; `buildings[].cells` are the plan's tile ids (were LotGrid cells); `grids` are two
  (the town's tile system, the farmland); a building's `use` now includes huts' and barns' (barn = granary: `store`).
- `SettlementPlan`: `city` (the structures plan) and `standing` replace `grids`; `SiteSpec` is a plan building
  (`building`, `storeys`, `door`) — no polygon, no materials; `free` lists buildings in build order.
- `LifeIO`: `raise(site, storeys)` replaces `townIO` (no stamping); `LiveSite` has no polygon.

## 2026-10-30 — round 117 (`flora`): plants from parameters — L-system trees, CA roots, species by fields, soft barriers

The user (DECISIONS round 117): "For plants, L systems are great for branches and then cellular autonoma for roots. I am
ok with stylized or low fidelity but I just want it to be readable and pretty and look integrated with the world. Plants
growing on fields and being instances that way into other geometry is key." And: "Waking through lead covered forest
floor with silver birches towering above and leaves falling and blowing in the wind would be breathtaking ... Make tall
grass that blows in the wind. Make leaves or dust." And (part 3): "plants making a barrier (even a soft barrier like
slowing you down or requiring you to cut through) is a good thing". ARCHITECTURE "Flora"; BACKLOG FL1-FL19.

**What was there.** vegplan.wgsl decides where trees stand (four species by a hash) and vegprep.wgsl draws them as
boxes, or with `?meshinst=1` as four hand-made low-poly meshes (MI3, "keep?" unanswered). Grass tufts and flowers were
quarter-cell boxes. Falling leaves were particles in the fall only. No L-systems, roots, tall grass, reeds or biome.

**Built.**
- src/flora, pure TS, unit-tested:
  - a stochastic L-system and a 3D turtle with tropism (rng, lsystem.ts);
  - a root cellular automaton (roots.ts: grow where exactly one neighbour is root, by soil, with a down-bias; the pipe
    model picks and thickens the visible surface roots);
  - a mesh builder (mesh.ts: faceted tubes, leaf clusters, birch's hanging leaf diamonds, conifer needle tufts,
    two-sided blades);
  - eleven species as parameters (species.ts);
  - generate(id, seed, {growth});
  - the game library (library.ts);
  - placement (fit by niche, the CPU ports of what the GPU stands);
  - passability (passability.ts);
  - viewer scenes (scene.ts).
- The game draws it, on by default on this branch (`?flora=0` for the old way):
  - vegprep writes every tree as one of its species' library variants;
  - meadows carry tall-grass clumps and wildflowers, the woodland floor ferns, shrubland its thickets;
  - florafield.wgsl (new) puts reeds on banks by water depth and moisture;
  - meshinst draws them all, through floralook.wgsl (sway and colour), which the viewer shares.
- Birch woods: vegplan.wgsl birchWood is world-scale value noise standing in for a biome field. Birches tower at 11-17
  cells and let a few leaves go all year (particles.wgsl).
- The woodland floor reads as leaf litter in drifts: meshdraw.wgsl, a look only, so the tiles inherit it.
- The contract src/api/contracts/flora.ts (FL1), on the world API. The viewer page flora.html (FL7). The perf test
  scripts/perf/flora.mjs (FL8).

**Why these choices.**
- *Parameters, not meshes.* One generator, many plants. Variants are seeds, and a species is one entry.
- *A fixed library of variants drawn by instancing,* not a mesh per plant. One indexed indirect draw a variant is what
  the phone affords for thousands of plants. The library takes ~70 ms to make at start.
- *Roots as cells.* That is what terrain, erosion and excavation speak (FL16 takes them into the world). Only the
  pipe-model main roots become wood; the first cut drew every root cell and roots were 60 % of a birch's triangles.
- *The packed vertex `w = part + sway`.* The instanced renderer's format and buffers stayed as they were.
- *No stored plants.* Where plants stand is still the succession field plus hashes. The CPU's ports are now pure
  functions tested against the GPU (test/gpu/flora-plan.test.ts runs vegPlan on Dawn against planTree for a 64² window
  with an origin).
- *A stand-in biome as noise.* No biome field exists yet (climate has temperature and moisture only). birchWood is the
  one place to swap one in.
- *Passability from the same plan.* What you can't walk through is what you see:
  - coverage = 1 − exp(−Σ fill·footprint·reach / area);
  - a tree blocks only its trunk (you walk under the canopy);
  - shrubland (succession 2.6-3.6) is the thicket. Under the woods only a fifth of its shrubs are drawn, so the forest
    floor is open: the first cut drew all of them and a wood was an impassable dark-green carpet.

**Found and fixed on the way.**
- api/plants.ts's CPU port of vegPlan hashed window columns without the window's origin, so in a streamed window its
  trees (treeAt, fell, logs) were another window's (FL9).
- In the atlas, the plants of a whole 1024² window were emitted every prep with no view cull: 33,780 flora instances and
  3.3 M triangles at zoom 14, the shadow pass drawing them all again. Now:
  - vegprep and florafield leave out plants whose box and shadow are off screen (floraput.wgsl floraSeen, the camera
    bound at 31 as renderprep's PrepCam);
  - grass, flowers and ferns thin out under 8 px a cell and are gone under 4.5 px (the ground's plant cover paints the
    meadow there);
  - only trees and thickets cast shadows.

**Measured** (scripts/perf/flora.mjs, Intel Xe-LPG iGPU, the phone tier q=low 412x915 dpr 2.6, the densest wood near
?at=13728,4768, every system in play; GPU ms a frame from the profiler; the GPU shared with other agents' checks, so
±1 ms):

| | zoom 14: flora instances / triangles | draw | shadow | GPU a frame | zoom 5: draw | GPU a frame |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| boxes (`?flora=0`) | — | 3.94 | 0.68 | 12.52 | 4.97 | 12.75 |
| flora, no cull (first cut) | 33,780 / 3.3 M | 4.95 | 2.65 | 12.03 | 4.77 | 10.57 |
| flora, culled + grass LOD + shadow kinds | 3,772 / 515 k | 5.58 | 0.61 | 13.34 | 5.26 | 12.21 |

So the flora costs ~+0.5-1.6 ms of draw at the close zoom over the boxes, and about even at zoom 5. The shadow pass is
back to the boxes' cost.

**Viewer** (flora.html): biome scenes, or one plant growing (the L-system re-made at fewer iterations as it grows). The
plants are generated in 7-100 ms a scene, 0.3-12 ms a plant. Triangles a plant:

| birch | conifer | broadleaf | giant | tall-grass clump | fern | ivy | reeds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ~1.9-2.5 k | ~1.6 k | ~0.6 k | ~1.4 k | 72 | 260 | ~390 | ~140 |

**Shared-system tweaks (for main to consolidate):**
- vegplan.wgsl: birch heights and birch woods.
- api/plants.ts: the origin, planTree, birchWood and vegCol.
- vegprep.wgsl: the flora instances, floraSmall, the view cull, binding 31.
- meshinst.wgsl: parts ≥ 3 go through floralook.
- render/meshinst.ts: draw(…, only) for the shadow kinds.
- renderer.ts:
  - the library;
  - the indirect buffer sized by kinds;
  - florafield;
  - the camera bound to vegprep.
- particles.wgsl: birch leaves all year.
- meshdraw.wgsl: the litter look.
- api/world.ts: `flora`.
- level.ts: `reclaimed.flora()`.
- vite.config.ts: flora.html.
- contracts/index.ts.

**Conflations flagged** (the user's principles):
- vegprep.wgsl both lays out box plants and writes flora instances, and is at the 8-storage-buffer limit. A flora kernel
  of its own for all the library's plants (florafield's shape) would free it (FL10).
- vegPlan's CPU port still exists twice (api/plants.ts planTree and flora/placement.ts standsAt for the small plants).
  They are tested against the GPU for trees only.
- MI3's question (meshes as the default for trees) is answered on this branch by doing it. Needs the user's yes.

### Round 117 (`flora`), follow-up: readable on the phone tier

Main, looking at the shots: the desktop birch wood (q=high) "is lovely". On the phone tier, though, the trunks and
branches "break into dotted white dashes and the canopy is speckle; it reads as noise, not a forest". The cause is that
the low tier renders at half scale (maxDpr 1 × renderScale 0.5): at zoom 14 a cell is 7 render pixels. A birch twig
0.05 cells across is then a third of a pixel, and a grass blade 1.4 px.

**Fixes.** The plants are now made for the pixels they'll get.
- The renderer passes render px a CSS px (the tier's dpr cap × render scale) to the library, which builds its plants for
  zoom 12 at that density (`generate(id, seed, {px})`):
  - wood is at least ~1.7 px wide, and twigs under half of that are left out;
  - leaf clusters are at least ~3 px and merged (fewer, bigger), so the crown's volume is about kept;
  - grass gets fewer, wider blades (≥ 1.7 px).
  - At desktop densities (px ≥ ~30) nothing changes (unit test).
- Grass, flowers and ferns thin by render px a cell, not CSS px: sparse under 11, gone under 5. At the phone's zoom 14 a
  full meadow of clumps read as static; the ground's plant cover paints it instead.
- The leaf litter is drawn in half-cell flakes, not per-pixel speckle.
- The thicket shrubs are lighter and 0.8 the size; the birch crowns are fuller (three leaf diamonds a site).
- Reeds stand only on a bank: open water and dry land both within two cells, in water at most 0.3 deep, never under
  the sea's level. The first cut stood them all over a shallow lake.

- desktop: m8d-flora1-z14.png.

The remaining speckle on the phone is the ground's own per-cell look at half scale, not the plants'.

## 2026-10-30 — round 119 (`flora`): the birches' cost on the phone

The user, verbatim (DECISIONS round 119): "I had some bad performance with the birches on mobile." Main: fix that
first; target the birch wood within ~1 ms of the old boxes on the phone proxy, measured with the GPU otherwise idle, and
a bench link the real phone can run.

**What cost.** These are counts at the showcase (?at=13728,4768), zoom 14, on the phone tier, after round 117's cull and
before this work:
- birches were their full ~1.6-2.5 k-triangle meshes at 90 render pixels tall;
- the thicket shrubs had no LOD: 600 of them were 128 k triangles at zoom 5;
- every vertex of every plant looped over all ~45 kinds to find its kind (meshinst.wgsl miKind), on the phone's
  vertex stage;
- the birches let leaves go all year at 0.12.

**Changed.**
- Levels of detail by height on screen in render pixels:
  - a tree is full from 150 px;
  - coarse from 55 px: made for 2.2 px a cell, so the trunk and main limbs stay (a birch's white trunk is what makes it
    read; the first coarse level, made for 1.5 px, lost it and the birches read as green blobs on the phone), twigs and
    roots gone, leaves merged, ~120-550 triangles;
  - far below that: ~20-30 triangles, a trunk and the crown's masses, from the same skeleton;
  - a thicket under 25 px is its far lump.
  - The library lays out the levels per variant (FL_<ID>_L1/L2), so a tree keeps its variant across levels.
- The kind rides in the vertex's w (+16 × kind, baked by render/meshinst.ts), so finding it is one step, not a search.
- Three variants a tree species (two for the giant): with three levels that is still ~40 kinds, a draw each. A flora
  kind holds at most 4096 instances, not 8192: 11 MB, not 23. The view cull keeps on-screen counts far under that.
- The birches' all-year leaf fall is halved (0.06).
- florafield skips off-screen columns before its 5 × 5 bank search. A bank also needs six dry columns of the 25: a lone
  dry line through held river water isn't one.

**Measured.** scripts/perf/flora.mjs, Intel Xe-LPG iGPU, phone tier, the GPU held alone by the runner's timing lease.
Flora and boxes were alternated twice (`--variants 1,0,1,0`), because single runs swung ±1-3 ms. GPU ms a frame:
